events.title: grm-0pen: cut a bounded jump table at the first target that does not decode as code
events.message:
grm-0pen: cut a bounded jump table at the first target that does not decode as code

deadly_towers' 30+ lone BRKs on zero filler in PRG_ALL_B2 were jump-table
targets. The bank-2 trampoline (fc2a: LDX/STX bank, ASL, TAX, LDA $8035,X
... JMP ($0000)) reads a word table that the lowest-target rule caps at 96
entries (in place, B2::fc3c), and that grm-pwuh's cross-bank refit kept
whole at 95 (B1/B3::fc3c). Only 6 are real: the ROM's 31 calls to fc2a
pass indices 0..5. From entry 6 on, the table points into 3-byte data
records (0c 00 03, 0a c0 00, 00 00 00), which decode as an undefined
opcode or a BRK within two steps.

New refinement JumpTableBound.codePrefix, applied in JumpTableBoundAnalyzer
after any rule bounds a table (or the cross-bank refit pins one): keep the
cases up to the first whose target bytes do not decode as code, but only
when the next 2 cases fail too. It only ever shortens a list a rule has
already capped, so it adds no phantom case (the grm-os9b line). The check
is InlineJumpTableDispatch.decodesAsCode: bytes only, so analysis order
cannot move it, and with stopAtCall it accepts at the first JSR. A first
version decoded past calls. It cut real tables on db3 (c2ac 31 -> 20,
ca2f 43 -> 4) and on cv3/megaman2, because NES helpers take INLINE argument
bytes after the JSR (db3 c7a0: LDA #0 / JSR $db47 / .byte $13). The
corrected rule leaves those rows byte-identical.

Rows that move, each checked against the ROM:
  deadly_towers: B2::fc3c and B1/B3::fc3c keep only the code prefix. 31 of
    the 33 grm-ktne BRK sites are no longer disassembled. 824f is the real
    JMP ($FFFC). 85a9 remains, from a bank-state bug after the far call
    (filed as grm-q4ga).
  dodge: W8000_M3_B1::80ed (AND #$7f / ASL / TAX / LDA $8161,X ...
    JMP ($0061)) 77 -> 27. Entries 0-26 are handlers (LDA $1e / BMI ...).
    Entry 27 on points into animation/frame data (33 34 33 34, 00 01 02 03,
    83 82 81 80). The dropped 82eb bank warning sat on that data.

SiteStateProbe now also prints incoming refs, the instruction falling into
a site, and the head of its fall-through run with that head's incoming
refs (what disassembled it). It skips an unresolvable site instead of
throwing.

Not addressed (filed as grm-jt7s): megaman PRG_LO_B5::99b5 (184 targets)
and megaman2 92e4, whose over-reads no rule bounds, so the refinement
never runs on them.

Gates: build-and-test check green. realrom check nes: 33 pass, plus
deadly_towers and dodge blessed below. Both are deterministic (0/3 solo
reruns match the old golden; all reruns agree).

  deadly_towers: refs.intoOverlay.intraOverlay 1915 -> 1578, instrs.inOverlay 4734 -> 4549, warnings 2 -> 1, symbols 350 -> 260
  dodge: refs.intoOverlay.intraOverlay 2532 -> 2497, instrs.inOverlay 11447 -> 11366, warnings 21 -> 20, symbols 239 -> 189

Realrom-Bless: deadly_towers
Realrom-Bless: dodge

events.title: debug: resolve a label through the live bases, for sym() and the stop's cause
events.message:
debug: resolve a label through the live bases, for sym() and the stop's cause

L2 of the stop hook (docs/stop-hooks-plan.md). A script can now name a label
instead of hard-coding an address that GEMDOS will move, and can ask why the
machine stopped.

`sym(name)` resolves through the symbol table and the program map's live bases.
Its rule is `labelAddress()` — the definition's own line when it shares one with
its data (`msg: dc.b "HI"`), otherwise the first line at or after it that emits
anything in *any* section, because `buffer:` above `ds.b 256` is bss. That is
deliberately not `labelSite()`, the break-here rule the remote `breakpoint
<label>` verb uses (the first code line, since a label alone on its line has no
code of its own): a label is not an address the way a watchpoint is not a PC, and
one lookup answering both questions would be wrong for one of them. Both refuse
an equate — `count equ 5` emits no bytes, so its line has no address and the line
after it belongs to somebody else — and `LineMap::nextAddressLine()` exists
because `nextCodeLine()`, the break-here rule, skips exactly the entries the
address rule needs.

`reason` / `at` describe the stop as far as the IDE can honestly tell: the
transport reports a prompt, not a cause, so `"breakpoint"` is the armed
breakpoint whose resolved address is this PC, `"step"` is the controller's step
flag, and a pause, an exception and a watchpoint all stay `"unknown"` rather than
being guessed at. `at` is nil, not an empty string, when there is no breakpoint
to name, so a script tests it once.

A breakpoint can run a script of its own instead of the project's hook, set from
its gutter menu. The path is absolute or relative to the source's directory
(`resolveScriptPath()`, the rule the project's own `hooks.scriptPath` follows and
where *New script…* writes one) — never relative to whatever working directory
PiST happened to be launched from, which the person typing it cannot see.

Tests: tst_debug pins both resolution rules, the stop's cause (including that an
unarmed address matches nothing) and the script-path rule; tst_stophooks covers
the engine's `sym()` binding and the runner's stop values, including `at` as nil
after a step; tst_emulatorhost proves `sym()` against a real machine — `start`
equals the PC, `msg` reads the program's own "HI"; tst_hrdb runs the same script
over the fork, which is what R8's typed intents are for. Full suite green.

events.title: docs: record stop hook L2 — the two label rules, and the proof on both transports

docs: record stop hook L2 — the two label rules, and the proof on both transports

The plan said `sym()` was L2 and that the runner exposed no reason, so both had
to be rewritten rather than appended to: §6's identity paragraph now describes
the three values a script gets, §7 lists `sym()` and the two stop globals, and
D8 records the decision that the break-here rule and the address rule are two
rules — with the equate refusal that follows from both, and why
`LineMap::nextAddressLine()` was needed. §9 gains the gutter's per-breakpoint
script and the path rule; §12 counts the suite (19 stop-hook cases) and names
what each new case pins; §13 marks L2 implemented; §17 says what is still
unverified, which is now only the archives and the dialog's own validation.

PLAN.md §9 gains the session-level evidence: `sym()` was checked against a real
machine's PC and its own data, and the same script ran over the hrdb-main fork,
so a *name* surviving GEMDOS relocation is verified rather than argued.

will look for them, glm-features §1's status is no longer "not started", and the
README documents `sym()`, `reason` and `at`. The starter script and the dialog

events.title: IWM: write drive registers on the rising edge of LSTRB only
events.message:
IWM: write drive registers on the rising edge of LSTRB only

A Sony drive latches its control register when LSTRB (PH3) goes high. Accessing
the LSTRBH address while LSTRB is already high makes no new edge, so the drive
does nothing. Snow wrote the register on every access, so touching LSTRBH five
times during one STEP stepped the head five tracks.

Only write the register when LSTRB was low, the same check the ISM path already
does in ism_write_phases().

Fixes #384

debug: author the stop-hook script in PiST, and paint Lua in the editor

Run ▸ Stop hooks… asked you to invent a file elsewhere and then find it again,
which is the friction the feature exists to remove. The dialog now offers
*New script…*: MainWindow::createStopHookScript() writes hello.s →
hello.hooks.lua beside the source through files::write(), from a starter whose
comments are the API reference, opens it in an editor tab and switches the hook
on. An existing script is adopted, never overwritten; an empty setting offers
the conventional path when one already sits beside the source; and the rule
recognises its own output — with the script focused it *is* "the source" by
buildSourcePath()'s rule, and naming a script after a script produced
hello.hooks.hooks.lua, which tst_gui caught.

A .lua tab is now painted by LuaHighlighter — keywords, -- and --[[ ]] comments,
short and long strings, numbers, and the hook API names — chosen by path and
re-chosen on setFilePath(), because a rename can change the extension. Exactly
one of the two highlighters is live and both are document-owned, as the assembly
one always was.

Tests: tst_gui gains the dialog's create gesture (no handler, no button), the
window operation end to end (file beside the source, starter content, tab
opened, adopted rather than overwritten), and three highlighter cases including
the path swap. Full suite green; the CI flag path was verified by configuring
with -DPIST_LUA_TARBALL and confirming no fetch happened.

events.title: ci: pre-seed the pinned Lua tarball instead of fetching it in configure
events.message:
ci: pre-seed the pinned Lua tarball instead of fetching it in configure

CMakeLists.txt pins Lua 5.4.8 by sha256 and downloads it from lua.org when
configure runs. Every other external dependency this project has — vasm, vlink,
Hatari, EmuTOS — is instead fetched by the workflow with the same kind of pin,
so this one made every CI run reach lua.org from inside CMake: an unverified
input to the build. Both workflows now fetch the tarball themselves, verify the
checksum, and hand it to configure with -DPIST_LUA_TARBALL, which CMake
re-verifies. The CMake download stays for a developer's first build.

tests/tst_toolfetch's pin cross-check is deliberately untouched: it exists
because the *application* fetches vasm and EmuTOS and therefore holds a second
copy of those pins. Lua's consumer is CMake, so extending that check would mean
bolting on a CMakeLists reader rather than extending the comparison.

events.title: fix(ipc): pause and wait pc's timeout answer once the machine has stopped (beads-veb0) (#120)
events.message:
fix(ipc): pause and wait pc's timeout answer once the machine has stopped (beads-veb0) (#120)

* fix(ipc): pause and wait pc's timeout answer once the machine has sto…

…pped (beads-veb0)

A pause only stops the machine between frames. In the threaded GUI loop
the frame in flight runs to its end, and the stop is announced when the
frame runner parks. Two replies went out before that: the text IPC
`pause` answered OK right after cpc_pause(), and the deadline of
z80_run_until_ephemeral() (wait pc, step to, step over) returned Timeout
right after cpc_pause_if_epoch(). A read that followed either reply saw
the firmware clock still moving.

The bounded wait #118 added for wait vbl moves into the core as
cpc_wait_announced_stopped(), next to cpc_wait_until_idle(), so the walk
in z80_view.cpp can use it too. It stops waiting as soon as the caller's
abort predicate fires (the server shutting down), so exit is not held up.
`pause` and the walk's Timeout now return once the stop is announced.

test_pause_replies_once_stopped and test_wait_pc_timeout_ends_stopped run
Faithful unpaced (~14 ms per frame), as #118's test does. Before the fix
both failed 3 runs in 3 (5 TIME ticks after the reply). After it, 5 in 5
passed in GUI mode and they also pass headless.

events.title: 事前登録追補: l4-t4 追補1 — CALL の変数番地・USR の識別値・BSAVE の媒体構成
events.message:
事前登録追補: l4-t4 追補1 — CALL の変数番地・USR の識別値・BSAVE の媒体構成

第1回の公式結果（全132走が関門通過）で次が分かったための追補。
- CALL は定数番地がすべて ERR 2 で、変数で渡したときだけ実行された → 破壊・引数・境界の腕を変数で書き直す。
- USR の引数 1 の符号化 01 00 が全型で HL+6 に一致し偶然一致の疑い → 引数を 12345 系にし、HL・DE・BC の ±32 を照合、23456 とのクロス対照を置く。書換腕は位置確定後の追補2へ。
- BSAVE/BLOAD は全腕 ERR 33。両ドライブに空データディスクを入れ、公式がディスク BASIC にならなかったのが原因で、関門が見逃した
  → ドライブ1 に参照用システムディスクの複製（読まない）・ドライブ2 に空データディスク、ファイルは "2:"。
  ディスク BASIC 有効の陽性対照と「最初の誤り番号が一様なら失敗」の関門を追加（公式では必須、自作は未実装として既知）。
第1回の事前登録・腕定義・署名は書き換えない。

events.title: fix(core): a pauser is no longer starved of the pause mutex (beads-m1lz) (#119)
events.message:
fix(core): a pauser is no longer starved of the pause mutex (beads-m1lz) (#119)

* fix(core): a pauser is no longer starved of the pause mutex (beads-m1lz)

The frame runner holds g_pause_mutex for every machine frame and lets go
of it for a few microseconds before the next. std::mutex promises no
order, and the thread that just unlocked usually takes it straight back,
so a pause lease (or cpc_pause) asked for on another thread waited behind
frame after frame of an unpaced -H machine. On a 2-core MSVC runner
EmuFramePacingTest.HeadlessTurnHoldsOffAPauseLease never got its lease
and CI cancelled it after 4.5 minutes; on an M-series Mac one acquire
took up to 0.9 s.

g_pause_mutex is now a FifoMutex (a ticket lock): whoever asked first
goes first, so a waiter is in at most one holder late.

Tests: ALeaseBesideBackToBackFramesIsGrantedPromptly times 50 lease
acquires beside back-to-back frames (worst 534-864 ms before, under
250 ms after). Both lease tests now run beside a runner with a watchdog
that stops it at a deadline, so a starved wait fails instead of hanging.

events.title: SCSI: only tick the targets that use ticks
events.message:
SCSI: only tick the targets that use ticks

The SCSI controller is ticked on every bus tick and calls tick() on each
attached target through its trait object, but only the CD-ROM does
anything there (audio playback). Disks, the Ethernet adapter and the
printer use the default, which does nothing.

Add ScsiTarget::ticks(), false by default and true for the CD-ROM, and
have the controller skip the loop when no target needs ticks. Whether
one does is cached and found out again when a target is attached or
detached, and after a save state is loaded.

No functional change. Saves about 1% of the host time on a Mac II with
a hard disk.

events.title: fix(ipc): wait vbl's ERR 408 answers once the machine has stopped (beads-wrkg) (#118)
events.message:
fix(ipc): wait vbl's ERR 408 answers once the machine has stopped (beads-wrkg) (#118)

* fix(ipc): wait vbl's ERR 408 answers once the machine has stopped (be…

…ads-wrkg)

The timeout path of `wait vbl` paused the machine and answered ERR 408 at
once. A pause only stops the machine between frames: in the threaded GUI
loop the frame in flight ran on after the reply, so the firmware clock
moved on a machine the reply (and its context) called paused. A slow CI
Mac saw it as "machine left running after ERR 408".

The timeout now waits, bounded, for cpc_announced_stopped(): the core
announces the stop when the frame runner parks. The frame step is already
disarmed by wait_frame_step_until() before the pause.

test_wait_vbl_timeout_ends_stopped runs the Faithful tier unpaced (~14 ms
of host time per frame), so the pause nearly always lands mid-frame: it
failed 3 runs in 3 before the fix (5 TIME ticks after the reply) and
passes 5 in 5 after.

events.title: MDC 1.2: take the VBL interrupt disable bit from the low byte
events.message:
MDC 1.2: take the VBL interrupt disable bit from the low byte

The VBL interrupt disable is bit 1 of the 32-bit CRTC register at
$20013C, which is in its bottom byte at $20013F. The emulated card took
it from the top byte at $20013C, so the long write of $00000002 that
disables the interrupt enabled it instead.

With the original Mac II ROM (v1), System 7 finds the card when it rescans
the slots and runs its primary init, which disables the VBL interrupt.
The interrupt then fired before any driver had installed a slot
interrupt handler, and the system error ("unserviceable slot interrupt")
left the machine on a grey screen with no video device.

events.title: ASC: interrupt when a FIFO drains to exactly half full
events.message:
ASC: interrupt when a FIFO drains to exactly half full

ASCTester on a real IIci and LC 475 shows that the half empty flag sets
on the sample that takes a FIFO from 513 to 512, not from 512 to 511:
256 sample periods after writing 768 samples into an empty FIFO, where
Snow took 257. Go back to that threshold.

We changed it in an attempt to fix a hang observed on the Portable, but
at the time only observed once, and thus we ran out of a "theory" that
this was the cause of the problem (not a bad theory per-se but it ended
up not being correct :-)

We now have identified the real cause of the Portable hang (and have a
repro case), so let's remove this. Fix for the hang in the next commit.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: ASC: don't set the full flags on a FIFO clear
events.message:
ASC: don't set the full flags on a FIFO clear

Clearing the FIFOs with bit 7 of $803 also set the full flags of both
FIFOs in $804, with the FIFOs empty. The original ASC doesn't do that:
on a real IIci, $804 reads $00 right after a FIFO clear (ASCTest).

In fact these flags trigger an obscure bug/hang on the Mac Portable:

The stale flags stay until $804 is read. The Portable ROM's start-up
test of the sound chip ends with a FIFO clear in mode 0, and nothing
reads $804 afterwards, so the flags are still there for the first sound
after boot. Under System 7.5.5, the sound output driver checks $804 for
"FIFO B full" before writing the first samples of a sound: it sees the
stale flags, writes nothing, and with the FIFOs left empty, no interrupt
ever comes

What happens next depends on the sound. A synthesized sound such as
Simple Beep is paced by wait commands on the Time Manager, so it
completes anyway, just silently. A sampled sound only completes when the
FIFO interrupts have played its buffer, so it never does, and the next
alert sound waits for it forever. The first beep at boot plays the
selected alert sound, or Simple Beep when it can't load it in time,
which made the hang look random.

To reproduce on a Portable with System 7.5.5 and no sound at start-up
(for example without QuickTime, whose start-up alert beeps): boot, open
the Sound control panel, click a sampled sound such as Quack (it stays
silent), then click any other sound: the Mac hangs. The Mac II family
doesn't run into it, as its start-up code doesn't clear the FIFOs in
mode 0.

events.title: Portable: run the power manager handshake as the firmware does
events.message:
Portable: run the power manager handshake as the firmware does

The power manager model sent each byte of a reply a fixed number of CPU
cycles after the host had taken the previous one (100), without
checking that the host had released /PMREQ in the meantime.

A host that took longer, e.g. when running from slower ROM, still had
/PMREQ low from the previous byte, which the model took as the host
taking the next one: the byte was skipped, and the host read the rest
of the reply one byte off.

The command bytes had similar fixed delays.

Instead, run the handshake on the levels of /PMREQ and /PMACK, a byte at
a time, as the firmware does it:
- receiving: wait for /PMREQ low, take the byte and pull /PMACK low,
  wait for /PMREQ high and release /PMACK;
- sending: check /PMREQ is high, present the byte and pull /PMACK low,
  wait for /PMREQ low and release /PMACK. The byte stays on the bus
  until the next one, as the host reads it before it sees /PMACK high.

The firmware gives up on a command when the host doesn't keep up, and
so does the model, with timeouts from the firmware's polling loops
(9 polls of /PMREQ when receiving, 256 rounds when sending) and the time
from one byte of a reply to the next at which it checks /PMREQ. The
data bus is released while receiving and after a reply.

The timings assume the M50753 runs at half its 3.93216 MHz crystal, 8
CPU cycles per cycle, as other MELPS 740 parts do; at the full crystal
rate the host as Snow runs it would not keep up with the firmware's
receive loop. The time to run a command is not known and stays 10 CPU
cycles.

Functional change, to match the hardware more closely: the handshake
no longer depends on the host answering within fixed delays. The ROM
issues the same commands as before at boot.

This is needed to prevent failures when adding the ROM wait states.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: M68k: drop unused bounds from CpuSized
events.message:
M68k: drop unused bounds from CpuSized

Nothing uses CpuSized values through WrappingShl, WrappingShr,
WrappingAdd or FromBytes, or needs the AsMut bound on their bytes.

WrappingShl was only used by the byte at a time bus path, now gone.
WrappingShr came with ADDX/SUBX and was never used. WrappingAdd dates
from the CPU skeleton and FromBytes from the generic registers; the
FromBytes and AsMut bounds of the impl came with MOVEP, which states
its own FromBytes bound. The 68040 work in PR #355 needs none of them
on top of the sized bus.

No functional change.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Portable: put the VIA and SWIM on their byte lanes
events.message:
Portable: put the VIA and SWIM on their byte lanes

The VIA is on the upper half of the data bus (D8-D15), at even
addresses, and the SWIM on the lower half (D0-D7), at odd ones, both
with their register selected by A9-A12 (Macintosh Portable schematic,
050-0219, sheet 9). Run them as byte devices on their lane, so a word
access reaches them once.

An access that the bus can't complete still logs a warning and reads 0.

Functional change, to match the hardware more closely: they used to
answer with their register on any byte, odd or even. Reading the other
lane now gives all ones, as what a floating lane reads as isn't
documented. Software uses the documented addresses, which behave as
before.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Portable: put the CPU GLU registers on the lower byte lane
events.message:
Portable: put the CPU GLU registers on the lower byte lane

The CPU GLU (Normandy) only connects to D0-D3 (Macintosh Portable
schematic, 050-0219, sheet 5), so its registers at $F0xxxx, $FCxxxx
and $FExxxx are on the lower half of the data bus, at odd addresses.
That is where Snow already decodes them, and the ROM reaches them with
word accesses (e.g. AND.W $FC0200 to test the SLIM adapter bit, TST.W
$FE0000/$FE0002 to switch the idle speed). Run them as a byte device on
that lane, so a word access reaches them once.

The register values keep their upper four bits as modelled, as what
D4-D7 read as on these registers isn't documented.

Functional change, to match the hardware more closely: they used to be
accessed on any byte, a word access reaching them twice. Reading the
upper lane now gives all ones.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: MacII: use a NubusSlot trait
events.message:
MacII: use a NubusSlot trait

The MacII bus and nubus/mod.rs have a pile of match on every card type
for each card API function.

Instead create a NubusSlot trait that exposes the overall API, and call
that, thus simplifying the bus code. It will also make it easier to add
other Nubus capable models.

The functions run on every bus tick and card access (tick, get_irq,
read and write) keep a static dispatch through the with_card! macro,
as going through the vtable there costs several percent of emulation
speed.

No functional change.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: MacII: sync VIA accesses to the VIA clock
events.message:
MacII: sync VIA accesses to the VIA clock

The VIAs are 6800-style synchronous devices, clocked at 783.36 kHz on
the Mac II family (Guide to the Macintosh Family Hardware, 2nd
edition, chapter 3). An access now waits for the next edge of the VIA
clock and lasts half a VIA clock cycle, as MAME models it. The cycle
stalls up to that edge, the CPU ticking the bus through the stall, so
the VIA is read and written in its state at that time rather than as of
the last bus sync.

Functional change (timing), to match the hardware more closely: VIA
accesses took 3 clocks, they now take between about 10 and 30.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Portable: put the SCC on its byte lane
events.message:
Portable: put the SCC on its byte lane

The SCC is on the upper half of the data bus (D8-D15), with A/B on A1
and D/C on A2 (Macintosh Portable schematic, 050-0219, sheet 7), so its
registers are at even addresses, as the Developer Note lists them. Run
it as a byte device on its lane, so a word access reaches it once.

The Developer Note puts the read registers at $FD0000 and the write
registers at $FD8000, and the CPU GLU that makes the SCC strobes has
A15 as an input. What a read of the write half or a write to the read
half does isn't documented, so the SCC is still read on reads and
written on writes all over its range.

Functional change, to match the hardware more closely: it used to
answer with its register on any byte, odd or even. Reading the other
lane now gives all ones, as what a floating lane reads as isn't
documented.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Portable: add the idle speed wait states once per bus cycle
events.message:
Portable: add the idle speed wait states once per bus cycle

At idle speed the CPU GLU injects 64 wait states into every RAM and ROM
bus cycle (Macintosh Portable Developer Note, chapter 6, "Power
management hints"). Snow polled the GLU every 2 cycles for each byte,
as the byte interface did, so it charged 128 cycles per byte, 256 for
a word, and only for RAM below $900000. Charge 64 wait states per RAM
or ROM bus cycle instead.

The SLIM wait states at $50xxxx, which aren't documented, keep their
previous length: 32 cycles per byte.

As the wait states no longer depend on the state of anything, the
cycle no longer stalls for them: they are returned at once. The GLU's
DTACK counter goes away from the save state.

Functional change (timing), to match the hardware more closely: a bus
cycle at idle speed now takes 68 clocks instead of 132 for a byte or
260 for a word, and ROM accesses at idle speed are slowed down too.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Compact: sync the VIA port A lines on VIA writes only
events.message:
Compact: sync the VIA port A lines on VIA writes only

The overlay (Plus and earlier), the floppy SEL line and the alternate
screen buffer select are VIA port A outputs: on the real machines they
are wires from the VIA pins to the address decode, the IWM and the video
circuit. A pin only changes when the CPU writes the VIA's port A output
or data direction register, or when a reset turns the pins back into
inputs, which read as 1 with their pull-ups. Nothing else in the model
drives the port A inputs.

They were copied to the bus, the IWM and the video after every write
cycle, RAM writes included. Copy them after a VIA write and on reset
instead, the only times they can change. After a reset they now follow
the VIA at once rather than at the next write cycle.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: MacII: move the address decode into access()
events.message:
MacII: move the address decode into access()

Now we tackle the conversion of the MacII family.

Similar in spirit to Compact, though we go straight to the table
based decode this time around.

RAM, ROM, the extension ROM and the NuBus slots run as 32-bit ports
(though the cards are still reached a byte at a time by the underlying
NuBus code) as before.

The VIAs, SCC, SCSI controller, ASC and SWIM are byte-wide chips and
run as 8-bit ports.

The only functional change here is timing, to match the hardware more
closely and avoid more churn (as our MacII timing was quite off already):

- a word or long access to an I/O chip now takes one bus cycle per
  byte, as dynamic bus sizing does on the real thing, where it was
  charged as a single cycle; this slows down SCSI pseudo-DMA, which
  moves data with long accesses;
- a word at offset 1 of a long word takes a single bus cycle, where any
  misaligned word was charged two;
- otherwise a bus cycle still takes 4 CPU cycles, with no wait states.
  (this will be brought down later).

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: MacII: approximate NuBus wait states
events.message:
MacII: approximate NuBus wait states

NuBus runs on its own 10 MHz clock: a transaction takes at least a
start and an acknowledge cycle, plus the time to cross between the
NuBus and CPU clocks. With a card that adds no wait states of its own,
an access from the 68020 takes around 6 to 8 CPU clocks.

Charge NUBUS_WAITS (4) on top of the 3 clocks of the bus cycle for the
standard and super slot spaces, to be refined per card later (e.g. slow
video RAM).

Functional change (timing), to match the hardware more closely, as an
approximation.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Portable: read and write RAM and ROM a word at a time
events.message:
Portable: read and write RAM and ROM a word at a time

RAM and ROM went through the generic path, which matches on the region
for each byte of the transfer. Give them their own handlers that move a
whole word at once.

The 68000 transfers a byte or an even-addressed word, so both bytes of a
word are in the RAM or both are past its end, and they are in the same
dirty page. Past the end of the RAM, reads return 0 and writes are
ignored, as before. The ROM keeps the byte path for the part of its
window past the end of the image. The boot overlay (ROM over RAM) stays
on the generic path.

No functional change.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: MacII: sync the VIA1 port A lines on VIA1 writes only
events.message:
MacII: sync the VIA1 port A lines on VIA1 writes only

The overlay, the floppy SEL line and the internal drive select are VIA1
port A outputs (PA4 and PA5): on the real machine they are wires from
the VIA pins to the GLUE and the SWIM. A pin only changes when the CPU
writes the VIA's port A output or data direction register, or when a
reset turns the pins back into inputs, which read as 1 with their
pull-ups. Nothing else in the model drives PA4 or PA5: the only port A
input it changes is the SCC wait/request on PA7.

They were copied to the bus and the SWIM after every write cycle, RAM
writes included, and the drive select also on every bus tick. Copy them
after a VIA1 write and on reset instead, the only times they can change.
After a reset they now follow the VIA at once rather than at the next
write cycle.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Compact: keep the open bus value without a loop
events.message:
Compact: keep the open bus value without a loop

The 68000 transfers a byte or an even-addressed word, so the value left
on the data bus is either both lanes from a word or one lane from a byte.
Set them directly instead of looping over the bytes of the transfer,
which runs on every bus cycle.

No functional change.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Compact: decode addresses with a table
events.message:
Compact: decode addresses with a table

This changes the decode logic to be table based. This appears to be
more efficient at runtime, and will allow us to more easily have
different tables with and without overlay and for different Compact
models to better reflect the subtle decode differences between the
various Compact machine generations.

A Region enum lists the possible regions. A region() function maps
address ranges to regions and is used to build the map, indexed by
boot overlay and A23..A17.

access() then looks up the region for the address with a simple index,
rather than going through a chain of range compares for every bus cycle.

It then matches on the region enum which should be faster and runs the
cycle on its device directly.

In the map the SCC, IWM and VIA only answer at the top of their range,
which doesn't fill their 128KB block, so their arms still check the
address. That is only to match the current Snow behavior, we will
change that to match the hardware which doesn't decode those bits in the
following commits.

No functional change.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Compact: fixup the address map for the SE and Classic
events.message:
Compact: fixup the address map for the SE and Classic

The SE and Classic glue (BBU) decodes more address lines than the
earlier PALs and leaves the rest of the address space floating. Map
them as Apple documented (Tech Info Library 8295):

  $000000-$3FFFFF  RAM
  $400000-$43FFFF  ROM
  $580000-$5FFFFF  SCSI
  $900000-$9FFFFF  SCC read
  $AA0000-$AFFFFF  expansion slot (empty)
  $B00000-$BFFFFF  SCC write
  $D00000-$DFFFFF  IWM
  $E80000-$EFFFFF  VIA

with nothing anywhere else. The SCC, IWM and VIA now answer all over
their range rather than only at its top, and access() no longer checks
the address bits below the table blocks for them. The ROM image above
$440000, the RAM image at $600000 and the phase read are gone.

The Classic keeps its ROM up to $47FFFF, as its 512KB ROM holds a ROM
disk, and the extension ROM stays at $F80000.

Functional change, to match the hardware more closely.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: bus: let a bus opt into the new access types
events.message:
bus: let a bus opt into the new access types

This modifies the Bus trait so it gains SIZED, which tells the CPU to
run its bus cycles through the new access() rather than read() and
write(), one byte at a time.

This is temporary. Once all busses are converted, SIZED will go away
and the old read/write path will be removed.

SIZED defaults to false and access() to unimplemented, so existing
buses carry on unchanged. read() and write() get unimplemented defaults
too, so a bus that is converted can drop them.

A bus also names the data bus of its CPU, Bus68000 or Bus68020, as
its Cpu type, which access() takes its BusAccess for. Testbus, which
serves the tests of both CPUs, takes it as a parameter.

No functional change, nothing sets SIZED yet.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Compact: move the address decode into access()
events.message:
Compact: move the address decode into access()

This is the beginning of "porting" the Compact machines to the new
SIZED bus type.

We take bus cycles through access() as one 16-bit cycle each, instead of
the CPU handing over the bytes of a word one at a time through read()
and write(), which are gone.

decode() maps an address to the target device read() and write()
functions.

access() uses the resulting function tuple to pass to bus_access_word()
for now. This mimics the existing behavior.

The debugger's memory view uses the same decode.

The wait states are the same as before as well for now. The bus stalls
the cycle 2 CPU cycles at a time while it has to wait, the CPU ticking
the bus through each stall before presenting the cycle again, as the
byte interface polled:

- RAM: while the video has it.
- VPA: at least 2 cycles, up to the next low edge of the E clock, for
  each byte of a word as the byte interface did.

The open bus latch and the values derived from VIA port A are updated
once per cycle.

There is one functional change that I allowed in this one as it keeps
things simpler and matches the hardware more closely: a word access
to one of the byte-wide chips (SCSI, SCC, IWM, VIA) now accesses it
once where it used to be accessed once per byte in the old model.

Devices still answer on every byte address of their range as the old
model even when not a correct reflection of the hardware: a word read
gets their byte on both halves, a word write writes its low byte.

Word accesses to those devices are not expected in practice.

Everything else, the timing included, is unchanged.

Subsequent commits will change things to further mimic the actual
hardware behaviour.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: MacII: 3-clock bus cycles and RAM/ROM wait states
events.message:
MacII: 3-clock bus cycles and RAM/ROM wait states

The asynchronous bus cycle of the 68020 and 68030 takes 3 clocks, plus
the wait states the device asks for, where the sized bus path charged
a flat 4. The 68000 keeps its 4.

On the Mac II family, every RAM or ROM access involves one wait state
for the memory, plus one for the address translation by the AMU or the
68851 on the 68020 machines (Guide to the Macintosh Family Hardware,
2nd edition, chapter 3): a RAM or ROM access now takes 5 clocks on the
Mac II and 4 on the IIx, IIcx and SE/30. The extension ROM is treated
as ROM.

Functional change (timing), to match the hardware more closely. This
commit makes RAM and ROM accesses take 5 clocks instead of 4 on the Mac
II, and leaves them at 4 on the IIx, IIcx and SE/30. It also makes I/O
and NuBus accesses go from 4 to 3 clocks, until the following commits
add their wait states.

Also update the 68020 privilege violation test as it expects the
exception to take 34 clocks (the 68000 figure), but it now takes
27 clocks.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Portable: wire the ASC like the real hardware
events.message:
Portable: wire the ASC like the real hardware

The ASC's data bus is wired to D8-D15, the upper half of the data bus,
and its A0 to /UDS, with A1-A11 on A1-A11. A 74AC244 copies D8-D15 to
D0-D7 on reads that assert /LDS while the ASC is selected (Macintosh
Portable schematic, 050-0219, sheet 10). So:
- a byte access reaches the register at its address, odd or even, a
  read of an odd one coming back on the lower half through the buffer;
- a word access asserts /UDS and reaches the register at the even
  address only: a read gets its byte on both halves, a write writes the
  upper byte.

Functional change, to match the hardware more closely: a word access
used to reach both registers, one per byte. Byte accesses behave as
before.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Compact: read and write RAM a word at a time
events.message:
Compact: read and write RAM a word at a time

The 68000 transfers a byte or an even-addressed word. Both bytes of a
word are in the same RAM page, and in the same framebuffer when they are
in one, as the framebuffers start on an even address and have an even
length.

Read and write a word in one go: one framebuffer check, one dirty page
update and one copy per word instead of one per byte. RAM is accessed on
most bus cycles, so this is a measurable speedup.

No functional change.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Portable: sync VIA accesses to the VIA clock
events.message:
Portable: sync VIA accesses to the VIA clock

The VIA is clocked at C16M / 20 (783.36 kHz) by the CPU GLU, which also
makes its chip select and /DTACK; the 68HC000's E clock and /VMA only go
to the expansion connector (Macintosh Portable schematic, 050-0219,
sheets 3, 5 and 9). So VIA accesses are not VPA cycles: like on the Mac
II, an access waits for the next edge of the VIA clock and lasts half a
VIA clock cycle. The cycle stalls up to that edge, the CPU ticking the
bus and running the power manager through the stall, so the VIA is read
and written in its state at that time rather than as of the last bus
sync. The GLU's exact /DTACK timing isn't known; MAME charges a flat
50 clocks per VIA access instead.

This relies on the power manager handshake waiting on the host and on
the ASC interrupt fixes: with slower VIA accesses, the previous
handshake lost bytes, and the start-up code took a stale ASC interrupt.

Functional change (timing), to match the hardware more closely: VIA
accesses took 4 clocks, they now take between about 11 and 30.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: MacII: hold off back-to-back SCC accesses
events.message:
MacII: hold off back-to-back SCC accesses

The SCC needs 2.2us between accesses for its internal lines to settle,
and on back-to-back accesses the GLUE holds off the second one for
that time (Guide to the Macintosh Family Hardware, 2nd edition,
chapter 3). Keep track of when the SCC is ready again and add the
wait states to an access that comes earlier.

Functional change (timing), to match the hardware more closely.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Portable: sync the SWIM SEL line on VIA writes only
events.message:
Portable: sync the SWIM SEL line on VIA writes only

The SWIM SEL line is wired to the VIA's PB5 pin. The pin only changes
when the CPU writes the VIA's port B output or data direction register,
or when a reset turns it back into an input, which reads as 1. Nothing
else in the model drives PB5: the power manager and the SCC write
request only drive PB1 and PB7.

SEL was copied to the SWIM after every write cycle, RAM writes included.
Copy it after a VIA write and on reset instead, the only times it can
change. After a reset it now follows the VIA at once rather than at the
next write cycle.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: bus: remove the byte at a time bus path
events.message:
bus: remove the byte at a time bus path

Every bus now runs sized bus cycles, so the CPU no longer needs the old
path that went through read() and write() one byte at a time.

The CPU's sized read and write become its only read and write. Bus
loses SIZED, read() and write(), and access() no longer has a default.
BusResult goes, and so do BusIterator, which nothing used, and the
unused bus_write() emulator call. Testbus keeps read() and write() as
its own methods for the tests.

No functional change.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Compact: improve device decode on 128K, 512K(e) and Plus
events.message:
Compact: improve device decode on 128K, 512K(e) and Plus

On those machines, BMU1 selects the SCC, the IWM and the VPA space from
A23-A21 only. Within the VPA space, the VIA selects itself on A20=0 (its
CS1, with /VMA on /CS2) and the TSG drives the phase read on D0 when
A19=0. So each of them answers all over its address range:

  $800000-$9FFFFF  SCC read
  $A00000-$BFFFFF  SCC write
  $C00000-$DFFFFF  IWM
  $E00000-$E7FFFF  VIA and phase read both (Apple: do not use)
  $E80000-$EFFFFF  VIA
  $F00000-$F7FFFF  phase read

Snow only decodes them at the top of their range, and the phase read
only during the boot overlay.

This gives these models their own address map and removes the checking
of the lower address bits. The range where the VIA and the phase read
are both selected is given to the phase read, as nothing uses it. The
SE and Classic keep the previous map, and the checks, for now.

Functional change, to match the hardware more closely.

Sources: Macintosh Hardware Memory Map (B. Smith, B. Howard, April
1983) and the BMU1 equations at
https://retro.co.za/ccc/mac/ReverseEngineering/PALs.html

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: CPU: run bus cycles on sized buses
events.message:
CPU: run bus cycles on sized buses

When the bus is SIZED, run operands as bus cycles through access()
instead of byte by byte through read() and write().

68000: one 16-bit cycle per word, the CPU ignores the port width. The
address error check still follows the first word, and long writes in
high to low order still do the high address word first.

68020/68030: dynamic bus sizing. Each cycle presents what is left of
the operand and continues after the bytes the port took, translating
the address once per cycle rather than once per byte.

For now, every cycle still takes at least 4 CPU cycles plus the however
many wait states the bus returns. This is going to change for
>= 68020 but for now we aim for parity with the old model first.

A bus that can't take a cycle yet answers with a stall: the CPU spends
those cycles, ticks the bus through them, and runs the cycle again.
That way only the CPU drives time.

Note: There's a subtle semantic quirk with stalls: The bus is expected
to include the stalled duration in its final response "waits" as a
stall is effectively wait time, just spent *before* the access. This
keeps some of the logic simpler down the line.

The total cycle is thus still 4 + waits (for now, the 4 will become
3 on 68030 in a subsequent commit).

The bus is built for the data bus of the CPU (its Cpu type), which is
checked at build time.

No bus is SIZED yet, so no functional change.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: bus: add the new bus access types and helpers
events.message:
bus: add the new bus access types and helpers

This is groundwork to model the bus the way a 68k sees it rather than
one byte at a time. The end result will enable us to much better model
the timing characteristics of various Mac models beyond the classic ones.

These are just type definitions and helpers, unused yet, no functional
changes.

A BusAccess is one bus cycle as the CPU presents it:

 - the address
 - the number of bytes left in the operand (SIZ0/SIZ1)
 - and the write data (if any, right-aligned)

The bus terminates it with a BusResponse:

 - the width of the port that answered (DSACK0/DSACK1), ignored
   on 68000
 - the read data
 - and the wait states.

The BusResponse can also alternatively return a BERR or a Stall for
holding the bus for a number of ticks, typically to sync with the VIA
clock or the E Clock or the video RAM contention.

The access machinery will make the 68020(030) split large accesses to
small ports like the real chip. This will allow us to model machines
like the LC or LC II with a 32-bit CPU bus but 16-bit RAM and 32-bit
ROM. The 68000 always issues one 16-bit cycle and won't break it up.

The busses will have an access() method replacing the old read()/write()
which allows to keep a bunch of the decoding logic common.

The bus-side implementation of access() will typically use helpers
provided here to actually perform the access. Those helpers take the
device read() and write() callbacks as arguments.

The "base" helper is:

bus_access::<BUS_W, DEV_W, OFFSET>(args...)

It runs a cycle against a device of DEV_W bytes at lane offset OFFSET
of a BUS_W port, handling the byte lanes so devices only see their own
bytes, right-aligned.

Then simplified "wrapper" helpers are provided for the common cases:

bus_access_long/_word/_byte() for devices as wide as their port, and
bus_access_word_lane/_byte_lane() for devices on part of a wider port,
like the byte-wide chips of the 68000 Macs.

There's a bunch of compile time checking to ensure invalid combinations
won't build such as long helpers on a 68000 CPU etc...

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Compact: put the VIA and IWM on their real byte lanes
events.message:
Compact: put the VIA and IWM on their real byte lanes

The VIA is on the upper half of the data bus (D8-D15), addressed at
even addresses, and the IWM on the lower half (D0-D7), at odd ones.

Run them as byte devices on their lane instead of word devices. Now,
a word access reaches them only once.

Functional change, to match the hardware more closely: they used to
answer with their register on any byte, odd or even. Reading the
other lane now gives all ones, as what a floating lane reads as isn't
documented. Software uses the documented addresses, which behave as
before.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Portable: put the SCSI controller on its byte lane
events.message:
Portable: put the SCSI controller on its byte lane

The 53C80 is on the upper half of the data bus (D8-D15), with its
register selected by A4-A6 (Macintosh Portable schematic, 050-0219,
sheet 9). Unlike on the SE, its /IOR and /IOW come from the CPU GLU
rather than from the data strobes, so it is read on reads and written
on writes. Run it as a byte device on its lane, so a word access
reaches it once.

Functional change, to match the hardware more closely: it used to
answer with its register on any byte, odd or even. Reading the other
lane now gives all ones, as what a floating lane reads as isn't
documented.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Portable: add the RAM wait state
events.message:
Portable: add the RAM wait state

There is one wait state when the CPU accesses the static RAM, permanent
or on the expansion card, for a nominal bus cycle of 320ns (Macintosh
Portable Developer Note, chapter 5, sections 5.6 and 5.8). Add it to
RAM accesses, including writes to the RAM under the boot overlay. The
GLU's idle speed and SLIM wait states still replace it.

The ROM has two wait states (section 5.7), but with them the power
manager model loses the reply to the extended PRAM read the start-up
code makes at $900E22: the handshake is timed in CPU cycles calibrated
on the current timing rather than the real power manager. The start-up
code then puts the stack at an odd address and the boot fails with an
address error. ROM accesses keep no wait states until the power
manager model is fixed.

Functional change (timing), to match the hardware more closely: a RAM
bus cycle now takes 5 clocks instead of 4.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Portable: move the address decode into access()
events.message:
Portable: move the address decode into access()

And now we tackle the Portable. As usual, we start with the basic
transformation to access() and the decode table with minimal behaviour
changes.

Everything still behaves as the byte interface did:
- every device is accessed one byte at a time, so a word access to a
  byte-wide chip still reaches it twice, with its register on any byte;
- an unimplemented address still reads 0 and never bus errors;
- Normandy's wait states are still polled every 2 cycles for each
  byte: the bus stalls the cycle 2 CPU cycles at a time, and the CPU
  runs the power manager and ticks the bus through each stall.

Functional change, as usual to avoid churn (and to match the hardware
more closely): in a long write in high to low order, it will now reach
the device in address order rather than odd byte first, as a
word is one bus cycle.

This only matters for a long write to a byte-wide chip.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: MacII: wait states for the IWM, SCSI and ASC
events.message:
MacII: wait states for the IWM, SCSI and ASC

The GLUE inserts one wait state for IWM accesses and SCSI accesses
without hardware handshake, two for ASC reads and one for ASC writes
(Guide to the Macintosh Family Hardware, 2nd edition, chapter 3).
SCSI accesses with handshake (pseudo-DMA) hold /DSACK0 until the
transfer is done, which is not modelled.

Functional change (timing), to match the hardware more closely.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: MacII: read and write RAM and ROM in one access
events.message:
MacII: read and write RAM and ROM in one access

RAM and ROM transfers were done a byte at a time, each byte masked and
bounds checked on its own.

A transfer the CPU makes on the 32-bit bus stays within an aligned long
word, so its bytes are in the same RAM page. When they are all within
the RAM or ROM array, read or write them as one slice, with one dirty
page update. The byte path stays for the transfers that run past the end
of the array, which read open bus.

No functional change.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Compact: wire the SCC strobes correctly
events.message:
Compact: wire the SCC strobes correctly

The SCC is on the upper half of the data bus. Its /RD comes from the
address decode of the read range (A21=0) whatever the direction of
the access, and its /WR is /LDS, asserted by any access to the odd
byte. So, as the 1983 hardware memory map describes:
- a byte read at an even address of the read range reads it;
- a byte write at an odd address of the write range writes it, with
  the byte the 68000 puts on both halves of the bus;
- a byte read at an odd address of the read range, or a word access
  to it, asserts both and resets the SCC (Z8530 hardware reset); the
  word access also adjusts the phase of the video timing, which is not
  emulated;
- an access to the write range that doesn't assert /LDS does nothing.

Functional change, to match the hardware more closely: the SCC used
to answer reads and writes on any byte of both ranges, and the odd
reads at $9FFFF7/$9FFFF9 used for the phase adjust read as 0 during
the boot overlay.

Its floating lane now reads as all ones, which is also what it latches
when a read strobes its /WR, as what a floating lane reads as isn't
documented.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Portable: add the ROM wait states
events.message:
Portable: add the ROM wait states

There are two wait states when the CPU accesses the ROM (Macintosh
Portable Developer Note, chapter 5, section 5.7; also on the PowerBook
100, for a 383ns bus cycle). Add them to ROM reads, including under the
boot overlay. The GLU's idle speed and SLIM wait states still replace
them.

With the power manager handshake now waiting on the host, the slower
ROM no longer upsets the extended PRAM read the start-up code makes,
and the machine boots as before.

Functional change (timing), to match the hardware more closely: a ROM
bus cycle now takes 6 clocks instead of 4.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Testbus: implement sized accesses
events.message:
Testbus: implement sized accesses

Make Testbus SIZED so the CPU tests run the new bus path, the 68000
single step tests included (cycle counts and bus transactions). Ports
answer with the CPU's data bus width, unless port_widths says
otherwise for the address.

Add tests for 68020 dynamic bus sizing: long reads and writes, aligned
or not, on 32, 16 and 8-bit ports.

No functional change to the emulation, Testbus only serves the tests.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Portable: hold off back-to-back SCC accesses
events.message:
Portable: hold off back-to-back SCC accesses

The SCC needs at least 1.8us from the end of an access to the start of
the next one, and the hardware holds off the next access until then
(Macintosh Portable Developer Note, chapter 5, section 5.14). Keep track
of when the SCC is ready again and add the wait states to an access
that comes earlier, as on the Mac II.

The CPU GLU also makes the SCC's /RD and /WR from A15 as well as the
direction of the access: the Developer Note puts the read registers at
$FD0000 and the write registers at $FD8000. What an access to the other
half does isn't documented, so say so where the SCC is accessed; the
SCC is still read on reads and written on writes anywhere.

Functional change (timing), to match the hardware more closely.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Portable: give the power manager time to dispatch a command
events.message:
Portable: give the power manager time to dispatch a command

The power manager model presented the first byte of a reply 10 CPU
cycles after taking the last byte of the command, a figure kept from
the previous model. The firmware takes much longer: it goes back to its
main loop, dispatches the command through its handler table,
runs it and starts the reply, at least about 110 cycles of its
internal clock without the command itself. A host that polls /PMACK
slowly, e.g. through VIA accesses synchronized with the VIA clock,
missed /PMACK going high between the two and gave up.

Take 110 cycles of the power manager clock (880 CPU cycles) from the
end of a command to the start of its reply.

Functional change (timing), to match the hardware more closely.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Compact: put the SCSI controller on its byte lane
events.message:
Compact: put the SCSI controller on its byte lane

The 5380's data bus is wired to D8-D15, the upper half of the data
bus, with its register selected by A4-A6. Its /IOR is /UDS and its
/IOW is /LDS, whatever the direction of the access.

So a byte access to the even address reads it and one to the odd
address writes it, with the byte the 68000 puts on both halves.

A byte write to the even address only makes it output its register,
a byte read from the odd address makes it latch its floating lane,
and a word access does both.

Functional change, to match the hardware more closely: it used to be
read on reads and written on writes, with its register on any byte.
Reading the lane it doesn't drive now gives all ones, as what a
floating lane reads as isn't documented.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: Compact: sync to the E clock once per VPA bus cycle
events.message:
Compact: sync to the E clock once per VPA bus cycle

The 68000 synchronizes a VPA bus cycle to the E clock once. The byte
interface did it for each byte, so a word access to VPA space waited
for two E clock edges. This matters for the phase read at boot on the
128K to Plus, which reads words.

Functional change (timing), to match the hardware more closely.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Herrenschmidt <benh@kernel.crashing.org>
events.author: ozbenh

events.title: MacII: decode the I/O space on $50xxxxxx only
events.message:
MacII: decode the I/O space on $50xxxxxx only

The GLUE decodes the I/O devices at $50000000-$50FFFFFF, repeating
every 128KB, and leaves $51000000-$5FFFFFFF undecoded (Guide to the
Macintosh Family Hardware, 2nd edition, figure 3-7). Snow also mapped
the I/O devices at $51xxxxxx; that now bus errors like the rest of the
undecoded range. The extension ROM stays at $58000000.

Functional change, to match the hardware more closely.

events.title: copperhf: NUL-terminate the mounter's BSTRs
events.message:
copperhf: NUL-terminate the mounter's BSTRs

The boot-ROM mounter built each partition's device-name BSTR
("copperhf.device", for fssm_Device) as the last field of its AllocMem
block, sized for the length byte and characters only. Filesystems use
BADDR(fssm_Device) + 1 as a C string: the ROM FastFileSystem and AROS's
AFFS pass it straight to OpenDevice. So the byte after the name decided
whether the partition mounted.

With a 4-character partition name and a 16-entry DosEnvec, which is
HDToolBox's default "CDH0"/"CDH1" layout, the block is exactly 152 bytes
and leaves no zeroed AllocMem slack. The byte after the name is then the
first byte of the next allocation, the BootNode AddBootNode makes, i.e.
the high byte of a pointer. In memory below 16 MB that byte is 0 and the
name happened to terminate. In an A3000's motherboard RAM at $07xxxxxx
it is not, so OpenDevice returned -1, FFS gave up, and the partition was
listed in the early boot menu but never mounted. The ROM scsi.device
terminates its strings, which is why the same image mounted when
attached there.

Both BSTRs the mounter builds, the partition name and the device name,
now end in a NUL, with the longword pad computed to leave room for it.
The ROM is rebuilt with the pinned gcc-v16.2 image.

tests/copperhf_mounter.rs gains an AROS autoboot of a 4-character
partition on the A3000 profile. It fails against the previous ROM (AROS
reports it cannot open "copperhf.device" followed by garbage) and passes
with this one. Document the terminated names in
docs/internals/copperhf.md.

events.title: fix(debug): a breakpoint a step walk steps onto is hit once (beads-w88g) (#117)
events.message:
fix(debug): a breakpoint a step walk steps onto is hit once (beads-w88g) (#117)

* fix(debug): a breakpoint a step walk steps onto is hit once (beads-w88g)

The step-out walk single-steps the frame it leaves and stopped at a user
breakpoint with the CPU at the boundary before that opcode's fetch. A probe
stop parks after the fetch, so the next run fetched the opcode, the probe
latched, and the machine stopped at the same breakpoint again (hit count 2).

The walk now runs the machine through that fetch (Machine::run_to_fetch,
subcycle_bridge_park_on_fetch) and judges the breakpoint there, as the probe
path does: the stop is published like a probe stop and the next run carries
on with the instruction. The probe, dropped from the tick list while nothing
was armed, is recomposed first so a breakpoint set while paused is seen. An
interrupt taken before the fetch is recorded as an entered frame instead.

Covers text IPC step out, DevTools Step Out, KCPC STEP out and step over of
an RST, which all share z80_step_out_until().

events.title: Fix CIA timer reload from a zero counter (reload0)
events.message:
Fix CIA timer reload from a zero counter (reload0)

A count arriving at a counter that is already zero is itself the
underflow and does not swallow the following count, and the early reload
of a zero counter does not swallow it either when the counter was loaded
with zero in the previous clock. A timer running with latch 0 therefore
counts a newly written latch from the cycle after its reload, which is
what the reload0 hardware references show, while the normal reload-and-
hold sequence (timerbasics `01 0c 0c 0b`) and the cascade/CNT tables are
unchanged.

reload0a and reload0b now pass; CIATimerPipelineTests covers the
reload0b rows for both timers.

events.title: Mark the operations the original ran at x87 single precision
events.message:
Mark the operations the original ran at x87 single precision

Direct3D 7 sets the x87 precision control to 24 bits when the device is
created unless the application passes DDSCL_FPUPRESERVE, which the game does
not. From then on every add, subtract, multiply, divide and square root
rounds to single precision, whatever the declared types; integer operands are
loaded exactly. X87Single.h marks these operations: X87S_ADD/SUB/MUL/DIV,
X87S_SQRT, and X87S_FILD/X87S_LOAD for integers converted to float as an
operand. Under MSVC6 they expand to the original tokens (an extra pair of
parentheses changes MSVC6's floating-point code); other compilers round the
exact result once to a 24-bit mantissa, with error-free transformations and
no fused multiply-add.

OpenCMR2's tools/x87s_rewrite.py marked 805 operations, 5 square roots and
231 integer loads with a Clang plugin over the sources parsed with MSVC6's
headers; a second run finds nothing. Four compound assignments were written
out by hand. Float operations need no mark: other compilers already round
them to single precision.

This matters for the fixed-point math tables, built right after the device:
at single precision 8 sqrt, 12 sin and 339 tan entries differ from double
precision, and the CPU runs of the super special stages, which replay their
controls open loop, were recorded with the single-precision tables. Captured
from the original under Wine with the control word forced to 0x007f, the
tables match these expressions bit for bit and the Greece super special
opponent finishes; at 0x027f it gets stuck in sector 36, as in the port. The
step scheduler also counts each step once at single precision: both of its
boundaries round alike, so the duplicated steps seen at double precision do
not occur.

Bytes: 2923 -> 2924 exact (OptionMenu_DrawResultsRallyInfo; no function
lost or worse), 0 data issues.

events.title: debug: run a Lua script at every debugger stop
events.message:
debug: run a Lua script at every debugger stop

A stop hook is a project setting — Run ▸ Stop hooks…, a `hooks` object in
`.pistproject` — naming a Lua script evaluated at every stop (breakpoint,
watchpoint, pause, step, and the entry stop) with the machine held stopped. It
may call readmem/writemem/readreg/writereg, log to the console, and continue().

The trigger is the *published* stop, not the raw stoppedChanged(true): at that
signal the register batch has not landed (MainWindow queues the attach from
there) and the entry dump may still be printing, so a script would read a stale
machine. The runner is entered one event-loop turn later, outside the
transport's single-entry drain, because a nested read-back loop spun inside it
could never see the answer it waits for. A scripted write is waited to
completion before the continue() it asked for — resume() prunes everything
without keepOnResume, so a write queued in the same frame would be dropped
silently. Steps carry their own flag in DebugSessionController: `s`/`n` are not
running→stopped transitions, so stoppedChanged never fires for them.

The engine is Lua 5.4.8, pinned by checksum and linked statically. Both
candidates were measured first (docs/stop-hooks-plan.md §5 D4): Lua adds
~345 KiB and stops a runaway script in-thread from its count hook, where Qt's
QJSEngine adds 8,770,048 B and can only be interrupted from a second thread.
Its MIT notice is hand-listed in collect-notices.py, because a statically linked
library is invisible to that script's artifact scan.

Tests: tst_stophooks (16 cases, no emulator — the engine against a fake HookApi,
the runner against a fake backend whose commands complete a turn later, which is
the only way the write-before-continue order and the stale-copy refresh are
visible), tst_settings (the project round-trip), tst_gui (the Run-menu doorway),
and tst_emulatorhost (a script's write, read back from a real emulator).

events.title: copperhf: mark queued requests NT_MESSAGE so WaitIO waits for them
events.message:
copperhf: mark queued requests NT_MESSAGE so WaitIO waits for them

BeginIO cleared IOF_QUICK and rang the doorbell but never touched the
request's ln_Type. Exec decides whether a request is still in flight
from ln_Type alone, and a request reaches BeginIO as NT_REPLYMSG:
OpenDevice leaves a fresh one that way, and a reused one keeps it from
its last reply. Kickstart's WaitIO stops waiting as soon as it reads
NT_REPLYMSG and unlinks the request from its reply port; AROS's
SendIO/DoIO clear the field and its WaitIO/CheckIO only wait while it
reads NT_MESSAGE. Either way WaitIO could return before the INT2
handler replied the request.

Whether it did depended only on how soon the CPU took the completion
interrupt after the doorbell. The precise core always took it first.
With [cpu] jit, which recognizes interrupts at batch boundaries,
HDToolBox 3.2 on a 68040 or 68060 reached WaitIO first on its very
first HD_SCSICMD. On a fresh request ln_Succ is NULL, so the unlink
wrote 0 to AbsExecBase at $4; the next level-2 interrupt then loaded
ExecBase as 0, dispatched through the CPU autovector table and RTE'd
into garbage, and the machine reset in a loop. A real fast CPU can
lose the same race.

BeginIO now sets ln_Type to NT_MESSAGE, the state PutMsg leaves a
queued message in, with a compiler barrier ahead of the doorbell write.
A held TD_ADDCHANGEINT is marked the same way, so CheckIO reports it
in flight until TD_REMCHANGEINT replies it. The ROM is rebuilt with the
pinned gcc-v16.2 image.

chftest_m4 gains a subtest that sends a CMD_READ under Disable(), so
INT2 cannot reply it, and requires CheckIO to report it in flight, and
the change-interrupt subtest now checks the held ADDCHANGEINT the same
way. Against the previous ROM both fail on AROS, and the new subtest
fails on Kickstart 3.2 with the precise core as well as under JIT.
Document the in-flight marking in docs/internals/copperhf.md.

the way disc_insert() does; every tape caller goes through it.

accepted by Google Play. A ReplaceSilkNativeLibraries target in the csproj
swaps them in after the AAR's native libraries are resolved; the 32-bit
armeabi-v7a libs are kept unchanged (16 KB pages only apply to 64-bit devices).

events.title: test(kcpc): chip polling test asserts its claims, not the host's speed (beads-pkv9) (#114)
events.message:
test(kcpc): chip polling test asserts its claims, not the host's speed (beads-pkv9) (#114)

* test(kcpc): chip polling asserts where reads were served, not how man…

…y (beads-pkv9)

test_polling_every_chip_changes_nothing required more than 50 reads
during a 100-frame step. A reader gets about one read per frame boundary
its round trip catches, so the count measures the host: on the efficiency
cores under full load it was 36-41 (CI macOS: 50), with registers, RAM
and the gate's counters all as they should be. The count also missed the
bug it stood for: a gate that took every read under a pause lease
(fallback_ms=0) still passed with 5533 reads.

Assert the claim instead: each step saw the running machine at least once
per reader, and the core's own count has no read under a lease (fallback
and busy 0) and at least as many boundary reads as the clients saw reads
of a running machine.

* test(kcpc): chip polling compares interleaved frame-rate windows (bea…

…ds-pkv9)

The frame-rate half of test_polling_every_chip_changes_nothing compared
one 2 s window alone with one beside the readers, within 3 frames a
second. A host hiccup lands on whichever window is open: PR #113's macOS
run read 49.7 and 46.5. On the efficiency cores of a loaded Mac the old
comparison failed 2 runs of 6 ((49.7, 39.3), (49.6, 45.7)), and its
alone window alone ranged 43 to 50.

Take four interleaved pairs of 1.5 s windows and compare the best of
each: a hiccup has to hit every watched window to fail it, a cost of
reading is paid in all of them. A gate that made each read cost the
runner 10 ms still fails it (0.6 frames a second).

The lease check allows the gate's safety net its odd read: a saturated
host stalled the runner past the quarter second twice in 378 reads.
At most one read in twenty may be taken that way; a gate that leases
every read (fallback_ms=0) took 39506 by lease and none at a boundary.

events.title: AGA 16+ colours: finer PNN histogram for the base palette
events.message:
AGA 16+ colours: finer PNN histogram for the base palette

PNN starts from a 24^3 OKLab histogram, which is coarse for large
palettes: the bin count moves S2 by about +-1 per image and more bins
win on the mean. quantize::plain_pnn_bins picks 48 bins for AGA
lores/hires (plain, --best candidates, DPF) with 16+ colours, and
copper::encode_copper uses the same for AGA --sliced. The AGA EHB
sliced seed palette uses 48 bins; plain AGA EHB uses 64 (32 and 48 swing
per image by up to -7 S2 there).
OCS, HAM, VGA, GBA and every other PNN user keep 24 bins. The --best
bins sweep skips plain's own bin count and also tries 24.

examples/*.jpg at 320 wide, mean S2 / time, 24 -> new bins (plain):
lores AGA d4 41.18 / 0.13 s -> 42.08 / 0.16 s
lores AGA d5 60.65 / 0.16 s -> 61.34 / 0.19 s
lores AGA d6 71.91 / 0.22 s -> 72.86 / 0.25 s
lores AGA d7 79.77 / 0.34 s -> 80.18 / 0.35 s
lores AGA d8 84.16 / 0.63 s -> 85.10 / 0.77 s
DPF AGA      41.18 / 0.14 s -> 42.08 / 0.17 s
EHB AGA      54.72 / 0.08 s -> 55.99 / 0.22 s
sliced AGA d5 67.87 -> 68.32, d8 83.62 -> 84.85, EHB sliced 72.96 -> 74.12
d2-d3 gain nothing and keep 24 bins. A faster PNN neighbour search was
not attempted: 96 bins costs about 1.4 s per plain d8 encode.

Score floors for lores d8 AGA plain and --best rise to 83.2.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Plain --best at 64+ colours: sweep PNN histogram bins
events.message:
Plain --best at 64+ colours: sweep PNN histogram bins

The plain lores/hires --best jitter sweep varies dither strength, palette
diversity {3, 4} and pre-image jitter. At 128+ colours
apply_palette_diversity is a no-op, so half of its 81 trials repeated the
other half, and none of them is pair-fitted. The PNN histogram
resolution moves S2 more (about +-1 per image). From 64 colours up, when
the quantizer is PNN, --best now encodes plain plus PNN at 48/64/80/96
bins per OKLab axis, each with pair fitting, and keeps the best S2
(plain wins ties). Below 64 colours the jitter sweep scored as well or
better and stays; other dither strengths added under 0.05 S2 for twice
the trials. With the Metal quantizer the jitter sweep also stays.

pnn_quantize and quantize take the histogram bin count (default 24).

examples/*.jpg at 320 wide, AGA lores --best, mean S2 / time vs the
previous commit:
d7 79.95 / 8.84 s -> 80.78 / 1.85 s
d8 84.31 / 3.97 s -> 85.72 / 2.32 s

events.title: fix(debug): wait bp reports an I/O breakpoint stop as one, with the real PC (beads-llnn) (#113)
events.message:
fix(debug): wait bp reports an I/O breakpoint stop as one, with the real PC (beads-llnn) (#113)

* fix(debug): wait bp reports an I/O breakpoint stop as one, with the r…

…eal PC (beads-llnn)

The probe's I/O hit was published through the watchpoint fields, so
`wait bp` answered `OK PC=7F89 WATCH=1 WP_ADDR=7F89 ...` for the
firmware's Gate Array write: a watchpoint nobody set, and a PC that was
the port. The hit hook was given hit.addr as the PC for every kind of
hit, which is the breakpoint's address for an exec stop but the watched
address or the port for the others.

The hook now gets the PC the registers show (the one KCPC's EVT_STOPPED
announces), and an I/O stop says what it is:
`WATCH=0 IO=1 PORT=XXXX DIR=IN|OUT [VAL=XX]`, in `wait bp` and in the
step/wait replies that report a stop elsewhere.

fix(gui): auto-pause only runs a machine it stopped itself (beads-z6yz) (#112)

* test(gui): auto-pause runs a machine somebody else stopped (beads-z6yz)

The focus and pointer handlers move into cpc_auto_pause(), unchanged, so
the decision can be tested without a window. Six of the new tests fail:
returning to the window runs a machine stopped by the user, a breakpoint
or a KCPC PAUSE.

* fix(gui): auto-pause only runs a machine it stopped itself (beads-z6yz)

Getting the main window's focus or pointer back called cpc_run()
unconditionally, so a machine stopped at a breakpoint, by the user's
Pause or by a text-IPC or KCPC PAUSE ran again as soon as the pointer
crossed back into the window.

Losing the window now pauses only a running machine and remembers the
pause as a claim: the stop and resume epochs it left. The core already
counted runs; it now counts the stops somebody asked for too. Getting the
window back runs the machine only while both epochs are unchanged, so any
stop or run in between drops the claim. Claim and run are checked under
the pause mutex, and under another actor's lease the chain's flag, not
CPC.paused, says whether the machine is stopped.

events.title: input: steer --mouse-to-after in screenshot pixels, a field at a time
events.message:
input: steer --mouse-to-after in screenshot pixels, a field at a time

The pointer servo gave up on targets it could reach. Guests sample the
mouse counters at vertical blank and rewrite the pointer sprite's
control words, so counts injected while field N is drawn reach the
display in field N+1, readable only once that field completes. The
servo assumed the answer was visible at its next poll, and the frame
loop polls once per step_frame quantum, an instruction budget rather
than a field. It saw no motion, and when one field was polled twice it
stacked two 64-count deltas that the guest's 8-bit counter difference
reads as -128. After three still polls (about two fields) it reported
the pointer stuck where it started. KS 3.1 on an A500 fails the same
way as KS 3.2 on an A1200; nothing about it is AGA.

The servo now counts completed fields: a poll that finds no new field,
or no answer yet to the delta in flight (up to five fields), returns
ServoStep::Wait, and the frame budget and stall detector count fields
and answered moves. The CCP loop steps on Wait and refuses to spin on a
machine that completes no field.

Its coordinates did not match the screenshot either. --mouse-to-after
was documented as taking --screenshot-after pixels, but the servo
worked in rendered-field coordinates, while a scheduled capture frames
the field through the TV aperture: rows doubled and cropped, columns
resampled onto the glass. present_common::CaptureFieldMap maps between
the two per axis, built from the capture's own sampling and the field
placement (now a pure FieldPlacement::for_field shared with
post_process_rendered_field). The window steers --mouse-to-after
targets and places --pen-after positions in capture pixels, and both
input recorders write pen-after lines in them (the headless control
server from the configured overscan and TV centre). The control
protocol's input.mouse_to and input.pen keep capture.screenshot
coordinates.

Tests: servo unit tests against a guest that samples once per vertical
blank under irregular polling; window and CCP convergence at the real
frame-loop cadence (both failed before); the map against the pixels a
capture actually shows under full, TV and centred framings; pen
scheduling and recording. The pointer fixture gains a blank playfield,
since Denise only shows sprites on lines bitplane DMA has opened. Docs:
headless guide, AGENTS.md, configuration, control protocol, peripherals.

feat(config): discover the Amiberry binary beyond PATH on Windows

The Windows installer never adds itself to PATH, so the server failed to
find Amiberry.exe unless the user had put it there by hand. Resolve the
executable as AMIBERRY_BINARY, then PATH, then the Inno Setup uninstall
key's InstallLocation (HKCU before HKLM), then the default install
directories under %LOCALAPPDATA% and %ProgramFiles%. AMIBERRY_BINARY
works on every platform, and macOS and Linux/FreeBSD keep their existing
behavior apart from honoring it. When nothing is found the bare name is
kept, so exec-time PATH lookup and the existing error messages still
work.
