events.title: Fix: BaseDocument FileSystemWatcher duplicate Changed subscription and disposed watcher reuse
events.message:
Fix: BaseDocument FileSystemWatcher duplicate Changed subscription and disposed watcher reuse

- SubscribeDocumentFileWatcher added a new Changed handler on every SetFilter call, so filter changes stacked handlers and file changes fired multiple times.
- DisposeWatcher() disposed the watcher but left the field assigned; it is called from both OnFormClosing and OnFormClosed, so the second call re-used a disposed watcher.
- Remove the previous Changed handler before re-subscribing and recreate the FileSystemWatcher after dispose, since the document owns the watcher and a disposed one cannot be reused.

events.title: Space audit: ~2.7K free in the image without changing the game
events.message:
Space audit: ~2.7K free in the image without changing the game

The image goes from ~240 B free to ~2,700 (2,565 B of level arena in one run).

- compact.mjs step 0 promotes the most-referenced RAM variables into the 88 free
  zero-page bytes (~775 B of code, and a cycle per access). A buffer in the
  unbroken run after an undeclared indexed buffer stays put (omEn's masked loop
  clears four bytes named nowhere else). One loop at power-on (@ZPCLEAR, in
  klPark's once-only path) zeroes zero page, as the image's scratch loaded as zeros.
- sharedPair: moveYT/moveXT, absSinT/absCosT, posYT/posXT (a quarter turn apart)
  and rsT/rbT (7 apart) each share bytes, asserted entry by entry.
- embedIn: rowLo/HiT, sndV1H/sndV2H and qIdxAT/qIdxBT are aliases into tables
  that already hold them.
- compact.mjs gives no RAM to equates nothing names.
- Removed: the 1/2/3 and Q/W palette keys, SNDTEST, oSWall, amDX/amDY, hlvOf;
  lvlLo is emitted only where it is called; four tail calls.

Bugs fixed on the way: rfCz cleared the render cache with X running to 255 over
160 bytes, stamping $ff on the next 96 at every boot and death restart -- now
bounded, and ccf (which inherited X = 0 from it) sets X itself. FALLNOW's first
forced fall no longer lands on frame 0, before anything is rendered.

Checked with tools/regress.sh against 8a9f6dc (draws the same) and
fpsr.mjs suite (docs/TESTING.md has the numbers; level 5's walk trips the
rig's open low-fps margin issue).

project.status: DOS reconstruction playable; native x64 port unfinished and development active
project.notes: Reconstructs the original Japanese PC-98 Touhou 4 executables MAIN.EXE, OP.EXE, MAINE.EXE and ZUN.COM from maintained source. The primary handoff reports accepted authored-function counts of OP 93/93, MAIN 493/495, MAINE 72/72 and ZUN 3/3, while explicitly separating function acceptance from whole-file exactness. The repository builds a standalone DOS game and maintains a separate unfinished Linux/Windows x64 port. ReC98 is a pinned source-routing and migration input, but product source no longer includes masters.lib or ReC98 product includes. Current upstream evidence reports original/reconstructed DOS agreement across four bundled demos for consumed input, score, RNG, nine complete actor/effect pools and 22 state blocks. Native x64 now uses a 17.723227 ms cadence derived from 15,984 original records; a fresh GNU build reports 69 CTests and scoped Linux/Xvfb routes. Boss combat/death, full raw RGB, physical scanout, broader paired routes and Windows input/audio remain open. Evidence: https://github.com/N0zoM1z0/th04/commit/e6589fe6b74e9583a5634e6759395dc1a80eb543 https://github.com/N0zoM1z0/th04/blob/e6589fe6b74e9583a5634e6759395dc1a80eb543/README.md

project.status: Source-reviewed; no independent build or runtime verification
project.notes: C64 Studio/RetroDevStudio is a Windows Forms retro-development IDE with implemented ASM/BASIC parsers, media/graphics editors, build configurations and external-emulator debugging. Linux support is through Wine/PlayOnLinux, not a native Linux GUI build. Lowercase readme.md describes integrated assembler, BASIC dialects, tape/disk/cartridge output and graphics/media editors. Compiling.cs instantiates actual ASM and BASIC parsers and manages build configurations; the WinForms csproj targets .NET 10 Windows, 3.5 and 4.8. Limitations: MIT license for C64 Studio plus separately listed LGPL-3.0 and other dependency terms; GitHub's NOASSERTION summary should not replace this inspected license text. README binary framework list lags the current csproj; avoid asserting one version from README alone. Linux is an upstream-described Wine/PlayOnLinux workflow, not a native Linux GUI build. README reports success under PlayOnLinux/Ubuntu and testing under Linux Mint 21.3 with Wine, so runnable=true is an upstream-only compatibility-layer claim. Current csproj frameworks are net10.0-windows, net3.5 and net4.8; the README’s older .NET 6 binary list is not substituted for current project configuration. No compilation was performed. Linux profile requires Wine/PlayOnLinux plus the appropriate .NET Framework installation; README’s concrete Wine example launches net4.8. Windows Forms is the native UI. No minimum hardware CPU/RAM is established by the ARM64 configuration or framework lists. README enumerates C64/C128/VIC-20/MEGA65 source/media support and assembly/BASIC dialects, while Compiling.cs instantiates real parsers. The sampled material does not explicitly establish the complete accepted source-CPU set; no 6502/4510/45GS02 inference is made from those machine names. C64Studio.csproj explicitly lists Platforms=AnyCPU;ARM64. target_cpu=ARM64 records an explicitly configured IDE build target only; AnyCPU is not a physical CPU and the retro output machines do not become host CPU claims. No ARM64 build was reproduced. C64Studio repository and RetroDevStudio source namespace identify one continuing IDE project, not separate roots. Inspected license.md grants MIT for C64 Studio and lists separately licensed dependencies including LGPL-3.0; GitHub NOASSERTION does not replace the actual notices. Canonical repository root was compared against the 1,444-project authored baseline and research indexes corresponding to main b23885e5dfb2c38cffab58e650ae700ec65da958; no project-root collision was found. GitHub fork=false alone is not proof of independent authorship. AI evidence: No explicit AI-assisted development evidence found in inspected README/source excerpts or relevant tree filenames. This is not evidence of no AI use. Development usage remains null; no model or tool is invented. Repository pushed_at was observed as 2026-10-05T16:58:16Z; last_activity remains null pending a commit-level check. No independent compilation, program execution, gameplay, physical-drive operation or original-binary comparison was performed. A 2026-10-11 upstream fix now applies StartIndex consistently when serializing swizzled and interleaved palette ranges; this is a bounded asset-export correctness fix, not build or runtime verification. project.status: active; v3.0.376 bounded original-media startup and FM Towns HUD work
project.notes: Clean-room Dungeon Master-family engine using authenticated original media. Current primary documentation records bounded startup/runtime coverage for DM1 on DOS, Atari ST, Amiga and FM Towns; CSB on Amiga, Atari ST and FM Towns; and DM2 on DOS, Amiga, FM Towns and Macintosh. The latest receipts correct DM1 Amiga HD and DM2 FM Towns boot assertions and expand the cross-game startup matrix and diagnostics. These source-owned handoffs do not establish full campaign, save, display or audio parity; Nexus and Theron's Quest remain explicitly bounded, with authentic level/campaign consumers still incomplete. Evidence: https://github.com/yeager/firestaff/blob/main/README.md https://github.com/yeager/firestaff/blob/main/docs/PROJECT_STATUS.md https://github.com/yeager/firestaff/commit/7791b08de76e https://github.com/yeager/firestaff/commit/17a20bdb465e The newest authenticated-media pass discovers the DM1 Amiga 3.6 archive from configured data roots, covers its root-menu scan, records an Amiga startup-media matrix and wires DM1 PC34 soundtrack selection to WAV playback. These remain bounded startup/audio receipts rather than full-game parity. Evidence: https://github.com/yeager/firestaff/commit/d3b50c77c364455674d783c6bf4d4755777dbc44 https://github.com/yeager/firestaff/commit/ec51d5c1b2f58b51b235fc2145abb384d55b597c https://github.com/yeager/firestaff/commit/da1e85756e618dd321ec42257cb31afbb2b341d1 v3.0.376 receipts now cover DM1 Amiga 2.0 resume, the published Linux x86-64 AppImage under QEMU on an ARM64 VM, and the DM2 FM Towns selected-hero HUD icon sourced from authenticated interface data. They do not establish native x86-64 hardware, physical input, aura/panel completion or full visual parity. The release also publishes Android and iOS arm64 artifacts; publication alone is not runtime verification. Evidence: https://github.com/yeager/firestaff/releases/tag/v3.0.376 https://github.com/yeager/firestaff/commit/e0cf778c39b039918d6b1ae1ebf18e23ec423b1a https://github.com/yeager/firestaff/commit/f0c58017d243551f9dbf30ae5b28fb25172bd10e https://github.com/yeager/firestaff/commit/1be613b14f3cef9e2323a3e2b6ed840e13f6c480

project.status: active; v0.6.0 multi-host packages and monitor/CRTC timing update
project.notes: Emulates CPC 464/6128, Plus and GX4000 with per-model CRTC/Gate Array timing, disc and tape support, a debugger and embedded RASM. Inspected src/core includes Z80, CRTC variants and debugging code. README calls expansion hardware and UI work in progress; SHAKER compatibility is upstream's claim. v0.4.0 adds host-backed M4 TCP/DNS/server and plain-HTTP operations, a folder-backed FAT16 IDE/CF interface for SYMBiFACE II/III, and LambdaSpeak 3 Epson/DECtalk command handling using host voices. The release documents tests with Duke's TCP/telnet examples, SymbOS and LambdaSpeak software; these upstream compatibility claims were not independently reproduced. Evidence: https://github.com/WacKEDmaN/CPCSyntaxError/commit/c909c7f7e465dc54640248cbd91a4d78a1c45656 v0.5.0 adds guided and manual RAM cheats, CDT/TZX tape recording and turbo loading, HFE read/write, IPF read support, image writeback, a 300-rpm real-time floppy model, Multiface II, RS232C endpoints and folder-backed M4 DSK images. The bundled IPF decoder retains its non-commercial licence; upstream compatibility tests were not independently reproduced. Evidence: https://github.com/WacKEDmaN/CPCSyntaxError/commit/35ca66c5bb974eb0b1113e08980ea166cf93362a v0.6.0 adds successful CI builds and release assets for Windows x64, Linux x86-64 and universal macOS arm64/x86-64, plus monitor H/V hold controls and Compendium-backed CRTC sync timing. Upstream explicitly says the Linux and macOS packages were not yet desktop-tested. Evidence: https://github.com/WacKEDmaN/CPCSyntaxError/commit/2b74f27e5c466376321eb7aa6587d994e08a6670 https://github.com/WacKEDmaN/CPCSyntaxError/releases/tag/v0.6.0 https://github.com/WacKEDmaN/CPCSyntaxError/actions/runs/38114012270

events.title: fix(libretro): latch the BIOS and PAL options at content load (#858)
events.message:
fix(libretro): latch the BIOS and PAL options at content load (#858)

check_variables() re-runs whenever ANY core option changes, and it
re-applied 'BIOS (Cartridges)' and 'PAL' every time. retro_load_game()
resolves vjs.useJaguarBIOS after its option read (a GPU-only/jagcrypt cart
forces the boot ROM on; CD boot mode sets it from bootConfig.showBootROM),
and the DSP reads that flag at runtime. So on such a cart, touching an
unrelated option silently turned the boot-ROM flag back off mid-session.
PAL rewrote vjs.hardwareTypeNTSC live, so the clock macros switched
standards while the AV timing (negotiated only at load) did not.

Both are now applied only before content is loaded, the same way
internal_resolution is. After load a change only logs a one-shot "takes
effect on restart" notice. 'BIOS (Cartridges)' gains the "Restart
required" sublabel marker, and moves from the live list to the load-only
list in test_option_explain case 8; settings guide section 7 lists it.

Test: test_cart_needs_bios gains a mid-session arm. It loads a GPU-only cart
with bios=HLE and pal=disabled, changes an unrelated option, then PAL
itself, and checks that useJaguarBIOS stays 1 and the standard stays NTSC.
develop fails 3 of its 4 checks (useJaguarBIOS=0 after the unrelated
change, NTSC flipped); with the fix all pass.

Closes #858

events.message:
Server runs with --no-wasm-code-gc on V8 13.6 (Node 24)

V8 13.6's process-wide wasm import wrapper cache can free a wrapper twice
when wasm code GC runs while cart instances come and go. The server died
twice on 2026-10-10 during cartwheel WebGPU gates: 'Check failed:
jit_page.has_value()' under Runtime_TierUpWasmToJSWrapper ->
WasmImportWrapperCache::Free, and glibc 'corrupted size vs. prev_size'.
Upstream fix: V8 9b8ca54d5a, not in any Node 24 release
(nodejs/node#66366).

A private server driven like the gates (3 sessions, WebGPU and GL loads of
the cartwheel dual carts, 333 frames, screenshot, debugState, shutdown)
crashed at 65 and 76 WebGPU loads before; with the flag, two runs of 200
loads (150 WebGPU each) ran clean with RSS flat at 1.4-2.1 GB. The re-exec
wrapper adds the flag; the test checks the server process has it.
events.author: monteslu

events.title: fix(crash_detect): test the raw DSP PC for dsp_pc_escape
events.message:
fix(crash_detect): test the raw DSP PC for dsp_pc_escape

dsp_pc_valid() canonicalised the PC to 24 bits, by symmetry with the GPU,
where GPUReadWord and the 68K bus really do alias $FD012786 to $012786.
The DSP does not: DSPExec's own PC-escape bail-out tests the UNMASKED
dsp_pc against exactly this predicate (<= $E3FFFF, or DSP local RAM
$F1B000-$F1CFFF) and drains the slice without fetching.  A DSP PC that
fires the new check is one the core refuses to execute, so a fire is a
non-executing DSP by construction.  The mask hid Music Demo's HLE runaway
to $C1903000 (#853); an interrupt kept vectoring the DSP back into its ISR,
so the opcode counter moved and dsp_wedge never fired either.  The log line
now prints the raw PC too.

Evidence (1200 frames):
- True positive: d14bb22 + this change alone flags Music Demo with
  dsp_pc_escape at frames 5 and 606 -- pc=$C1903000 in HLE (previously
  silent) and $FFFFFFEF under --bios.  With the #853 DSP fix as well: clean
  in both modes.
- No new lines on the cart corpus: all 160 cart ROMs, HLE and --bios, every
  CRASH-DETECT line identical to the fix-only core, and audio + video
  byte-identical (the watchdog is observe-only).
- NOT swept: CD discs.  A CD title whose DSP sits at a high-byte PC would
  now log dsp_pc_escape, which matrix_diff.py reports as a new crash
  signature at release -- a detection gain, not a regression; read it that
  way.

Suite: `make TEST_EXPORTS=1 test` exit 0 (test_crash_detect_cd_wedge 12
cases, test_crash_detect_inframe 33 cases; audio clipping/presence pair ran
and passed).  c89-lint clean.

Refs #853

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: JoeMatt

events.title: fix(dsp): instructions behind a D_FLAGS store use the pre-store register bank (#853)
events.message:
fix(dsp): instructions behind a D_FLAGS store use the pre-store register bank (#853)

Music Demo (2002) (ScatoLOGIC) enters its DSP program at $F1B020 with a
store to D_FLAGS (REGPAGE=1 + I2S interrupt enable) immediately followed by
`movei #$F1B00C,r31` -- the stack pointer its bank-0 I2S handler uses via
`load (r31),r28`.  DSPWriteLong switched the register bank inside the
store, so the movei landed in bank 1, bank-0 r31 stayed 0, the first
interrupt pushed to $FFFFFFFC and the handler returned to garbage:
dsp_pc_escape at frame 5 under the real BIOS ($FFFFFFEF), and a runaway to
$C1903000 in HLE that the watchdog's 24-bit mask hid.

CAUSE / MODEL
JTRM v8 p.109 (p.59 for the GPU): "writing a value to the flag bits and
making use of those flag bits in the following instruction will not work
properly due to pipe-lining effects" -- at least one other instruction must
lie between.  The instruction already in flight behind the store still runs
with the OLD flags.  d220aa2 modelled that only for `jump` (Wolfenstein 3D's
`store; jump (r3)` epilogue, via dspPreStoreBank).  This generalises it:

- A DSP-issued D_FLAGS store no longer repoints dsp_reg/dsp_alternate_reg.
  The switch is deferred and committed (DSPUpdateRegisterBanks) when the
  existing retire delay runs out, so every operand of the instruction
  behind the store -- sources and destination, movei/moveta/movefa
  included -- uses the pre-store bank.  No per-operand check: the only
  hot-path change is the commit inside the already-present
  `if (dspFlagsRetireDelay)` countdown.  dspPreStoreBank is gone; jump's
  plain RM now reads the pre-store bank naturally.
- A taken jump/jr commits before running its inline delay slot (the second
  instruction behind the store, so Wolf3D's delay slot keeps the new bank
  exactly as before) and again at the redirect (Doom's `jump (r15); store`
  epilogue at $F1B028: the target still sees the new bank).
- Interrupt dispatch and host (68K/GPU) D_FLAGS writes already call
  DSPUpdateRegisterBanks, so they commit too.
- Window length unchanged: DSP_FLAGS_RETIRE_DELAY = 2 (the store + one
  instruction), JTRM v8's "at least one".  Software Reference v2.4 p.46
  (two; four for an indexed STORE) and Hardware Bugs & Warnings #11 (two
  NOPs) are documented as programmer margins; the indexed-store extra
  latency is not modelled.  Music Demo needs exactly one slot.
- Savestate: a window that straddles a frame boundary now leaves the live
  bank != the flags-implied bank, so the remaining delay rides in bits 1-2
  of the DSP chunk's existing active_bank byte (v17 extended in place, no
  layout change; older states hold 0/1 = no window).  Before this, a load
  silently dropped the window -- a run-ahead hole for Wolf3D's jump too.

The pipelined DSP executors (DSPExecP/P2/Comp) are declared but never
defined, so DSPExec is the only path.

GPU: same gap, not fixed here.  GPUWriteLong's G_FLAGS case swaps banks and
dispatches interrupts inside the store with no retire model at all; adding
one is the whole d220aa2 + this change again, so it is a follow-up.

TESTS
- test/test_dsp_unit.c Tests 17-21 (CI, no ROM): store REGPAGE then movei /

events.title: fix(netlink): fit the reply wait into one video frame instead of overrunning the vsync
events.message:
fix(netlink): fit the reply wait into one video frame instead of overrunning the vsync

Doom (2P) over RetroArch netplay stuttered, and toggling Network Link
Latency Hiding changed nothing.  Measured in a deterministic two-instance
netpacket simulation (test/tools/netlink_sim.c: virtual clock, RetroArch
netpacket semantics read from netplay_frontend.c): Doom's tic exchange is a
chain of single-byte hops, each side's byte depending on the other's, so the
link only advances while the core is blocked in JLinkAwaitReply.  The
per-frame wait budget was 2*EWMA+2 ms clamped to [4,15] ms and ignored what
the rest of the frame costs: with a few ms of emulation the frame finished
past its vsync, the frontend skipped the next one, and the core ran at 30 Hz
(audio at half rate) with ~13 ms of dead time per frame.  Every frame overran
at 3 ms/way (30 overruns/s); a slower device overran by more.

The budget is now what is left of ONE frame after the measured emulation cost
(EWMA of frame time minus time spent waiting, taken in retro_run just before
the frontend calls: audio_batch_cb blocks on a full audio buffer and video_cb
on vsync, neither is emulation) and a 3 ms margin for those calls.  The margin
widens by 1 ms (max 8) whenever a frame that waited is still followed by a
late frame start, and decays after 60 clean frames, so an unmodelled frontend
cost (hi-res present on iOS) corrects itself.  The per-reply timeout stays
adaptive, so a silent peer still costs little.

Sim, Doom 2P deathmatch, wait enabled, old -> new image updates/s
(emu = virtual emulation ms per frame):
  3 ms/way, emu 2:      14.5 -> 22.2, overruns 30/s -> 0
  3 ms/way, emu 6:      11.1 -> 22.2, overruns 30/s -> 0
  3 ms/way, emu 10:     11.2 ->  9.6, overruns 30/s -> 0 (waits only ~4 ms)
  Wi-Fi jitter+spikes:  8.6/8.2/8.1 -> 9.6/10.7/9.8 over 3 seeds, overruns
                        28/s -> 0
  4 ms of unmodelled post-hook cost: overruns 30/s -> 0.5/s via the margin
Wait disabled is ~9 image updates/s on every link, so on a jittery link the
old wait was no better than off: that is why the toggle appeared to do
nothing.  Network spikes themselves stay (a byte-synchronous protocol cannot
hide them).

Also: netlink_delay_proxy gains --jitter-ms/--spike-pct/--spike-ms/--seed
(Wi-Fi model), netlink_game gains --trace, and test/tools/netlink_sim.c +
netlink_sim_clockpatch.py record the simulator (measurement-only clock hook,
never applied to src/).  No regression since 693f42a (#250): identical results
in the sim, and nothing in the arm/pump/flush path changed.

events.message:
feat(libretro): restart-required sublabels, per-content option hiding, demotion OSD test (#850)

Follow-ups to #841 (#847).

- Restart marker: the info (sublabel) of every option that is read only at
  content load now starts "Restart required: applied when content is
  loaded." Static strings in libretro_core_options.h, so no re-push and no
  amendment slot is spent. Verified per option against where libretro.c
  consumes it: internal_resolution (latched in retro_load_game),
  enhancement_hooks (latched; check_variables only compares and logs),
  gdb_stub/bind/port/wait/halt_timeout (read only inside retro_load_game),
  bios_type (vjs.biosType used only by cart boot-ROM staging), cd_bios_type,
  cd_boot_mode and memory_track (consumed in open_disc_and_resolve_boot /
  CD BIOS staging), jgd (JGDLoadROM, only from the cart ROM loader) and pal
  (documented restart-only; see below). Redundant "requires a restart"
  sentences dropped. `bios` is deliberately NOT marked: check_variables()
  rewrites vjs.useJaguarBIOS live.
- Option hiding: with content loaded, the cartridge-only options (BIOS,
  Cart BIOS Type, GameDrive + SD card, enhancement hooks, blit memo) are
  hidden for CD content, alongside the existing CD-only hiding for carts.
  They share the one show_cart_options gate, so the visibility_force_push
  after a definitions re-push re-hides them. CD-only (not RAM-loaded
  executables). All SET_CORE_OPTIONS_DISPLAY calls go through
  option_display_push(), which reads the return value (libretro.h: "call
  is available"), latches a refusal and stops asking; reset in retro_deinit.
- Harness: records SET_CORE_OPTIONS_DISPLAY (a definitions push resets
  every row to visible, as RetroArch's rebuilt manager does), option
  descs, and can refuse the call. test_option_visibility now runs its disc
  half against the in-tree synth_jagcd.chd, so CI covers the CD side.
- test_option_explain cases 7-10, all on in-tree yarc.j64: runtime
  demotion OSD notice (synthetic enhancement row + underrun feed: one
  notice with the demotion reason, one re-push, nothing repeated, no
  SET_VARIABLE), the restart marker swept over every registered option,
  visibility surviving a re-push, and a refusing frontend.

Not changed: pal and bios still have live writes in check_variables()
(vjs.hardwareTypeNTSC / vjs.useJaguarBIOS), so a mid-session toggle
half-applies; out of scope here.

Closes #850

project.display_title: uDump — native Atari TOS ROM dumper
project.status: Creator-released TOS ROM dumper v1.03; native build untested
project.notes: Identity: Miro Kropacek/MiKRO identifies uDump 1.03 as a TOS ROM dumping utility for ST, STE, TT and Falcon. The entire five-file tree contains its C implementation, build recipe, author README and license; this is the canonical non-fork repository. Classification: A native preservation tool that obtains the TOS header, identifies version/country and machine cookies, selects ROM size and writes a named image. It handles EmuTOS and CT60 cases and copies ROM through a bounded buffer to avoid a documented extra-read bus error. It does not reconstruct or emulate TOS execution. Source CPU: uDump copies ROM bytes and parses header/cookie metadata rather than disassembling or interpreting the captured instructions. The ROM platform is recorded, but no original CPU analysis is claimed. Target CPU: Makefile uses m68k-atari-mint-gcc with explicit -m68000 and links libcmini startup/runtime into udump.tos. This establishes a native Motorola 68000 target without implying that all supported Atari models have the same minimum RAM or firmware. Build: The Makefile declares a libcmini-based native .tos build. The creator publishes a uDump 1.03 binary archive and earlier release notes explicitly discuss the distributed executable; runnable=true records that released utility, not a local run. The current source build was not reproduced, so compilable remains null and no gameplay or historical byte-match claim is made. Limitations: No cross-compilation, execution, real-machine ROM capture or binary comparison was performed. Runtime profiles: README names ST/STE/TT/Falcon and the source selects TOS ROM sizes and CT60/EmuTOS variants, but it does not specify a complete minimum-memory or OS-version configuration. The 16 KiB transfer buffer and -m68000 flag do not establish a runtime minimum. AI: The full five-file inventory, README, C implementation, Makefile and all 12 returned commits show no explicit generative-AI development disclosure. Usage is unknown, including later maintenance of the historical code. Relationships: uDump depends on libcmini and m68k-atari-mint system bindings; it is a separate focused application, not a duplicate runtime-library or TOS-reconstruction record. Its TOS/EmuTOS/CT60 support describes the data captured and machine handling, not ownership or reimplementation of those systems. project.notes: Planar-native compatibility layer and converter for porting SDL 1.2 games to ST/STE, used by several ports. The README documents cross-compilation with m68k-atari-mint-gcc, runnable TOS examples under Hatari, byte-identical BLiTTER/CPU checks on target, and measured stock-ST/Mega-STE behavior. The 26 September update adds per-step YM tone/noise effects and preserves their millisecond timing at both 50 and 60 Hz. SDL source/assets are inputs to the porting library, so source CPU is not applicable. The current OVCACHE sweep adds an 8 MHz cache-off control to the prior 16 MHz paths; upstream reports 150/150 frames on a real Mega STE at 8 MHz and at 16 MHz without cache. This is a tested configuration, not a minimum requirement. project.title: sid-analyzer — SID structure, MIDI and project exporter
project.display_title: sid-analyzer — SID structure, MIDI and project exporter
project.status: experimental pre-release; upstream claims not independently reproduced
project.notes: Rust SID program analyser with executable-player tracing, SID-bus captures, note/effect inference, MIDI and Pertylizer exports; distinct generic analysis tool. Cargo workspace specifies Rust 1.98 and mos6502/midly dependencies; runner.rs runs 6502 calls with cycle/wall-clock guards and captures register events. README carefully distinguishes PSID playback from limited RSID inspection/export and calls musical analysis/export approximate. Experimental Rust SID structure/tracing/MIDI/Pertylizer exporter with generic mos6502 execution. It has no playback UI or complete mixed SID-to-WAV renderer; exports are approximations. Cargo install/build/test commands and substantial source were reviewed, but no successful build or fixture execution was established in this review. All build flags remain unknown. Pinned Rust 1.98/dependency availability was not independently checked. Requires Rust 1.98 to build; optional SQLite needs native C/C++ tools, and licensed SID inputs must be user supplied. RSID export is refused without an explicitly unreliable override, CIA/interrupt hosting is incomplete, most exports primary-SID only, and MIDI loses subframe timing. No host hardware minimum. Build/tool prerequisites: Rust 1.98; Native C/C++ toolchain for optional bundled SQLite; User-supplied licensed SID files. Documented commands: cargo install --path crates/analyzer --bin sid-analyzer --locked; cargo build --release --workspace --locked; cargo test --workspace. RSID export refused by default without unreliable override; incomplete CIA/interrupt hosting. Secondary-SID capture available but most exports primary-chip-only; MUS/STR emulation unsupported. MIDI loses sub-frame timing; digi WAV is separate PCM, not full mixed SID rendering. No local build/fixtures run; pinned toolchain/dependency availability not independently checked. Analysis/export suite using mos6502; separate Pertylizer application consumes outputs. GitHub reports fork=false; that metadata alone does not establish independent authorship. Canonical root was screened against the approved 1,320-project catalogue plus discovery-source/decision indexes; no root collision was found. Upstream/related links: https://github.com/pertyjons/pertylizer. Rights: GPL-3.0-or-later for own source/docs; third-party notices preserved; users supply tunes and databases. Exporting does not by itself GPL-license output, but input music rights remain. AI evidence: README says artifacts support AI-assisted analysis; this is capability, not an explicit AI-development attribution. Agent files alone are insufficient. Reviewed 2026-10-05; no independent build, execution, gameplay, hardware test or byte comparison was performed. project.notes: Native C64 6502/Kick Assembler RPG with original code, maps and graphics according to README and main.asm, inspired by pokered's organization. Do not classify as a Pokémon Red disassembly/port despite the repository metadata description. README claims eight original monster species, thirty maps, battles, NPCs, menus and disk saves. build.bat regenerates assets/maps, validates assembly, assembles and creates a D64; main.asm imports real engine/data modules and documents resident-engine/streamed-data layout. Original Pokémon-inspired native homebrew RPG. README and source claim original code, graphics and maps; pokered informs organization. No disassembly, port, source-reconstruction or other RE method is asserted for the homebrew itself. README describes a presently playable set of maps, battles, NPCs, menus and disk saves with screenshots and play controls; runnable/playable=true are scoped to that upstream development-build claim. The provided batch recipe hard-codes author-specific tool paths. No assembly, testing, full-game completion or byte comparison was independently verified. Native Commodore 64 development build. Disk saves require the D64 path; the all-in-one PRG fallback cannot save. Upstream shows VICE launch and keyboard/joystick controls but establishes no additional CPU/RAM minimum. Build/tool prerequisites: Windows batch environment as provided; Java/Kick Assembler; VICE and c1541; Python 3. Documented commands: build.bat main.asm; python tools/map_editor.py. build.bat hard-codes the author's Windows Java, assembler and VICE paths and needs adjustment. Disk saves only work from D64, not PRG fallback. No local play/test performed; README does not establish a finished game. No root licence file found. Original homebrew inspired structurally by pret/pokered, not a derived Pokémon game-data/source port. GitHub reports fork=false; that metadata alone does not establish independent authorship. Canonical root was screened against the approved 1,320-project catalogue plus discovery-source/decision indexes; no root collision was found. Upstream/related links: https://github.com/pret/pokered. Rights: README and assembly header claim original assets/code; no root licence grant found. Pokémon-inspired naming/inspiration is distinct from a formal rights clearance. AI evidence: AI_DEVELOPER.md and .claude workflow files are present, but reviewed README/latest commits do not explicitly attribute development to an AI. Do not infer authorship from configuration. Reviewed 2026-10-05; no independent build, execution, gameplay, hardware test or byte comparison was performed. runtime_profiles.name: Enhanced Atari ST build
runtime_profiles.notes: The root README describes the enhanced Atari ST MC68000 build and Atari floppy/TOS distribution. No minimum RAM is stated here.

evidence.excerpt: Buildable Elite sources for the MC68000: the enhanced Atari ST version in src_atari, a separate native Amiga port in src_amiga, and the preserved original Atari ST version in src_orig.

runtime_profiles.name: Default OCS build
runtime_profiles.os: Kickstart 1.3; Workbench 1.3 or later for icon launch
runtime_profiles.notes: The documented baseline is PAL OCS with 512 KB Chip RAM plus 512 KB expansion RAM. The delivered image runs on a stock MC68000 and switches to wider routines automatically on 68020+ CPUs.

evidence.excerpt: Target: PAL OCS, MC68000, Kickstart 1.3, 512 KB Chip RAM plus 512 KB expansion RAM.
Double-click it to launch the game from Workbench 1.3 or later.

runtime_profiles.name: 68020-only build
runtime_profiles.notes: The explicit cpu=68020 build assembles only the native 68020 forms. The README does not restate a separate RAM minimum for this variant, so RAM is left unspecified.

evidence.excerpt: cpu=68020 still assembles the native forms only, for a tighter image that needs an MC68020.

The enhanced Atari output uses a TOS launcher and disk image; the Amiga version supplies native bitplanes, input, Paula audio and AmigaDOS handling. The documented Amiga baseline is PAL OCS/MC68000, Kickstart 1.3 and 512 KB Chip plus 512 KB expansion RAM; an explicit 68020-only variant is available. The original build is explicitly not byte-identical; do not infer byte identity for the enhanced versions. Real Amiga hardware remains unverified. project.title: c64engine native EasyFlash game engine
project.display_title: c64engine native EasyFlash game engine
project.status: Native 6510 engine/demo with EasyFlash packaging and VICE regression tooling.
project.notes: Identity: Roland Leißa's c64engine supplies a native 6510 engine/demo with bitmap scrolling, multiplexed sprites, tile streaming, music and a cartridge boot path. Classification: This is original retro-development tooling, not recovered historical game code. The engine, authored demo assets, cartridge packer and regression utilities are one coherent repository-root project. Source CPU: No historical input program is reconstructed: the inspected materials describe original native engine development, so an original-source CPU field does not apply. Target CPU: The project-local architecture document explicitly states that the engine is written entirely in 6510 assembly. The inspected source directly programs VIC-II/CIA and the C64 memory mapping registers. Build: The author documents generating engine.crt and running the demo; architecture notes also report a verified PRG boot. Compilation and execution are author-reported, while complete-game playability and original-binary matching remain unclaimed. project.title: Amiga Game Kit
project.display_title: Amiga Game Kit: native game build, test and asset pipeline
project.status: Source reviewed; no independent build or runtime test
project.notes: Identity: Amiga Game Kit is a coherent root-scoped toolkit plus demonstration games, native debug runtime, test scenarios and asset pipelines. The reviewed README, template, build script and profile implementation agree on that scope. Classification: Modern retro-development tooling integrates native C/ACE compilation, reproducible joystick/frame scenarios, golden-image checks, serial state capture and game-asset conversion. Emulator-driven testing is a development aid, not a catalogue entry for an individual game running through a guest CPU wrapper. Example games remain supporting material of this root entry. Source CPU: No historical executable is being recovered by this toolkit. Original-binary platform, CPU and source-language fields stay empty rather than being copied from its Amiga output. Target CPU: tools/build explicitly sets M68K_CPU=68000, M68K_FPU=soft and an m68k-amigaos toolchain. This records the native game output architecture; no host CPU is inferred from Python or Docker. Build: The inspected script invokes Docker/CMake against ACE and creates a bootable OFS ADF. README supplies dependencies and upstream example-test claims, but this pass did not install the toolchain, compile games, execute tests or compare historical binaries. All independent build flags remain unknown. Runtime profiles: Profiles.py documents A500 OCS 512 KiB chip plus 512 KiB slow, ECS/Kickstart 3.1, AROS and experimental A1200 AGA configurations. These are selectable test profiles rather than a universal minimum for every generated game, so no project-wide minimum runtime profile is imposed. AI: The README expressly says several bundled games were built by an AI agent and selected graphics generated with Retro Diffusion; the latest commit corroborates those generated assets. Thus usage is true for this repository. Claude Code, Codex and Cursor appear as supported integrations, which alone does not establish that each authored the toolkit, so only Retro Diffusion is a specifically evidenced tool label. All 55 available commit messages were reviewed; none names Claude, Codex or Cursor as a contributing author. CLAUDE.md is only an @AGENTS.md pointer, while AGENTS.md gives generic repository procedures. Relationships: ACE, bebbo-derived GCC and vAmiga are explicit dependencies. ACE already has its own tracker entry; this repository adds an orchestration/test/asset layer rather than mirroring that library. Root scope covers its integrated examples. README states MIT for AGK, MPL-2.0 for ACE and the used vAmiga core, and MIT for Moira; it says the GPL GUI is not used. These are upstream declarations, not a dependency-wide licensing audit. Evidence: https://github.com/codebase/amiga-game-kit/blob/6acced96fd328458e074f6e303633866ce5dc5aa/README.md https://github.com/codebase/amiga-game-kit/blob/6acced96fd328458e074f6e303633866ce5dc5aa/templates/game/CMakeLists.txt https://github.com/codebase/amiga-game-kit/blob/6acced96fd328458e074f6e303633866ce5dc5aa/tools/build https://github.com/codebase/amiga-game-kit/blob/6acced96fd328458e074f6e303633866ce5dc5aa/harness/agk/profiles.py https://github.com/codebase/amiga-game-kit/commit/6acced96fd328458e074f6e303633866ce5dc5aa https://github.com/codebase/amiga-game-kit/blob/6acced96fd328458e074f6e303633866ce5dc5aa/CLAUDE.md https://github.com/codebase/amiga-game-kit/blob/6acced96fd328458e074f6e303633866ce5dc5aa/AGENTS.md

events.title: Snapshots: a load powers on as the state's machine (#17)
events.message:
Snapshots: a load powers on as the state's machine (#17)

* add images and modern software section to README

* Snapshots: a load powers on as the state's machine

A state for another ROM, RAM, Microdisc fit, VSync setting or pulse is
no longer refused by name: the menu reads the ROMs it needs from the
card, powers on as that machine with the guest parked, and loads it
(design.md §10.6). The core says what a state needs (snapshot_machine)
and checks the field's shape, which is the build's, before anything a
power-on changes; a Microdisc on a 16K is not a state. snapio splits
into snapio_check and snapio_load so the menu can power on between the
passes.

A machine waiting on a tape request or busy on a disc command is
powered on the same way first: a Microdisc with drive A empty waits in
its EPROM's boot read for ever, which refused every load with a
message cut to "the tape or disc is".

Checked on the host (test_snapshot, test_snapshot_rom on all four
machines, test_vsync, test_disc, each run on to the original's state,
with planted bugs caught) and by the owner on a Pico 2 W.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* milestones: the owner's check of a state whose ROM is missing

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* milestones: the missing ROM named, the machine as it was

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Snapshots: power on again only after a torn load; keep the EPROM

From the review of #17. snapio_load counted every second-pass failure
as a part-changed machine, though snapshot_load refuses before changing
anything for all but a failed read of the RAM: that one is now
SNAP_TORN, and only it powers the machine on again. stage_roms read
microdis.rom from the card on every power-on with the Microdisc, even
with the EPROM already in the socket: it now puts that one back, as it
does an unchanged ROM.

project.notes: Identity: Mark Seelye's ScottFree64/128 ports Alan Cox's DOS ScottFree 1.14b C interpreter. The inspected source includes a native game loop, Commodore I/O, assembly parsing and C128 banked-memory support. Classification: This is a substantive native source port with platform optimizations, not a guest-CPU wrapper or a new disassembly of individual adventure binaries. No reverse-engineering-derived-port method is asserted. Source CPU: The upstream lineage is explicitly the DOS ScottFree 1.14b C source. The inspected material does not establish its original executable's exact CPU target, so source_cpu stays empty. Target CPU: The Makefile selects cc65's c64 or c128 target and links project-specific 6502 assembly routines. The code establishes a native 6502-family output independently of the C implementation language. Build: The README shows a completed cc65 build transcript and playing instructions for distributed C64/C128 D64/D81 images. These support author-reported compilation, execution and playability; original-binary matching is not established. Limitations: No independent build or gameplay test was run. Upstream cautions that some boundary-pushing modern adventures may fail through memory limits or format quirks. Runtime profiles: Documented operation covers C64 and C128, including C128 40/80-column modes and disk/emulator loading. No explicit minimum CPU model or RAM profile was established. AI: The README, source headers and inspected repository tree contain no explicit development-AI disclosure; usage remains unknown. Relationships: The repository credits Alan Cox's ScottFree source, ScottKit definition corrections and a shortened cc65 C128 memory driver. Bundled third-party adventure data is convenience content, not separate reconstruction work by this author. Both source headers credit Curdt/TEK and 1993 development. The archive also includes sprite data, per-part include files, screenshots and a disk image; it does not claim to preserve every demo part. Classification: This is an original-author historical source archive with substantive graphics, Copper, interrupt, scripting and 3D/mirror code. It is source preservation rather than binary-derived reverse engineering, and the two related parts belong in one repository-root record. Source CPU: The original sources use Motorola 68k data/address registers, MOVEM, DBF, RTE and Amiga custom-chip addresses. The inspected files do not select an exact processor variant, so retain the broad m68k architecture rather than asserting a minimum 68000. Target CPU: The preserved output remains native m68k assembly for Amiga custom hardware; no translated host implementation is present. Build: The complete tree contains no common makefile or build instructions. mirror.s includes setup.i, which is absent from that tree, and the source retains historical assembler directives and fixed test addresses. The supplied disk image does not prove these published sources currently rebuild, so all build flags remain unknown. Limitations: No compilation, execution or byte comparison was performed; the missing setup.i is a concrete reproducibility gap. Runtime profiles: The author README and selected code do not state a reliable minimum CPU, RAM, chipset or OS configuration. Fixed source addresses and the existence of an ADF are not used to infer runtime requirements. AI: README, source headers, complete tree and all four returned commits disclose no development-AI use. Historical source dates do not establish non-use in every later maintenance action. Relationships: The README explicitly identifies Curdt's contribution to TEK's Rampage and releases his sources under the Apache licence. Embedded manager code credits Captain Bifat/TEK; the archive's own authorship statement is not a new ownership claim over every third-party contribution or the full disk image. project.notes: Identity: Mårten Rånge/Lance preserves the third version of his 1993 STE replay system and explains its history and implementation in a detailed first-person README. PT_SRC50.S contains the replay/Paula emulation implementation, PT_INFO.S documents use and compatibility, and REPLAY.S/REPLAY50.S provide integration examples. Classification: This is a substantive original-source music-development library/archive: it combines a ProTracker replay routine with native STE Paula emulation and self-generating mixer code. The historical source and retrospective explain earlier reverse-engineering lineage, but the current archive is not mislabelled as a new binary-derived reconstruction. Its emulator classification concerns sound-chip behavior, not a game-specific guest-CPU wrapper. Source CPU: The preserved historical STE implementation uses 68000 registers and instructions, supervisor/user switching and Atari hardware access; the author explicitly discusses 68k instruction timing and its 8 MHz STE implementation. The record describes this preserved ST-family source rather than treating the use of Amiga music formats as proof of an analyzed Amiga binary. Target CPU: PT_SRC50.S and REPLAY.S directly implement the native 68000 replay routine and STE DMA/LCM1992 output path. There is no portable host or alternate CPU output established by this archive. Build: The archive contains complete substantial assembly and example integration sources, with the author documenting its historical release and later use. A present-day build/run is not established: PT_SRC50.S expects an external modules\*.mod input, and the examples use period-style include paths with no modern build automation. Limitations: Current compilability, runnable output and byte equivalence stay unknown. Historical success and author performance estimates are not independent tests of the archived checkout. Runtime profiles: PT_INFO.S explicitly targets STE and warns that this original version is not Falcon-compatible because of stack techniques and the missing LCM1992. Neither it nor the reviewed source establishes a complete minimum-memory runnable configuration, so no minimum runtime profile is inferred. AI: The author history and inspected original-source files contain no explicit AI-development disclosure. The age of the original code does not justify asserting non-use across the repository's later history. Relationships: The author explains an early derivation from a recovered Dr. Doom STE replay routine and use of a lightly patched ProTracker player, with the Paula emulator rewritten for version 3. README points to later bug fixes by Mrs Beanbag/RiFT, Paulo Simoes and SMFX; their changes are not attributed to this preserved original version, and the lost UCDM plugin source is not claimed to be present. Classification: The source implements format detection, SCP capture, standard ADF/D64 conversion, direct retry reads, reports, hashes and conflict-safe publication of complete logical images. Its DOS path additionally implements targeted head-by-head adaptive rereads and multi-SCP sector merging. This is independent recovery automation around an existing decoder, rather than a claim to have reimplemented Greaseweazle's flux codecs. Limitations: The multi-SCP handler explicitly rejects Amiga and C64 modes. Advanced adaptive two-pass sector recovery is DOS-only; Amiga/C64 use direct Greaseweazle retry reads. Complete ADF/D64 standard sectors do not preserve all copy-protection or unusual flux data, so SCP remains the archival master. Source CPU: This tool reads floppy flux and disk-image sector data rather than reconstructing any original executable CPU instruction set. Supported disk platforms do not establish source CPUs. Target CPU: The AutoIt source, README and v1.3.4 release establish Windows as host, but no explicit x86/x64 target selection or minimum processor architecture was found. No architecture is inferred from AutoIt or Windows. Build: The repository supplies a substantial AutoIt source script and tagged v1.3.4 release, whose inspected release assets list is empty. Root README describes a compiled EXE but no such artifact was verified. No AutoIt compilation, hardware capture, recovery trial or independent image comparison was performed; all build flags remain unknown. Limitations: The 100_PERCENT_OK label means all expected standard sectors were reported present; it is not historical binary equivalence or completeness of copy-protected flux. Runtime profiles: The creator README explicitly requires Windows 7 or later, Greaseweazle gw.exe and compatible hardware/drive for physical capture. Record the documented OS requirement, leaving CPU/RAM unclaimed. AI: Inspected README, complete current root, source and both available commit messages include no explicit AI development attribution. The README's self-evaluation tone is not evidence of AI authorship. Relationships: The README explicitly credits and requires Keir Fraser's already-tracked Greaseweazle tools. This separate AutoIt implementation adds workflow, reporting and DOS-sector rescue logic and is not a mirrored copy of those tools. The root license is MIT. events.title: fix(core): mirror 1, 2 and 4 MB cartridge images across the cart window (#851)
events.message:
fix(core): mirror 1, 2 and 4 MB cartridge images across the cart window (#851)

Flip Out (2 MB) executes `cmpa.l $A02000.l,a2 / blt / illegal` at $11EEAA.
A cart only drives the address lines it has, so a 2 MB image repeats at
$A00000 and the read returns the cart's own word at $2000 and the branch is
taken.  We returned 0 (jagMemSpace past the loaded image is zero), so the
ILLEGAL fired: HLE looped ILLEGAL/RTE at $11EEB4 from about frame 320, and
BIOS mode trapped to the boot ROM's $E005DC vector at about frame 810.

Ground truth: the MiSTer Jaguar core (Jaguar.sv) ANDs a cart_mask into
abus_out[22:20], armed only for an image of exactly 1, 2 or 4 MiB (mask
000/001/011); every other size is left unmirrored ("not exact=don't
modify").  The JTRM is silent, and jag_sim's cart model has no size-based
decode.  So only 1/2/4 MiB images (measured after a copier header is
stripped) are replicated, at load time, so the read path is unchanged:
1 MB repeats every MB, 2 MB at $A00000/$C00000, 4 MB once at $C00000.
Copies stop at $DFFF00 (the CDROM overlay), MemTrack's claimed window still
wins because MTClaimsRead is tested ahead of the ROM read, and a GameDrive
banked image is untouched.

jagMemSpace is static, so the cart window past the image is now cleared at
load and again in JaguarDone: a previous title's mirror (or the CD BIOS)
used to survive a reload in the same process.  JaguarMirrorCart() is
re-run after TitleHookApplyROM patches so the repeats carry the patch.

Tests: test_cart_format gains 7 mirror cases (distinct markers per
megabyte, 1/2/4 MB mirror, 3 MB and 64 KB do not, header-stripped size,
no leak across reloads); test_flipout_851 steps Flip Out for 1000 frames in
HLE and BIOS and fails if the 68K lands on the ILLEGAL or a trap landing pad
(skipped, and recorded in the skip ledger, without the private ROM).
Corpus A/B (160 carts, 600 frames, HLE, both blitters): only Flip Out
changes, plus a 1-pixel difference in Fight For Your Life (4 MB) where the
blitter reads past the end of the image and now sees the wrapped ROM bytes
instead of zero.

Closes #851

events.title: fix(libretro): list zip/7z floppy images in disk control (#2408)
events.message:
fix(libretro): list zip/7z floppy images in disk control (#2408)

RetroArch hands block_extract cores an archive either whole or, when the
user browses into it, as "<archive>#<entry>". The core passed both to UAE
unchanged: Disc Control showed only the archive, UAE inserted whichever
image came first in archive order, and the '#' form left DF0 empty
because zfile opens members as "<archive>/<entry>".

Zip and 7z content now becomes one disk control entry per floppy image,
sorted by name. A browsed member is inserted first unless a valid saved
initial image applies, and an archive with no floppy images keeps the
previous single-entry behavior. Disc Control replacements convert '#'
paths the same way.

Positional media handling inserted nothing for an uppercase extension
(GAME.ADF) or a disk image outside the extension list (.scp, .fdi, an
extensionless ADF). The floppy list now matches case-insensitively, and
any file zfile identifies as a disk image is inserted into DF0.

events.title: tests: ipv6_socket_test finishes on a machine without tap0
events.message:
tests: ipv6_socket_test finishes on a machine without tap0

On the A3000 the test never finished.  The raw-connect section binds a raw
socket to 10.9.9.1, tap0's address under the emulator harness, sends to it
and then blocks in recv() for its own packet to loop back.  Without tap0
that address is off-link: the packet leaves by the real interface and the
recv() waits forever (ipv6_socket_test.c, "raw first send
synchronization").  The four ICMP-error sections fail for the same reason:
they need a local, non-loopback address to send to.

Where DEVS:NetInterfaces/tap0 exists, nothing changes: tap0 must come up
and its address is used.  Where it does not, the test uses the address the
machine's own interface sends from, and the five sections that need one
skip, with a line saying so, when there is none.  The two raw
synchronisation receives wait at most 5 s, so a packet that does not come
back is a failure, not a hang.

Each log line now goes to Output() as it is logged, not at exit: a stuck
run shows the last line it reached, and the transcript is no longer cut at
8 KB.

run-socket.sh -n stages no tap0; CI runs it.  Before this change that run
ends with no summary.

events.title: tests: take tcpdrill.device off DeviceList when the test ends
events.message:
tests: take tcpdrill.device off DeviceList when the test ends

tap_remove() called RemDevice(), which only calls the device's expunge
vector.  tap_expunge() declines, so the node stayed on Exec's DeviceList
while tap_remove() freed its base, and ipv6_socket_test and sockopt_test
never called tap_remove() at all, leaving a node whose vectors point into
the program's unloaded segment.

On the A3000 that is the reboot after a Break-ed ipv6_socket_test:
NetShutdown, then the first Avail FLUSH calls the dangling expunge vector.
The same sequence with the device removed does not reboot.

tap_remove() now unlinks the node itself under Forbid().  Both tests call
it after CloseLibrary() and check that tcpdrill.device is gone; the check
fails against the old RemDevice() code.

ButtonClickInteraction failed only after another test.  The ROM layout
change of v0.11.87 exposed this.  The run-to-run differences, found by
comparing per-frame RAM dumps and instruction traces of both runs:

- Musashi kept the CPU's data and address registers and the FPU state
  (registers, the FSAVE null-frame flag) across m68k_pulse_reset().
  Every reset now starts from the first run's state.
- Host file descriptors, which programs and the ROM see in fh_Args, came
  from whatever the process had open.  Files now get descriptors from
  600 up, and a new run closes the previous run's.
- Host state not reset between runs: the open-file table (exclusive
  opens keyed by handle addresses), the fd-kind table of the file-cost
  model, and the display's input state when the display stays
  initialised.

The remaining differences are the FileLock keys (host inode numbers of
the per-run temporary directories).

Not fixed here: with the FPU in its reset state (FSAVE null frames on
task switches), SIGMAth2 corrupts the free list.  That path is now the
same in every run but is not taken; it goes to Phase 240.

events.title: feat(tools): score BIOS-mode cart boot rows from the boot-ROM handoff, add BIOS_REJECT
events.message:
feat(tools): score BIOS-mode cart boot rows from the boot-ROM handoff, add BIOS_REJECT

The cart boot matrix scored real-BIOS runs from frame 0, so the identical
~490-frame boot logo animation and jingle counted as every title's "video"
and "audio", and carts the boot ROM rejects (red "Jaguar" screen) read as
"BIOS works".

cart_boot_probe now finds the boot-ROM -> cart handoff itself (68K or any of
its last 1024 instructions, via pcQueue, in $800000-$DFFFFF) and restarts
scored_* counters there; --post-handoff N runs N frames past it (--frames is
the cap) and stops early once the boot ROM sits on its BRA.S * halt loop.
Headerless RAM-loaded .jag files never run the boot ROM (bios_ran=0): whole
run scored, never a reject.

The classifier moves to test/tools/cart_classify.sh (so a unit test can feed
it synthetic logs) and gains BIOS_REJECT (boot ROM ran, no handoff, parked on
BRA.S *) and ? (bios_trap) (cart got control, then PC fell back into the
boot ROM: a crash, not a reject). Crash-watchdog signatures stay whole-run:
an early escape is a real bug (#853), not excused.

matrix_diff.py ranks BIOS_REJECT equal to GAME_CODE: GAME_CODE -> BIOS_REJECT
is a lateral scoring correction, and HLE GAME_CODE / BIOS BIOS_REJECT is not
an HLE-vs-BIOS asymmetry. BIOS runs get FRAMES+700 frames and a 150s default
timeout. docs/cart-boot-matrix.md prose updated; table not regenerated.

Closes #852

events.title: PCMCIA cards can save and load their contents

PCMCIA cards can save and load their contents

TPCMCIACard::TransferContents() saves or loads the contents of a card,
for debug state files. Linear cards copy their memory map under the
flush mutex and mark every page dirty, so the image file is rewritten
two seconds later. ATA cards copy their image and write it back to the
file at once (a read-only image keeps the contents in memory only, with
a message). The size must match the card; the network card has no
contents.

events.title: Debug state files hold the contents of the PCMCIA cards
events.message:
Debug state files hold the contents of the PCMCIA cards

Decided by Matt: debug files save the card contents like the flash,
but cards may be shared with other emulated Newtons, so contents that
changed since the state was saved are only overwritten when the caller
asks for it: TEmulator::LoadState(path, inOverwriteCards),
TMonitor::RequestLoadState(path, inOverwriteCards), and the Monitor
command "load overwrite <path>". Without it, the file is refused with
a hint. Fast start files are unchanged (the card must match).

File version 12, files up to 512 MB (two 128 MB ATA cards).

Tested with a 2 MB linear card: a changed card refuses the load, the
overwrite brings the saved contents back and into the image file, and
the round trip is identical.

events.title: native32: RaiseException(0x406D1388), MSVC's SetThreadName, returns
events.message:
native32: RaiseException(0x406D1388), MSVC's SetThreadName, returns

The guest wraps it in __try { RaiseException } __except (EXECUTE_HANDLER)
{}, but its __try frame is on the guest SEH chain, which Windows never
walks (eh32 handles C++ frames only). The exception went unhandled and
ended the process with 0x406D1388. Returning is exactly what the empty
__except does; every other code is still raised for real.

events.title: disasm32: every slot of an incremental-link thunk table is a function
events.message:
disasm32: every slot of an incremental-link thunk table is a function

An incrementally linked image routes every function through one table of
5-byte `jmp rel32` thunks, and every call and function pointer names the
thunk. A pointer-shaped value naming a byte inside a slot decoded across
the next slot and hid it, so a thunk reached only through a runtime
pointer went missing from the catalog and its first call faulted.

thunk_tables() finds runs of 16+ back-to-back E9 slots into the code;
each slot becomes a seed, and an entry off the slot grid is dropped
before the mid-instruction pass.

events.title: lift32: xadd and cmpxchg
events.message:
lift32: xadd and cmpxchg

Neither was lifted, so the inlined InterlockedExchangeAdd and
InterlockedCompareExchange of reference counts and spin locks did nothing:
a release never dropped its count. Tiberium Wars has 21 `lock xadd` and
`lock cmpxchg` sites. Lifted code runs under one machine lock, so the plain
read-modify-write is already atomic. Four difftest cases, matching hardware.

events.title: lift32: SSE and SSE2, and the x87 compares that set EFLAGS
events.message:
lift32: SSE and SSE2, and the x87 compares that set EFLAGS

lift32 had no SSE: every xmm instruction lifted as UNIMPLEMENTED, a no-op.
VC6-era titles never emitted any; a title built with /arch:SSE (VC 2005 and
later) does all its float math in it. Tiberium Wars had 212,000 such sites
(120,000 movss, 28,000 mulss), so every float in the game was wrong.

- runtime/recomp32: an xmm_t register file (g_xmm[8], _xmm in lifted code)
  and MXCSR, defined beside g_mm in every runtime and saved per guest thread
  by native32; helpers for the edge cases C gets wrong (cvt to int32 gives
  0x80000000 out of range, min/max return the second operand on NaN or
  equal, COMI's EFLAGS word, the cmpXX predicates).
- tools/lift/lift32_sse.py: the moves, scalar and packed arithmetic,
  compares (into EFLAGS as FK_EFLAGS, as sahf does), shuffles and unpacks,
  conversions, ldmxcsr/stmxcsr and the integer SSE2 forms MSVC's code uses.
  lift32 asks it first, so xmm forms of pxor/movd/movq are not taken for MMX.
- fcomi/fucomi and the popping forms: capstone names those fcompi/fucompi,
  so the existing fcomip branch never matched, and it compared st(1)
  whatever the operand. lahf (the `ucomiss; lahf; test ah, 44h` NaN test),
  and bsf/bsr, which were missing too.
- difftest: 103 new cases against Unicorn, every one matching.

The cause of the exec/getmsgnull and ref_expected_outputs_2 flakes: a
write to an unmapped address started lxa's interactive debugger.
exec/getmsgnull writes through ROM code bytes taken as list pointers,

and never in liblxa (tests, pylxa).  tests/rdd/test_stdin.py runs the
probe with debugger commands on its stdin.  Without the fix the test

events.title: lift32: lift `repz ret` as ret, and end extents at it (#78)
events.message:
lift32: lift `repz ret` as ret, and end extents at it (#78)

* lift32: lift `repz ret` as ret, and end extents at it

`repz ret` (F3 C3) is AMD's branch-prediction idiom for a plain ret, which
MSVC 2005 and later emit -- __security_check_cookie among them. lift32 left
it UNIMPLEMENTED, so a cookie that matched fell through into
__report_gsfailure and every /GS-checked function ended the process with
0xC0000409. generate.py's extent walk did not treat it as a terminator
either, so a body ending in one ran on into its neighbour. `bnd ret`
(F2 C3) is handled the same way.

events.title: Phase 237d: RawDoFmt registers, SetTaskPri byte, shell variables, mass-run names - v0.11.77
events.message:
Phase 237d: RawDoFmt registers, SetTaskPri byte, shell variables, mass-run names - v0.11.77

Each change is checked against AmigaOS 3.1 with a probe:

- exec: RawDoFmt()'s PutChProc sees D2-D7 the way it left them; they
  start as the caller's.  Whatever the PutChProc does to them, or to A2
  and A4-A6, does not reach RawDoFmt's own state.  The caller gets its
  registers back (exec/rdfregs: Fish PhxAss counts characters in D7 and
  no longer hangs).
- exec: SetTaskPri() stores the low byte of the priority and does not
  clamp it.  A "task" inside the exception vector table is on no list
  (exec/taskprilow: Fish Joey calls SetTaskPri(127, 1005)).
  exec/taskregs records that a new task starts with all registers 0.
- dos: a program started by lxa has the shell's local variables
  process, RC and Result2 (dos/procvar: Fish ShellTimer).
- massrun: each program runs as LXAREF:p/<id>/<name> on a volume of its
  own, as on the reference.  Fish Mkid fid/lid build their path into a
  small buffer, and Molec3D PCCopy depends on it too.  Password "loop" is
  listed as memory-dependent (the stack lies below the ROM on lxa).
  Formatter, Riff and ShellTimerDaemon are listed as environment-
  dependent: on the reference they rely on what an earlier program of
  the same batch left in memory.

events.title: fix(devices): conform 1442, 2501, 2310 and console to the IBM 1130 manual
events.message:
fix(devices): conform 1442, 2501, 2310 and console to the IBM 1130 manual

1442 Card Read Punch (rewritten):
- Control modifiers use IOCC low-byte positions: bit 13 Start Read
  (0x04), bit 14 Feed (0x02), bit 15 Start Punch (0x01), bit 8
  Stacker Select (0x80)
- Sense Device returns the DSW and resets level-0 (bit 15) or
  level-4 (bit 14) responses without aborting the operation
- Read/Write transfer via the IOCC address; Read Response and Punch
  Response DSW bits are reported; Operation Complete is a level-4
  interrupt for both read and punch
- End-punch is bit 12 (0x0008) and that column is punched
- Single hopper with read station -> punch station -> stacker flow;
  Start Punch feeds a card when the punch station is empty
- Level-4 ILSW bit 2 (0x2000)

2501 Card Reader:
- Operation Complete after every card; Last Card set in addition
- Word count taken from bits 9-15 of the first table word
- Not Ready or Busy reflects busy and empty-hopper states
- Run() no longer requests an interrupt when nothing was read

2310 / single disk:
- Device codes 0x04 (CPU disk), 0x11-0x14 (2310 drives 1-4)
- Seek direction is modifier bit 13 (0x04)
- Read-check verifies without transferring to storage
- IOCC address latched at Initiate Read/Write
- Sense Device with bit 15 resets Operation Complete
- Busy is cleared when a read or write finishes

Console keyboard/printer:
- Replaced stub with the manual's protocol: Write -> busy -> printer
  response on level 4; Control selects keyboard, key latches a
  card-code word, Read stores it and deselects; INT REQ and function
  keys; DSW bits 0-6 per the manual; level-4 ILSW bit 1 (0x4000)

events.title: fix(cpu): conform instruction set to IBM 1130 Functional Characteristics
events.message:
fix(cpu): conform instruction set to IBM 1130 Functional Characteristics

- Short-format effective address uses the next-instruction address
  (IAR+1) as the base, per the manual (e.g. /0500 + /78 -> /0579)
- MDX opcode corrected from 0x0A to 0x0E (01110); real IPL/DMS
  binaries now decode
- SRT is an arithmetic shift (sign propagates); right shifts with a
  zero count now advance the IAR; SRA counts >= 48 clear ACC
- Divide: remainder takes the dividend's sign; negative quotient
  overflow is detected
- STS zeroes bits 8-15 before storing Carry/Overflow in bits 14-15
- Memory addressing wraps (high-order bits beyond installed storage
  are ignored) instead of throwing
- XIO Sense Interrupt (function 011) implemented: ACC <- ILSW of the
  level being serviced, independent of device code

Tests updated where they encoded the old behavior; new tests added
for each corrected rule.

events.title: Save the fast start file on the monitor thread
events.message:
Save the fast start file on the monitor thread

On quit, the UI thread stopped the emulator, waited for the monitor to
halt, and then saved the state itself. Now it hands a save request to
the monitor thread with the new inHaltAfter flag: the monitor stops the
emulator, saves, and stays halted, so nothing changes after the save.
The UI keeps running and waits until the request is done
(TMonitor::IsStateRequestPending()). During the quit, the UI thread no
longer touches the emulated machine.

Found by Greptile in PR #225.

instead of 0.18 s; loading is unchanged at 0.13 s, so most of the time

it is being loaded (edited by hand, or a bug). The machine then ran on a
half-loaded state. Now LoadState() clears RAM and resets, as the fast
start path already did, so NewtonOS boots again from the flash. Files
that are refused before loading starts (identity, CRC, header) still
change nothing.

events.title: Don't let a huge or foreign file stop Einstein from starting
events.message:
Don't let a huge or foreign file stop Einstein from starting

ReadStateFile() allocated memory for the whole file before looking at
it, outside the callers' try blocks. A large file in place of
FastStart.state could throw std::bad_alloc at launch, before the file was
deleted, so every launch failed. Now the first 8 bytes must say
EINISNAP, files over 256 MB are refused, and an allocation failure is
reported like any other read error.

Found by Greptile in PR #225.

events.title: Don't block in a serial write while holding the DMA mutex
events.message:
Don't block in a serial write while holding the DMA mutex

The BasiliskII worker wrote to a blocking pseudo terminal while it held
mDMAMutex. Once about 1 KB waited unread, write() blocked, and save,
load, reset and the fast start on quit waited forever in Suspend()
(reproduced: the save request stayed pending). The TCP client had the
same pattern with a blocking socket, and connected while holding the
mutex.

Both now write without blocking. If the other side does not read, the
byte stays in DMA and is sent again in the next round; other errors
drop it, as before. The TCP client connects before it takes the mutex,
and a read without data no longer counts as a disconnect. PTY and Pipes
already opened their ports with O_NONBLOCK.

Found by Greptile in PR #225.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: MatthiasWM

events.title: Check values from a state file before they replace the current ones
events.message:
Check values from a state file before they replace the current ones

A refused value must not stay behind. The breakpoint count replaced
mBPCount before its check, while the breakpoint array kept its old size,
so a refused file left a count that later loads and resets walked past
the array. Breakpoints are now read into a local list and replace the
old ones only when complete (and realloc is checked). The pen sample
positions and the sizes of platform events and buffers are checked
before they are stored. The event queue only counts events that were
read completely, so a failed load leaves no half-read event with an
unchecked size, and both queue reallocs are checked.

Found by Greptile in PR #225.

events.title: Phase 237d: file waits, one-shell Execute, ReadArgs defaults, NULL remember key, floppy drives - v0.11.76
events.message:
Phase 237d: file waits, one-shell Execute, ReadArgs defaults, NULL remember key, floppy drives - v0.11.76

Each fix is checked against AmigaOS 3.1 with a probe:

- dos: a task sleeps while its file operations' 3.1 time passes, and
  other tasks run meanwhile.  exec wakes it when the time is up; when
  nothing else is ready, the clock skips ahead to that point.  System()
  sleeps until its child ends; it no longer polls.  Execute(cmd, in, out)
  runs one shell with the command at the head of its input, as 3.1 does.
  The resident shell costs no disk time.  Run is internal to the shell and
  starts a background CLI that loads the command itself
  (dos/runload: Fish Wicon).
- dos: ReadArgs() leaves the array entries of absent arguments as the
  caller set them; /M entries become NULL (dos/readargsdef: Fish Leggi).
- intuition: AllocRemember() with a NULL key links the node at address 0
  (intuition/remnull: Fish WBLander show, LifeCycles).
- trackdisk/dos: two floppy drives.  Units 2 and 3 return
  TDERR_BadDriveType.  There is one "trackdisk.device" task per drive, at
  priority 5.  DF0: and DF1: device nodes carry a FileSysStartupMsg for
  trackdisk.device (exec/tdunits: Fish NoClick, NoClick2).
- massrun: each reference batch of 25 programs is emulated on lxa with a
  fresh private system directory.  Each program gets a fresh copy of its
  own directory.

events.title: fix(dsp): take DSP interrupts at the DSP's next instruction, not in the event callback (#744) (#849)
events.message:
fix(dsp): take DSP interrupts at the DSP's next instruction, not in the event callback (#744) (#849)

Club Drive was silent under HLE. DSPSetIRQLine vectored the DSP
synchronously inside the I2S event callback; the 68K, which runs its
whole slice before DSPExec, then wrote D_PC=$F1B030 while DSPGO=1 (JTRM v8
p.110: D_PC writes only while the DSP is idle) and landed on the vector
with zero ISR instructions run; the game's init wrote IMASK=1 back and no
interrupt was ever taken again (DSP spins at $F1B120, LTXD 0). Pure I2S
phase luck: 5/97 first-tick phases silent on develop, 0/97 with the fix.

DSPSetIRQLine now latches the interrupt (IMASKCleared, already
serialized) and the DSP takes it at its next instruction boundary in DSP
time; a host D_FLAGS write ORs into the latch instead of dropping it.
The handoff-state hypotheses (R31, bank seeding) were tested and refuted.

Club Drive HLE: RMS 0.0 -> 2948.6, onset frame 6. Corpus A/B vs develop:
160/160 framebuffer streams identical in both modes; cart matrix audio
changed only for Club Drive HLE (better) and Cybermorph HLE (+5 samples,
neutral). Audio presence + clipping unchanged on Wolf3D, Doom, WMCJ,
IS1/IS2, Skyhammer, Atari Karts, Raiden, T2K, Zoop. test_dsp_unit 7/9/9a
updated to the new contract; Club Drive HLE presence check added.

Refs #744

An ARM/Thumb interpreter in the runtime (runtime/interp.cpp, armemu's
semantics in C++): code no module holds runs from memory as it is, in step
with the rest, until it returns to its caller; its calls to entries run
recompiled. A call to a non-entry is interpreted instead of stopping (the
--copy hint is kept), and a function the emitter cannot translate (bytes
that are no code as they lie: an overlay that decrypts itself) becomes a
call to it. The self-test's --interp runs every vector through it.

Overlays are told apart function by function: each overlay function's
extent (its code and the literal pools it folds) and crc32 are in its
module; a call into the overlays' area goes to the function whose bytes
are in memory as built, and every store there marks its 256-byte page so
the functions over it are checked again. Overlays stacked at several load
addresses, partly overwritten or decrypting themselves are followed; the
cartridge's epoch, the slots, the samples and the first instructions are
gone.

A program its crt0 decompresses carries its stored image as a segment of
kind "loaded", which the boot matches too.

Fixes: the emitter's Thumb `add pc, rB` read pc word-aligned (switches
whose add lies at 2 mod 4 jumped two bytes short; the instruction test now
has the switch at both alignments); discovery follows a known word pushed
alone and popped into pc as a jump (CodeWarrior's Thumb thunks into ARM);
the self-test's --auto keeps a vector only if it runs discovered code, and
leaves out segments outside the test's memory (an ARM7 autoload linked for
VRAM); display capture's source A is engine A's graphics whatever its
display shows (composed apart on a line shown from VRAM); the run's dump
writes VRAM too.

Checked on a 2010 cartridge with a compressed ARM9, 20 compressed
overlays stacked at five bases and a self-decrypting anti-piracy overlay:
the opening, the title (main RAM against melonDS's state: 12 482 bytes,
12 288 of them a stream's ring buffer) and the route into its first
dungeon; its self-test 137 231 vectors, no failure either way. Discovery
on five cartridges unchanged.

events.title: Import lisa-c: C cross-development for the Apple Lisa Office System
events.message:
Import lisa-c: C cross-development for the Apple Lisa Office System

Cross-compile C on the host into native Lisa Office System 3.x programs
and write them to a floppy image that runs in the granny-smith emulator.
Nothing is compiled or linked on the Lisa.

- Toolchain: Retro68's GCC for the 68000 (its `pascal` attribute gives
  the Lisa Pascal calling convention).
  - .github/workflows/toolchain.yml builds it from a pinned Retro68
    commit and publishes a trimmed, relocatable copy
    (tools/package_toolchain.sh).
  - `make toolchain` downloads it.
- Pipeline:
  - lisalink.py packs code into segments.
  - elf2lisa.py writes the Workshop 3.0 object format, with the jump
    table and the desktop-tool unit tables.
  - phrasec.py compiles phrase files (menus, alerts).
  - mklisafs.py writes an Office System 3.1 floppy file system from
    scratch.
- Runtime: startup code, PASLIB console glue, generated OS-call stubs,
  and a POSIX layer for picolibc (stdio, malloc, files, time). The heap
  and data live in Lisa data segments.
- Headers (include/lisa/): QuickDraw, events, windows, menus, alerts,
  Filer protocol. They call the Lisa libraries through generated
  register-saving thunks.
- Examples and tests:
  - examples/hellotool is a working desktop tool (launch, draw, menu,
    Set Aside).
  - tests/ holds Workshop console programs.
  - `make test` runs everything in the emulator and compares
    screenshots.
- emu/: scripts that drive gs-headless (Workshop runs, LOS tool
  install/open/close, floppy save).
- AGENTS.md and agent skills (lisa-build, lisa-desktop-tool,
  lisa-emulator).

No Apple software is included. The Lisa ROM and system disks
(media/), the library entry-point table and the reference screenshots
are supplied by the user and kept out of the repository.

events.title: dos32: save states (#77)
events.message:
dos32: save states (#77)

dos32_state_save / dos32_state_load write the whole machine to a file and
back: registers and FPU, the selector, vector and heap tables, the PIC,
PIT, VGA and DAC, the mouse driver, and memory up to the heap top plus
video memory with all-zero pages left out (about 8 MB for Theme Park).

Lifted code is the host's own call stack, so a state loads only where it
was saved: the host names the hook (`where`), and the load also checks the
host stack's depth below dos32_run (stable from run to run, unlike the
address) and the guest stack pointer. Anywhere else it returns -2 and
changes nothing.

events.title: dos32: dos32_mouse_move, the mouse as relative motion (#76)
events.message:
dos32: dos32_mouse_move, the mouse as relative motion (#76)

* dos32: dos32_mouse_move, the mouse as relative motion

The absolute pointer (dos32_mouse) maps the window position onto the
program's range on every event, which overrides whatever the program set
with int 33h AX=04h. Theme Park reads how far the driver's position moved
from where it last put its own cursor, then moves the cursor itself; with
an absolute pointer every host move dragged it back toward the window
position (the cursor drifted while laying paths), and nothing moved past
the window's edge, so edge scrolling barely worked.

dos32_mouse_move takes motion in screen pixels, scales it to the
program's range keeping fractions, and moves from the driver's current
position as a real driver does. Mickeys count the whole motion, clamped
at the edge or not. dos32_mouse switches back to absolute, so scripted
headless clicks are unchanged.
