events.title: Fix trimmed Release APK build in CI (#2)
events.message:
Fix trimmed Release APK build in CI (#2)

* Fix trimmed Release APK build in CI

PublishTrimmed=true (passed on the command line) made the Android build
expect trimmed assemblies under obj/.../linked/shrunk/, but the csproj
hardcoded AndroidLinkMode=None, which disables the _RemoveRegisterAttribute
target that creates that directory. CompressAssemblies then failed with
XACAS7023 (missing linked/shrunk/Microsoft.CSharp.dll).

Make the link-disabling properties conditional on PublishTrimmed so the
Android SDK defaults (AndroidLinkMode=SdkOnly) apply when trimming is
enabled, while local builds (MSB4018, no ILLink) keep trimming off.
Also root Microsoft.CSharp.dll since the app uses the DLR (dynamic) in
Freeserf.Core (Buffer.cs, Savegame.cs).

Co-authored-by: Copilot App <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

* Add RootMode metadata to TrimmerRootAssembly

The Android SDK's ILLink.targets references %(TrimmerRootAssembly.RootMode),
so the item must define it (MSB4096 otherwise).

events.title: fix(gpu): reject idle loops where a late load write-back fired (#811)
events.message:
fix(gpu): reject idle loops where a late load write-back fired (#811)

GPUIdleLoopProbe proves a loop idle by walking its body in program order,
so for `load (rX),rY / moveq #n,rY` it concludes the overwrite wins.
Since #819 the interpreter lets an external load's data land last (JTRM
Rev 8 p.136, TOM bug 13), so for such a loop the dataflow proof describes
a different loop than the one that runs (e.g. a later load whose address
comes from the overwritten register can really hit register space).

Snapshot gpu_load_wb_fixups at S0 and reject (memoised) when it moved by
S2. Cold path, once per probe; the per-instruction loop is untouched.
Same shape as the DSP guard.

Test: gpu_idle_probe_falsify gains a late-load loop that must not fire
(fails on develop, passes here) and a no-overwrite control that must
still fire, so the guard keys on the fix-up, not on external loads.

Refs #811

events.title: ndskit: function discovery, the ARM7's ModuleParams, a Ghidra export
events.message:
ndskit: function discovery, the ARM7's ModuleParams, a Ghidra export

recomp.discover finds the functions of a DS program without symbols. It
reads the program where it runs, in segments (the main block and each
autoload at its destination), and descends ARM and Thumb code with the
mode carried through interworking: veneers and calls through registers
resolved by constants along straight lines, CodeWarrior's addls-pc
switches, hand-written jumps through tables of offsets, returns put in
lr ahead of a jump, conditional transfers with opposite conditions
ending a block, then code pointers, boundaries and prologues as seeds
to a fixed point. On the first port's ARM9 it covers 4 663 of the 4 680
functions Ghidra finds and 749 more, on its ARM7 535 of 536 and 390
more, with no descent meeting data or an undefined instruction on three
cartridges.

rom now finds the ARM7's ModuleParams, which has no footer, by its
shape: the autoload list ends exactly at the program's end.
ghidra/ExportFuncs.java exports Ghidra's functions with their mode for
the comparison.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: release: boot the sealed macOS emulator to its entry stop before shipping
events.message:
release: boot the sealed macOS emulator to its entry stop before shipping

The dmg checks proved the bundle resolves its tools and that hatari loads —
the banner check exercises the exec+dyld path only. A field report of the
0.9.0-alpha dmg showed the bundled fork dying at session start with no
stderr and only 'connection dropped': a failure beyond the banner path that
no step in the workflow could see. The seal step now assembles the demo with
the bundled vasm and boots it under the sealed hatari with the bundled ROM,
waiting for the debugger's entry-stop banner — the earliest state an IDE
session depends on — and naming stderr and stdout if the emulator dies or
never stops.
events.author: idontwantyourspamthanks

events.title: debug: report how the emulator died, not just that it did
events.message:
debug: report how the emulator died, not just that it did

The HRDB transport could end a session with 'The remote-debug connection
dropped' and nothing else: a dying child closes its sockets before QProcess
delivers the exit notification, the EOF handler ran first, and stop()
disconnected QProcess::finished on the way down — the crash that killed the
session never reached the log. A macOS field report of the bundled fork dying
at launch produced exactly that transcript and no diagnosis.

The disconnect handler now waits briefly for the child's exit notification,
so the already-connected finished handler speaks. Both backends report the
cause rather than a bare code: a CrashExit says which signal killed the
emulator, since 'Hatari exited (code -11)' is not a sentence anyone can act
on.

events.title: ndskit: rom, hw, lz, sdat, arm
events.message:
ndskit: rom, hw, lz, sdat, arm

The first modules of a game-agnostic toolkit for Nintendo DS reverse
engineering and static recompilation, born inside its first port and
to be split out into its own repository.

rom reads cartridge images: the header and its CRCs, the secure area's
state, both programs, NitroSDK's ModuleParams through the footer after
the ARM9 (autoloads, static BSS, compression, SDK version), overlay
tables, the FNT/FAT tree, the banner; it extracts the files with a
sys/ directory, undoes the SDK's backward LZ, and opens NitroROM images
kept inside a cartridge as archives (--nested). hw names both CPUs'
address maps and I/O registers. lz decodes the BIOS's LZ77, LZ11 and
RLE. sdat lists and extracts NitroSDK sound archives by their symbols.
arm decodes ARMv5TE/ARMv4T and Thumb into structured instructions
(targets, interworking, writes to pc), disassembles with literals and
register names, and finds who loads an address; against capstone 5 it
disagrees on no ARMv5TE encoding across every Thumb halfword and 1.39
million ARM words.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: fix(blitter): a blit hardware never finishes hangs the blitter, not the host
events.message:
fix(blitter): a blit hardware never finishes hangs the blitter, not the host

Phrase-mode blits below 8bpp never end on hardware.  INNER.NET builds the
inner-counter decrement (Inc0-Inc3) from the 8/16/32bpp decodes, so below
8bpp it is dstxp[0].  Phrase-mode X add truncates to a phrase boundary
(JTRM v8 p.71), so after the first write the counter never moves and
inner0 is never reached.  The synchronous accurate engine reproduced that
faithfully and never returned from retro_run (Music Demo --bios, #794;
Native Demo (bin) HLE).

Policy: hang the emulated blitter, never the host.

- BlitterNeverEnds() (blitter_mmio.c) is the single exact predicate.  The
  accurate engine, the dispatch path and the crash watchdog
  (CrashDetectBlitNeverEnds now delegates to it) all use it.
- The accurate engine runs the stuck step for exactly one destination
  wrap period, then returns.  That is 65536/ppp phrase writes (1024, 2048
  or 4096 at 1/2/4bpp), 65536 with the Y-add bit, +1 when the start X is
  not phrase-aligned.  Bounded at 65,536 writes.  It sets a stop flag only
  after the inner0/mask logic, so no write mask changes.  The collapsed
  pattern-fill and copy paths are bypassed for these blits.
  - The result is EXACT when repeating the step is idempotent on memory.
    Every observed homebrew hang has that shape: DEMO1B $2208, Chroma
    $2704, Native Demo $2718 (LFU clear, no accumulators).
  - Otherwise it is a defined one-pass approximation:
    BlitterNeverEndsApprox() flags Gouraud/Z/shade accumulators,
    comparator masks, ADDDSEL, LFU feeding back D, or LFU fed by a
    separately stepping source (Music Demo, JagMania).  The watchdog line
    now says never_ends=1 approx=1 for those.
- Dispatch then sets a sticky "blitter hung" flag, under both engines.
  - B_CMD status reads busy (JTRM v8 p.75): IDLE clear, outer-INNER and
    inner-DWRITE set, and the stuck inner count in bits 16-31.
  - Further B_CMD starts are ignored, because OUTER.NET leaves idle only
    on go (innert[0] = idle AND go).
  - The flag clears only in BlitterReset (reset / power-on).
  - Known limit: hardware still latches B_COUNT/B_CMD/pointer writes
    mid-blit (FDSYNC on countld/cmdld), so a B_COUNT write with inner 0
    would un-stick it.  JTRM p.70 calls that undefined; this model does
    not resume a hung blit.

Savestate: v16 extended in place, no bump.  A "BLH1" chunk (hung flag and
stuck count, 7 bytes) is appended strictly after #814's CDX1, with a room
check before writing.  It is read only for version >= 16.  A missing or
wrong magic, or an older state, loads as not hung.

Tests:
- test/tools/test_blitter_hung, ROM-free, accurate and fast engines.
  - The synthetic never-ending blit returns.
  - Exactly the 8 KB wrap period is written and the next phrase is
    untouched.
  - Status reads busy with count $DC, and a second start writes nothing.
  - serialize -> retro_reset clears the flag -> unserialize restores it.
- ROM-gated runs of Music Demo --bios and Native Demo (bin): 600 frames
  each, and the blitter ends hung.
- test_crash_detect_inframe gains 10 approx rows.

Closes #794
Refs #800

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: fix(hle): park ILLEGAL for uploaded executables so homebrew stops hanging the accurate blitter
events.message:
fix(hle): park ILLEGAL for uploaded executables so homebrew stops hanging the accurate blitter

Seven homebrew carts froze retro_run under the default (Accurate) blitter.
The blitter was the victim, not the cause:

- Raw BJL binaries and .abs images carry no vector table, and many end
  their 68K main with ILLEGAL (the Alpine/BJL "drop into the debugger"
  idiom; the GPU/OP keep running the demo).  HLE installed RTE stubs only
  for cartridges, and file.c guarded only Alpine/JagServer images, so the
  trap went through a zero vector to $0, ran the vector table as code and
  walked the stack down through $0, $FFxxxx and into TOM.
- There the 68K's own exception frames land on B_COUNT/B_CMD ($F0A238
  reaches $F02238 through TOMWriteWord's $FF3FFF mask): SR becomes B_CMD's
  low word ($2208 = S|IPL2|N for DEMO1B), the pushed PC becomes B_COUNT,
  and the write starts a blit with the zeroed A1 registers -> phrase
  mode, 1bpp, X=0.
- That blit never ends on real hardware either.  INNER.NET's inner-counter
  decrement (Inc0-Inc3) only uses the 8/16/32 bpp decodes beyond bit 0, so
  below 8bpp it is dstxp[0]; phrase-mode X add truncates to a phrase
  boundary (JTRM v8 p.71), so after the first write the counter never
  moves.  BlitterMidsummer2 matches the netlist term for term, which is
  why it spun forever; the Fast engine just shrugs the garbage off.

Fix: JaguarReset parks vector 4 at a BRA.S * loop at $1000 for every
non-cartridge, non-CD image -- the guard file.c already used for Alpine
and JagServer, now re-armed on every reset so retro_reset()'s RAM clear
cannot wipe it.  Only vector 4 is parked; skipped if the image covers the
vector or the loop.  No blitter semantics change, no savestate change.

Also:
- crash_detect: inframe_hang now also fires (never_ends=1) for a blit
  whose inner counter cannot decrement (phrase mode below 8bpp).  DEMO1B's
  blit (14.4M pixels) was under the 2^24 pixel rule and logged nothing.
  The "inner 0 = one step" assumption now cites INNER.NET's zero/underflow
  detect.  CrashDetectNoteBlit takes the destination flags and X.
- cart_boot_matrix.sh: CART_MATRIX_PROBE_ARGS knob so the matrix can sweep
  the Accurate blitter.  Folded into the row-cache id and default log dir,
  and refused without an explicit CART_MATRIX_OUT, so it can never reuse
  or publish over the Fast rows.
- test/tools/test_upload_illegal_park: ROM-free synthetic raw binary that
  ends in ILLEGAL must park at $1000, also after retro_reset (the old core
  hangs on it); plus a ROM-gated DEMO1B run under the Accurate blitter.
  test_crash_detect_inframe gains 11 never_ends rows.

Before/after, Accurate blitter, 600 frames: before, all 7 carts timed out
in HLE (120 s cap) and 6 of 7 in real-BIOS mode (90 s cap; JagMania
(Jul 8) completed); after, all 7 complete in both boot modes.
Chroma-Luma (bin) and JagMania (Jul 8) no longer hang but stay broken:
their raw-binary load address is inferred wrong (a JSR lands in font data
/ mid-instruction), a separate loader bug.

Native Demo (bin) HLE, already broken (68K wild by frame 2, GPU runaway at
frame 1), now takes a different chaotic path that reaches the same
never-ending blit at frame 170, so it hangs under Accurate where it used
to end on a black screen.  That is the #794 class below.

Music Demo (ScatoLOGIC) --bios (#794) is a cartridge in real-BIOS mode,
so this guard does not apply; its hanging blit is the same never-ending
1bpp phrase-mode shape and is now named by never_ends=1.

Closes #800
Refs #794

- src/isr.asm: η πρώτη διακοπή του παιχνιδιού. Αλυσίδα χειριστών στο #0103

  και μηδενισμός του μετρητή του Gate Array στο πάνω σπάσιμο. Τα σπασίματα
  πέφτουν σε κενές γραμμές (15, 176). Κόστος 1.177 us ανά frame, 5,9 % —
  εκτιμήθηκε 3,8 % πριν μετρηθεί.
- is_on: μετά από μακρύ di (δίσκος) περιμένει το VSYNC και ξεκινά την
  αλυσίδα στο βήμα· με σκέτο ei οι λωρίδες έμεναν στραβές ως δύο frames.
  Ο δίσκος κλείνει τις διακοπές, σβήνει τις λωρίδες και δείχνει Mode 0.
- src/hud.asm: γλύφος ένα byte ανά γραμμή, 80 στήλες, οι πέντε λογικές
  σειρές στις λωρίδες· τα κελιά της μπάρας είναι γλύφοι (η άδεια μπάρα
  περίγραμμα). hud_move: οι λωρίδες ΜΕΤΑΚΙΝΟΥΝΤΑΙ με το δαχτυλίδι σε κάθε

  και δεν μένουν πια σκουπίδια μετά από σκρολάρισμα — ούτε σε παύση, που ως
  τώρα τα κρατούσε για πάντα.
- tools/pack.py: font_m1 (808 bytes, η γραμματοσειρά σε Mode 1 και τα κελιά

- tests/test_split.py: κάθε pixel της εικόνας απέναντι στη μνήμη με το mode

Ο κώδικας του βρόχου, το hud_draw, το ui_panel και το βήμα κάμερας δεν

events.title: perf(rpi4): zero-copy native frames and faster AGA Denise line drawing (#2385)
events.message:
perf(rpi4): zero-copy native frames and faster AGA Denise line drawing (#2385)

* perf(rpi4): zero-copy native frames and faster AGA Denise line drawing

On Linux the native chipset surface is now a CPU-cached dma-buf that the
OpenGL renderer imports once as an EGLImage and samples directly, instead
of uploading the frame with glTexSubImage2D every vsync (about 1.4 ms of
main-thread CPU per hires frame on a Pi 4). Ownership moves with
DMA_BUF_IOCTL_SYNC: present drains the Denise queue and ends CPU access,
and frame writers reclaim the buffer before writing, so the GPU read
overlaps emulation. Any allocation, import or sync failure falls back to
texture uploads; other platforms are unchanged.

checkhorizontal1_aga() runs twice per CCK in every AGA line renderer. A
table-driven fast reject (Amiberry-guarded, exact for every counter
value) skips the compare chain at positions with no horizontal event,
and the wrapper is forced inline.

Jim Power A1200 title (AGA, cycle-exact memory) on a Pi 4 at 2.2 GHz:
41.7 -> 44.0 FPS.

* perf(denise): fast-reject OCS/ECS horizontal checks

checkhorizontal1_ecs() runs twice per CCK in every OCS/ECS line
renderer. Reuse the horizontal-event tables from the AGA fast reject:
positions with no horizontal event, burst edge or pending unaligned work
skip the compare chain and keep only the per-call csync delay. Counters
outside the tables take the full chain, so the result is identical.

Jim Power A500 title (OCS, cycle-exact) on a Pi 4: Denise thread
12.64 -> 12.07 ms per frame.

events.title: Fix Github deployment bug.
events.message:
Fix Github deployment bug.

The site broke in this morning's commit, "Fix multiple emulator bug". That commit updated `index.html` to load a new main file, `js/app.56ab902f.js`, deleted the old one, and never added the new one. Everything that kept its name updated fine. You're right that it was serving correctly before: the merge commit `b2762a0` just before it had everything.

That's what `git commit -a` (or `git add -u`, or "commit tracked files" in an editor) does. It commits changes and deletions to files git already knows about, but never adds new files. The build gives the main JavaScript file and its stylesheet a new name each time. That can happen even when the code hasn't changed: I rebuilt identical code and got a new name.

**To fix the live site now**, nothing new is needed. The file is in your local `docs/`, just not committed:

sh

```
git add -A docs
git commit -m "Add the missing app bundle"
git push
```

**To stop it happening again**, copy these from `sms-game-designer-src.zip` into the repository:

-   **`npm run build:docs`** builds straight into `docs/`, runs `git add -A docs` for you, then checks the result.
-   **`tools/check-site.mjs`** works out every file the editor will load and fails, by name, on anything missing. That includes files `index.html` never mentions, like the compiler worker and the examples. Inside a git repository it also lists files git doesn't know about yet, and gives the command that fixes it.
-   **`.github/workflows/check-site.yml`** runs that check on every push, so a broken `docs/` shows a red ✗ on the commit. One limit: GitHub Pages will still publish the broken version. The ✗ is a warning, not a block.
-   **`.gitattributes`** tells git to store `docs/` exactly as built. Git had been changing the line endings of one emulator translation file. That was harmless, but it no longer matched the emulator's file list.

I ran the checker against all four real deployments in your history. It got every one right --- working, broken, working, broken --- and also found the missing stylesheet I'd overlooked. I also reproduced the `git commit -a` problem in a test repository. Run before committing, the checker named the missing file and the fix.

The console noise isn't the editor. The `unload` policy violations come from browser extensions --- your stack traces name their scripts --- and the emulator wasn't running anyway, since the main file was missing.

**`sms-game-designer-editor.zip`** is a fresh build. It has a new main file, `app.5459f0e2.js`, and the corrected translation file. If you deploy it, replace `docs/` with its contents and run `git add -A docs` before committing. I tested exactly that in a scratch repository and it passed. The full test suite is at 298 passing.

events.title: fix(m68k): model the prefetch queue for self-modifying code
events.message:
fix(m68k): model the prefetch queue for self-modifying code

The 68000 holds the two instruction words after the one it is executing.
A write to a word already in that queue does not change what runs next;
the CPU executes the stale copy.  Xenowings' anti-tamper check depends on
it: `ori.l #$04000400,(a1)` turns the next two `addq.l #1,d6` into
`addq.l #3,d6`, and the check (d6 == $12071971) only passes if the old
pair runs.  This core fetched every word straight from memory, so d6
ended at $12071975 and the game jumped back to its loader a few frames
into gameplay (#811).

Model only what the queue makes observable, at no cost on the fetch path:

- The main-RAM write paths compare the address against a 32-byte window
  around regs.pc; on a hit, M68KPrefetchSnoop() records the word as it
  was before the write.
- At the next dispatch, the recorded words the queue really held are kept
  and swapped back into RAM for exactly that one instruction, then
  restored.  A stale IRC word survives to the following dispatch only
  when the instruction was one word long and did not branch.  The slow
  path is out of line so m68k_execute's loop keeps its size.
- Which words are queued depends on the bus-cycle order.  The
  read-modify-write forms, MOVE to -(An), PEA (An) and ADDX/SUBX -(An)
  prefetch before writing (next_pc and next_pc+2 queued).  MOVE to any
  other destination, MOVEM, MOVEP, LINK and the other PEA modes write
  first (next_pc only).  The order comes from Clock Signal's
  microcode-derived 68000 (TomHarte/CLK 68000Implementation.hpp:
  Perform_np, MOVE_bw, MOVEMtoM, LINKw, MOVEPtoM), not from the generated
  handlers, whose fill_prefetch placement is wrong for MOVE.
- Exceptions, interrupts, reset and an external PC change flush the
  queue.
- Queued words go into savestates through regs.prefetch_pc and
  regs.prefetch, which were always serialized and never used.  Old
  states load as "nothing queued", and STATE_VERSION is unchanged.

test/test_m68k_prefetch is ROM-free.  It covers both bus-order classes
(MOVE.W onto next_pc is stale, onto next_pc+2 is fresh; ORI.W onto
next_pc+2 is stale), a branch away and back, a second pass through patched
code, a data read of a patched word, and a savestate taken with words
queued.  On the old core it fails 5 of 9 checks.
xenowings_ingame_video now requires 600 consecutive lit gameplay frames
and no return to the loader.  The old core gives a streak of 2 and 10
returns to the loader; this change gives a streak of 990 and none.

events.title: refactor(quickdraw): share region-row algebra and oval/round-rect spans (#4188)
events.message:
refactor(quickdraw): share region-row algebra and oval/round-rect spans (#4188)

Start the shared QuickDraw raster module (quickdraw/raster/) described in
issue #4182, milestone M0a. This is a pure extraction: no output changes.

region_rows.rs takes the scanline interval operations that the 68K trap
path held as TrapDispatcher associated functions: endpoints_to_intervals,
intervals_to_endpoints, the merge-based intersection, union, difference,
xor, combine, inset, merge_endpoints (applying one inversion-point list),
endpoints_contain_point and the coordinate clamp, plus RegionBooleanOp.
The 68K call sites keep #[inline] shims, RegionBooleanOp is re-exported
from trap/quickdraw.rs, and the 68K picture parser's identical copy of
merge_region_endpoints now imports the shared one.

spans.rs takes compute_oval_spans and compute_rrect_spans from
trap/shapes.rs. TrapDispatcher keeps #[inline] shims, so the 68K shape
code and the PowerPC callers (oval drawing, OpenRgn recording, dialog
round-rect outlines) are unchanged.

The PowerPC region code now takes merge_endpoints,
endpoints_to_intervals, intervals_to_endpoints, union, difference and
xor from the shared module under their old ppc_region_* names; each
computed the same result as its 68K counterpart. PowerPC intersection
stays all-pairs: its callers intersect rows parsed from guest region
storage, which are not guaranteed to be sorted, and on unsorted rows the
68K merge pass can drop pieces. Each side keeps its own region parser
and malformed-region policy.

Tests keep the replaced 68K and PowerPC functions as references and
compare them with the shared code: 50,000 random row pairs per property
(arbitrary rows, including odd lengths, unordered and inverted pairs and
extreme coordinates) plus hand-picked empty, single-point, touching,

events.title: fix(devtools): Registers window corrupted a paused machine; settle the inject test with step frame (#68)
events.message:
fix(devtools): Registers window corrupted a paused machine; settle the inject test with step frame (#68)

* test(e2e): settle the inject key test with step frame, not wait vbl

beads-27a7. test_inject_launches_like_run lost its key ~2-7% of the time,
locally as well as on CI: the injected program sat in KM READ CHAR with the
key never delivered.

The cause is a real emulator bug, filed as beads-vwwq. A pause/resume about
3 s after a breakpoint stop corrupts the machine in ~2% of runs: the firmware
key-buffer counter (&B688) ends one above its contents, so KM READ KEY pops
a blank slot and spins forever at &1CF3. The test hit it because `wait vbl 50`
is a wall-clock sleep (beads-71pg) that resumes, runs ~3.3 s (~150 frames)
and pauses, right after `wait pc` stopped on a breakpoint.

`step frame 50` runs exactly the 50 frames the comment asks for, and a pause
that early is clean: 0/200 here, against 2/100 with wait vbl in the same
setup. The corruption itself stays open as beads-vwwq (P1).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_016V4AeC4Vf5ZDaApCT2LKFp

* fix(devtools): Registers window pushed registers to the machine every paused frame

beads-vwwq, the root cause behind the beads-27a7 e2e flake.

While the machine was paused, the Registers window rebuilt F from its
checkboxes and called subcycle_bridge_regs_to_machine() on every rendered
frame, edited or not. That is z80_poke(): it rewrites every register from the
host mirror AND restarts the CPU at a fresh instruction boundary. A pause
parks the board mid-instruction, so each paused frame silently dropped the
rest of the instruction in flight.

Traced with a watchpoint plus instruction trace: the firmware kernel's
PUSH BC at &B99E moved SP by one instead of two. The kernel's later POP BC
then lost its saved Gate Array port (&7Fxx became &03BB), and the next
ROM-switch OUT (C),C at &B9B2 hit &03xx, the PPI control register. Setting
port C bits made the AY keyboard read return &00 for every row, so the scan
pushed phantom keys (CTRL+SHIFT+cursor), and KM READ KEY could pop a blank
slot and spin forever at &1CF3.

A breakpoint stop opens DevTools, and SDL_VIDEODRIVER=dummy still runs the
GUI build with its render thread, so the e2e harness hit this whenever a
test paused after a breakpoint.

The window now pushes only when a field or flag actually changed.

- New unit test: a PUSH BC ROM parked mid-instruction, the paused window
  rendered over 20 frames; SP must stay odd. It fails at frame 0 without
  the fix.
- Before/after on the e2e sequence (Faithful, 7 parallel): pause at 1.0 s
  19/50 -> 0/50 failed; at 2.0 s 29/50 -> 0/100; original wait-vbl sequence
  ~2% -> 0/200.
- AGENTS.md: the dummy video driver does NOT mean headless.
- The inject test keeps `step frame 50` (wait vbl is a wall-clock sleep,
  beads-71pg) and its comment now records the cause as fixed.

Deliberate edits still poke mid-instruction; filed as beads-3yl2.

events.title: fix(dsp): late write-back of external loads (JTRM JERRY bug 13)
events.message:
fix(dsp): late write-back of external loads (JTRM JERRY bug 13)

DSP side of the GPU fix (#819): JTRM Rev 8 p.136 bug 13 'applies to both
Tom & Jerry'.  Xenowings' DSP joypad reader does load (r0=$F14000),r1 /
moveq #0,r1 at F1BBA0; on silicon the load data lands last, so r1 holds
the joypad row.  This core let the moveq win and r1 was always 0.

Same one-instruction model as GPUExec: the instruction immediately after
an external load writes the load's target without reading it and is not
a load/store.  External = outside F1A000-F1DFFF (JTRM p.98).  The armed
state lives in DSPExec locals and the loop runs that one instruction past
its budget, so nothing outlives a slice and no savestate change is
needed.  Test-ABI counter dsp_load_wb_fixups counts applications.

The idle-loop fast-forward rejects a loop in which the fix-up fired
during its probe: its dataflow proof orders the overwrite last.

Measured against the GPU-only baseline: fires only in Xenowings (one
site, F1BBA2 / EA F14000); 0 fires in 298 matrix runs and 148 3000-frame
input-driven runs of the rest of the corpus.  Frame hashes, 68K PCs and
audio (WAV md5) are identical to the baseline.

Refs #811

events.title: od-unix: initialize shared memory slots once at startup
events.message:
od-unix: initialize shared memory slots once at startup

Unix calls init_shm() without first calling preinit_shm(). Removing
clear_shmids() from the reset path left the slot table zero-initialized.
Cleanup recognizes only slot zero in that state, so rtarea consumes the
only available slot and later ROM allocations fall back to untracked
memory without ROM protection.

Call preinit_shm() from init_shm() and guard table initialization with a
static flag. This makes every slot available at startup while preserving
the live UAE Boot ROM allocation and its bookkeeping across resets.
events.author: reinauer

events.title: unix: honor gfx_vsync and disable vsync during warp mode
events.message:
unix: honor gfx_vsync and disable vsync during warp mode

Both SDL3 presentation paths hardcoded vsync on at renderer/context
creation (SDL_SetRenderVSync(renderer, 1) and
SDL_GL_SetSwapInterval(1)),
regardless of the gfx_vsync prefs setting or turbo_emulation. Since the
main emulation loop presents synchronously on the same thread in the
common case, every shown frame blocked for up to one host refresh
interval, capping overall throughput at roughly the display refresh
rate no matter how fast frames were actually produced. This defeated
warp mode (only marginally faster than realtime) and ignored an
explicit gfx_vsync=false config.

Track the desired swap interval dynamically from currprefs instead:
follow gfx_apmode[APMODE_NATIVE].gfx_vsync when not in turbo mode, but
always disable vsync while turbo_emulation is active so warp mode is
never refresh-rate limited.

(cherry picked from commit 2a9a3568872b7907750d9cdaef6661e2b62818f9)
events.author: Graham Bates

events.title: od-unix: preserve loaded ROM allocations across resets
events.message:
od-unix: preserve loaded ROM allocations across resets

init_shm() runs on every device reset, but the core reloads ROMs only
when its reload conditions are met. Freeing tracked ROM allocations
there leaves Kickstart missing, so kickmem_init() replaces it with
zero-filled memory and the guest fails to boot. Preserving only rtarea
leaves Kickstart and extended ROMs exposed to the same lifetime bug.

Keep allocations and their protection records intact in init_shm().
Leave release to mapped_free() when the core replaces a bank and to
free_shm() at shutdown. Remove the now-unused keep-bank exception from
the shutdown cleanup helper.
events.author: reinauer

events.title: unix: preserve per-frame vsync and reset backend state

Developer page: logs (debug + snoop), tasks, run, screens - in the app

Everything the terminal's debug/snoop/ps/kill/run/screen do, in the
desktop app and Wasabi phone:

- Logs: wasabi_logs.LogHub holds ONE subscription per stream (the
  daemon gives each to one listener) and shares it with every open
  window, starting with the first and stopping after the last; late
  windows get the last 2000 lines. Lines dressed as in the terminal and
  tagged (Wasabi's own, routine noise) so the page hides them by tick
  box; snoop task filter and entry logging; find, pause, clear, save.
  A terminal holding a stream is reported, and retried.
- Tasks (ps with headroom, Ctrl-C / Remove after a warning), Run (live
  output over /ws/run, return code, time limit, Stop = Ctrl-C), Screens
  (list, bring to front).

Fixed on the way: in a browser, wasabi desktop counted its window only
while the live Screen page ran, so leaving Screen for Overview ended the
program 5 s later with the window still open (tests ran with --stay and
missed it). The app now keeps /ws/hello open for its whole life, and
only that counts; a new offline test holds it.

Also: the log's mono font token pointed at a Radix variable that only
exists inside .radix-themes - tokens now carry real values.

Tested on the A1200 (test/developer.mjs: streams on, snoop lines,
tasks, a run with output and code, screens, Logs kept while away), at
phone size, and offline (171 pass).

project.display_title: Wizardry I–III: direct Go terminal recreation
subjects: Wizardry: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord
Wizardry II: The Knight of Diamonds
types: Apple II-origin game reconstruction or remake
project.status: Game implementation source reviewed; independent build and gameplay unverified
project.notes: Identity: One shared Go engine embeds three Wizardry scenarios. Reviewed game.go provides dungeon position, walls, movement and encounter state; combat.go directly implements party/monster actions, spells, rewards and traps. Classification: Direct reimplementation with binary/source-analysis-informed behavior. Although README labels it clean-room, source comments and recent fixes explicitly trace Pascal routine names and p-code addresses. This review does not endorse a strict clean-room claim. The DSK reader imports legacy character data, rather than executing an Apple II CPU. Source CPU: The implementation cites Pascal and UCSD p-code routines, including COMBAT2 and CINIT, but this is not an inspected 6502/65C02 machine-code build. No physical input ISA is assigned. Target CPU: The new implementation targets a modern language runtime, with no fixed host instruction set declared in the reviewed build or entry point. target_cpu remains empty rather than inheriting an Apple II processor. Build: Go module declares Go 1.24.0 and toolchain 1.24.4; Makefile builds cmd/wizardry. JSON scenarios, messages, monster/title material and a title bitmap are embedded. Author claims all scenarios are playable; that is not an independent result. Limitations: Static research only: no candidate compilation, execution, gameplay, hardware test or binary comparison was performed. All independent build/runtime verification flags remain null. Runtime profiles: Terminal rendering uses Unicode with optional Sixel and NTSC-style artifact colors; save files are scenario-specific under the user configuration directory. No modern machine RAM minimum or original Apple model minimum is established. AI: No explicit development-AI attribution was found in the inspected documentation, source and 20 most recent available commit messages (request capped at 20). This bounded negative finding does not establish non-use; gameplay opponent AI is not development attribution. Relationships: This is one trilogy implementation, not three separate projects. MIT licenses the repository code, but README’s assertion that no copyrighted material is embedded conflicts with its original-artwork description, embedded title/monster data, and a commit describing re-extraction of monster images. Original-derived asset rights remain unresolved; no blanket rights-clearance claim is made. Normalized root, title aliases and code lineage were screened against the current 1,833-project catalogue, source/decision indexes and 2,249-root prior-review union before primary inspection; no same implementation was found. Evidence: https://github.com/sshoecraft/wizardry/blob/39faa42d05356aadd915c23330d8f1e0292845d6/README.md https://github.com/sshoecraft/wizardry/blob/39faa42d05356aadd915c23330d8f1e0292845d6/engine/game.go https://github.com/sshoecraft/wizardry/blob/39faa42d05356aadd915c23330d8f1e0292845d6/engine/combat.go https://github.com/sshoecraft/wizardry/blob/39faa42d05356aadd915c23330d8f1e0292845d6/scenarios/wiz1/scenario.go https://github.com/sshoecraft/wizardry/blob/39faa42d05356aadd915c23330d8f1e0292845d6/engine/dsk.go https://github.com/sshoecraft/wizardry/blob/39faa42d05356aadd915c23330d8f1e0292845d6/go.mod https://github.com/sshoecraft/wizardry/blob/39faa42d05356aadd915c23330d8f1e0292845d6/Makefile https://github.com/sshoecraft/wizardry/blob/39faa42d05356aadd915c23330d8f1e0292845d6/LICENSE https://github.com/sshoecraft/wizardry/commit/04ad7eebc5a5f25a0aa5dc2a99de2796e5d3ae0d

project.notes: Identity: The original programmer identifies Totally as his unfinished-but-playable 1983 high-school side shooter. TOTALLY.S contains the actual player, missile, enemy, fuel/lives, collision, boss-stage and high-score state paths, rather than only a launcher. Classification: This is a source reconstruction from the author’s hand-entered machine code, assisted by SourceGen, not an intact original assembly listing. Unused gaps and patch chains were removed; DOS 3.3 raw-sector high scores were replaced with ProDOS file I/O; another 16 enemy images came from the author’s unfinished SEU project. Source CPU: README explicitly identifies the original hand-entered 6502 opcodes. The recovered game uses the 8-bit A/X/Y register set, zero-page pointers and Apple II keyboard, speaker, HGR and paddle soft switches. No native IIgs 65816 source is evidenced. Target CPU: The restoration emits Merlin-format 6502 code for Apple II, packaged as a ProDOS .SYSTEM. The browser-play link loads a disk image into Apple2TS; it is not a JavaScript gameplay rewrite or a separate native host-CPU port. Build: The inspected Python builder invokes Merlin32 and CiderPress II to assemble source and create Totally_Release.po. It can download Merlin32 when missing; prerequisites and paths remain environment-dependent. The maintained source intentionally differs from the historical binary through layout, I/O and content changes, so no byte-exact-original claim is made. Limitations: Static source review only. No candidate source or build script was executed, installed, assembled, launched, played, hardware-tested or byte-compared. All independent build flags remain null. Runtime profiles: ProDOS, Apple II high-resolution graphics and keyboard/joystick controls are directly supported by README and soft-switch accesses. The historic DOS 3.3 design and restored ProDOS build are distinct. No inspected statement establishes exact hardware/RAM or OS-version minima. AI: The inspected README, selected implementation/build files and first page of 10 recent default-branch commits contain no explicit development-AI disclosure. Gameplay enemy behavior is not evidence of generative-AI development. The bounded history sample and source inspection cannot establish non-use; usage remains unknown. Relationships: Root and normalized-title checks found no prior reviewed record. SEU is an acknowledged source of additional enemy art, not a second promoted project. It is substantive partial game code, not a full Apple II version of all A Dark Room mechanics; README itself calls space integration future work. Source CPU: README explicitly identifies the original as browser JavaScript and contrasts DOM/event-driven logic with the C port. No particular original physical CPU is established or required by that implementation; source_cpu remains empty. Target CPU: README explicitly states a MOS 6502 target via cc65 and the Makefile passes -t apple2 with a custom raw linker configuration. That direct target declaration supports 6502; no 65C02-only or IIgs-native output is claimed. Build: Makefile compiles main.c, logic.c and ui.c using cl65/apple2-raw.cfg. README documents DOS 3.3 disk insertion with AppleCommander and BRUN. The repository includes a blank disk and ac.jar, but the latest history removed the generated binary and no build/runtime check was done. Limitations: No candidate compilation, testing, launch, gameplay or byte comparison was performed. All four independent build flags remain null. Runtime profiles: 40-column Apple II text UI with conio keyboard polling and a realtime tick loop. README targets bare-metal/DOS 3.3 loading; no minimum RAM, Apple II subtype or reliable timing floor is established by this static sample. AI: No explicit development-AI disclosure was found in the inspected README, implementation/build sample, any available rights files, and the first 6 available default-branch commit messages (request cap 20). This bounded negative result does not prove non-use. Gameplay logic, assistant filenames, and repository age are not attribution evidence. Relationships: The linked doublespeakgames/adarkroom is the browser predecessor, while this is a distinct C/Apple II implementation. Root LICENSE is MIT, copyright 2026 Taciano Dreckmann Perez; that notice is not treated as clearing all inherited text/design or bundled tool/disk components. Six available commits plus a ten-result-cap AI query contained no explicit AI attribution; GEMINI.md filename alone is not evidence of use. The normalized root, title/alias and lineage screen found no same-code project in the 1,833-project baseline or expanded 2,249-root prior-review union. test(gpu): ROM-gated Xenowings in-game video check (#811)

State-driven: wait for the 652-wide main menu, press B, wait for the
LOADING MISSION DATA screen, then require a lit 326-wide playfield
frame within 900 frames. Fails on develop (every gameplay frame black,
best 1.1% lit), passes with the bug-13 late write-back (94% lit).

Only a handful of gameplay frames render today: a 68K self-modifying
integrity check at $350C needs the 68000 instruction prefetch, which
the core does not model, and sends the game back to its loader. The
check says so and is meant to be tightened once that lands.

events.title: fix(gpu): late write-back of external loads (JTRM TOM bug 13)
events.message:
fix(gpu): late write-back of external loads (JTRM TOM bug 13)

JTRM Rev 8 p.35: no score-board protection applies to writes, and an
external load's data is not written to its target register until the
transfer completes. p.136 (TOM/JERRY bug 13, 'Scoreboard failure on
successive writes') gives the consequence: after

    load  (r3),r2
    moveq 3,r2

the load data lands in r2 AFTER the moveq. This core wrote load data
immediately, so the second write won.

Xenowings (#811) swaps its object-list double buffer on the GPU with
load (r0),r2 / moveq #0,r2 / ... / store r2,(OLP): OLP got 0, the OP
walked the STOP object at $000000 every field, the GPU never got its
GPU-object interrupt, and in-game video stayed black.

Model the unambiguous case: the instruction immediately after an
external (non-local-bus) load writes the load's target without reading
it and is not a load/store; the load value is re-applied after it.
The armed state lives in GPUExec locals and the loop runs that one
instruction past its budget, so nothing outlives a slice and no
savestate change is needed. Test-ABI counter gpu_load_wb_fixups counts
applications.

Refs #811

project.status: Upstream reports multiple running targets; Atari MiNT compiles and runs but is too slow to be playable.
project.notes: Original tile-board game with complete C sources and Make/CMake build paths using SDL, SDL_image and SDL_mixer. Primary README explicitly lists Atari MiNT as a compiled and running target. Upstream explicitly says the Atari MiNT version is too slow to be playable. Target is MiNT with SDL, not an unqualified plain TOS/ST release. Atari build requires Makefile/toolchain adjustment. README explicitly calls Atari MiNT compilable and running but too slow to be playable. Other platforms are reported running. Global playable is left unknown because a single boolean cannot faithfully represent the MiNT exception; notes preserve it. No independent compilation, execution or benchmarking was performed during this catalogue review. project.title: Notegame — original Amiga music-symbol game and editor
project.display_title: Notegame — original Amiga music-symbol game and editor
project.status: Substantive source reviewed; build, runtime and binary parity independently untested
project.notes: The authors’ preserved 1994–95 Blitz Basic music-note identification game for Amiga, with an executable, original tokenized source, readable text exports and game-definition tooling. The 1,516-line Aikaar_V0.26.txt contains dated 1994–95 development notes and a v0.26 identifier dated 13 September 1995. Substantive inspected code covers requester-based player input, randomised symbol/question order, correct/incorrect answer handling, elapsed time, result history and score-file persistence. At source lines 747–776 randomlist separately shuffles SymbolOrder and AskingOrder and builds gadgets. Lines 997–1067 contain the event loop, sound/error feedback and timer updates; newhit records result data and saves scores at completion. The companion 569-line TeePeliTP.txt is a game-definition editor: it assigns textual names to selectable symbols and writes a .GAME definition beside a graphics file. Keep the related editor and test programs inside one game record. README describes the original Amiga 1200 / Blitz Basic 2 v2.10 / SuperTED v2.52 environment and current Aika: assignment and launch instructions. A prebuilt Aika-arvot executable, .GAME/.GFX data, IFF resources and fonts are present in the tree. README reports permission from co-author Tapio Pärepalo to release the Amiga game as open source in July 2023; LICENSE grants MIT rights for Lauri Ojansivu and Tapio Pärepalo. The September 2024 changelog and inspected conversion commit document exporting tokenized .bb2 source through AmiBlitz3 and converting Scandinavian characters to UTF-8. Historical comments intend compatibility with Kickstart 1.3 and 2.x and use ReqTools requesters; this is an upstream intent claim, not an independently verified OS support matrix. Development on Amiga 1200 does not establish an AGA-only or 68020-only minimum. The inspected GUI uses a 640x256, three-bitplane, high-resolution non-interlaced screen; minimum CPU and RAM remain unspecified. The repository bundles third-party-looking Amiga system binaries, reqtools.library and fonts. The authors’ MIT notice should not be treated as verified relicensing of every bundled dependency. Readable .txt files are converted exports alongside original tokenized .bb2 files. No compilation, detokenization-equivalence check, executable comparison or runtime test was performed. README’s mention of other Blitz variants on Windows/Linux/Mac does not demonstrate a port of this game; only the canonical Amiga source and target platform are proposed. Changelog labels early releases with June 2023 dates while README describes a July 2023 permission event; preserve the documented dates without constructing a more precise release/permission chronology. Original 1994–95 Blitz Basic game/editor sources are readable text exports, with tokenized originals and a runnable executable retained. events.message: notes: The authors’ preserved 1994–95 Blitz Basic music-note identification game for Amiga, with an executable, original tokenized source, readable text exports and game-definition tooling. The 1,516-line Aikaar_V0.26.txt contains dated 1994–95 development notes and a v0.26 identifier dated 13 September 1995. Substantive inspected code covers requester-based player input, randomised symbol/question order, correct/incorrect answer handling, elapsed time, result history and score-file persistence. At source lines 747–776 randomlist separately shuffles SymbolOrder and AskingOrder and builds gadgets. Lines 997–1067 contain the event loop, sound/error feedback and timer updates; newhit records result data and saves scores at completion. The companion 569-line TeePeliTP.txt is a game-definition editor: it assigns textual names to selectable symbols and writes a .GAME definition beside a graphics file. Keep the related editor and test programs inside one game record. README describes the original Amiga 1200 / Blitz Basic 2 v2.10 / SuperTED v2.52 environment and current Aika: assignment and launch instructions. project.status: Substantive source reviewed; build, runtime and binary parity independently untested
project.notes: A substantial native Blitz Basic tile-pair puzzle begun in 1992 and completed in 2020, with editable source, assets and disk/file releases. The 6,446-line editable source implements boot/resource loading, level selection and tutorials, tile validation, pathfinding, tile removal, end-of-level state, score persistence and autoplay; it is a complete game implementation rather than a rendering example. At source lines 1722–1755, xy2calc validates the old and new tiles, checks matching identity, invokes Pathfinder, removes the pair and checks the remaining matrix. Lines 1804–1843 distinguish blocked/empty cells, matching tiles, wildcard tiles and the dice reshuffle case. Level-selection logic uses embedded 8x8 tile matrices; source lines 5816 onward contain level data. SaveScores and LoadScores implement Score.sav persistence at lines 4075–4168. The manual explains two-turn connecting paths, timing penalties and saved progression. README documents Blitz 2 v2.1, SuperTed 2.24 and CIATrkrLib. Compiler object limits are explicitly supplied in Blitz2CompilerOptions.txt; the editable plain-text VSC source is distinguished from the generated Amiga/SuperTed representation. README/manual record the 1992 concept, 1996 continuation, June 2020 completion and October 2025 bugfix; latest commits are October 3, 2025. The manual credits ISK with the original Stone concept and Bonefish with a third-party cracktro whose source is not included. Source-available, not open source: README reserves rights and forbids redistribution, quotation or sale without written permission; asset notices also prohibit unauthorised music/graphics redistribution and preservation-site uploads. Catalogue with links and paraphrased findings, not copied source/assets. Editable source loads gfx/StoneSet.2020 at line 40, while the recursive tree contains gfx/Stoneset.2025 and no StoneSet.2020. This is a checked-in source/asset filename mismatch; no build or packaged-release execution was attempted, so its runtime effect is unverified. Build instructions describe Amiga OS 3.0 for the development setup. The separately stated game minimum is Kickstart 2.0 with 1 MB Chip RAM; these are not interchangeable requirements. README says designed for stock Amiga 500+ and 1200, and the manual explicitly describes an ECS A500+. No AGA-only requirement or universal compatibility with unexpanded A500 hardware is established. The third-party executable cracktro in the ADF release is not included as source. Release archives and the generated/tokenized Amiga source were not opened or tested. Substantial editable original Blitz Basic source is preserved, with 1992 concept and later development history. The checked-in release archive contains an AmigaOS Hunk executable, directly establishing the broad m68k source/output family. No narrower processor model is inferred from A500+/A1200 labels; A1200 development does not prove an AGA-only or 68020-only minimum. Build requires Blitz 2 v2.1, SuperTed 2.24 and CIATrkrLib with supplied compiler limits. Editable source loads gfx/StoneSet.2020 while the tree supplies gfx/Stoneset.2025. Runtime consequences were not tested. OS 3.0 is a development environment, not the game minimum. Manual states 1 MB Chip RAM and Kickstart 2.0. A500+ ECS and A1200 are upstream design targets, not a separately tested all-Amiga compatibility matrix. Development OS 3.0 requirement is distinct. No build/runtime test. Original title based on ISK Stone concept, not another count for its source representations or third-party cracktro. All-rights-reserved/non-redistribution source and asset notices are explicit. Catalogue links/paraphrases only; no broad rights grant or generative-AI usage inferred from a hypothetical future-AI-remake comment. License/asset review: Explicit all-rights-reserved/non-redistribution notices in README and asset readmes; GitHub reports no recognised license. Freeware runtime distribution is not an open-source grant. No explicit generative-AI usage attribution found. Manual suggests that someone could use AI for a future remake after 2045; that hypothetical is not evidence that the checked-in game used AI. Latest ten commits and selected source/readmes inspected. Source snapshot: commit 4fa00f788204a6c71983779df0d3bf0b45967af9; actual root Git tree 296689e25cf2702149748a28eae3baef1d9a845a verified through https://api.github.com/repos/wertstahl/blitzways/git/commits/4fa00f788204a6c71983779df0d3bf0b45967af9. All build flags remain null; no candidate was compiled, run, emulated or byte-compared. Repository creation and release dates do not establish a reverse-engineering start date. Evidence: https://github.com/wertstahl/blitzways/blob/4fa00f788204a6c71983779df0d3bf0b45967af9/README.md https://github.com/wertstahl/blitzways/blob/4fa00f788204a6c71983779df0d3bf0b45967af9/Manual.readme https://github.com/wertstahl/blitzways/blob/4fa00f788204a6c71983779df0d3bf0b45967af9/src/VisualStudioCodeSrc/Ways1.30.VSC.bb2 https://github.com/wertstahl/blitzways/blob/4fa00f788204a6c71983779df0d3bf0b45967af9/Blitz2CompilerOptions.txt https://github.com/wertstahl/blitzways/blob/4fa00f788204a6c71983779df0d3bf0b45967af9/extra/extra.readme https://github.com/wertstahl/blitzways/blob/4fa00f788204a6c71983779df0d3bf0b45967af9/extra/unused/copyright.readme https://api.github.com/repos/wertstahl/blitzways https://github.com/wertstahl/blitzways/commit/4fa00f788204a6c71983779df0d3bf0b45967af9 https://api.github.com/repos/wertstahl/blitzways/git/commits/4fa00f788204a6c71983779df0d3bf0b45967af9 CPU audit: original and output architecture are recorded as broad m68k from the documented Amiga Blitz source and stock A500+/A1200 release path; no narrower processor minimum is inferred.

project.status: v1.7.0 source SDK released; upstream-qualified Mode 7 fast profile, no independent or physical-hardware verification
project.notes: Source SDK for eight C64 graphics modes: polygon rendering and a distinct Mode 8 2.5D DDA bitmap renderer. PowerShell/Python scene builder emits 6510/6502 assembly for 64tass; example JSON and guides are included. Mode 8 has no wall UV textures or room-over-room, and is not the historical character-cell renderer. Upstream qualifies stock VICE x64sc; real hardware has not been tested. Code/data are PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0. The repository documents Codex-assisted use of the SDK, not independently verified AI authorship of the engine. v1.7.0 adds an opt-in Mode 7 Q8 fast profile with eight-pixel projective blocks, alternate logical-row sampling and upper-row reconstruction; standard remains the default. Upstream's Turbo6510 64 MHz figures are scene-specific emulator measurements, and physical hardware remains unqualified.

events.title: Fix disk-type tagging bugs in the HDD disk library, add a SCSI catalog entry
events.message:
Fix disk-type tagging bugs in the HDD disk library, add a SCSI catalog entry

Three copy paths into the browser disk library dropped diskType, so every
image ended up tagged 'smd' regardless of its real type:

- smdDoCopy (catalog copy) never passed the catalog entry's own diskType
  to storeImage. Copying the Winchester or NDIX catalog entry silently
  tagged it smd, so the Winchester tab and the NDIX window's own filter
  never showed it.
- smdDoGatewayCopy already had driveType in scope (the remote unit's own
  type) but never passed it through either. No new UI needed, just the
  missing field.
- Local file import had no type source at all. Add a "Tag Imported Disk"
  dialog (smdAskImportType) shown before the file is stored. Its options
  come from smdEnsureCatalog() reading hdd-catalog.json at runtime, unioned
  with disk-types.js's real controller types, so a type the catalog adds
  later appears in the picker without a JS change.

Add a SCSI catalog entry (SCSI0.IMG, not committed - matches the existing
/*.IMG gitignore rule for SMD0.IMG/WD0.IMG) and copy it into the WASM
build folder the same way SMD0.IMG already is.

Verified headless: copying the Winchester and SCSI catalog entries now
stores them tagged winchester/scsi; the import dialog offers
smd/winchester/scsi/floppy/nd500 and reports the chosen type back.

events.title: grm-mej.8: a partly known live-mirror read-back stays RESTORED_BANK
events.message:
grm-mej.8: a partly known live-mirror read-back stays RESTORED_BANK

rcransom's cd57/ef85 FUN_fed1 restores (LDA $bfff / PHA / ... / PLA / JSR fed1)
reached the $bfff read with the bank partly pinned, so the mirror hook answered
the ROM byte partly known and stopped() collapsed the scan to RESOLVED, dropping
the ReadBack. fed1's prologue then discards the caller's register value, so the
call had neither a value nor a restore and warned. X1 was no longer the blocker:
it pairs both PLAs at the shipped caps.

restoredKeepingValue keeps both the partial value and the ReadBack when a
read-back-shaped read (identity accumulators, plain absolute, live-bank mirror)
is not fully known over the register's byte; a fully known byte still stops
RESOLVED. Applied to the resolveLoad branch, the mirror branch, and the
grm-zsxz save-slot carrier. Every consumer of a call's read-back gates on the
argument NOT having resolved, so a surviving partial value leaves it unused.

rcransom re-blessed: cd57/ef85 warning -> RESTORED note (warnings 22->20,
notes 6->8), nothing else. build-and-test.sh check: SUITE OK. realrom check
nes: fail=3 = rcransom (intended) + wizwarr (held) + shenlong 97 (known flap).

project.notes: Identity: A native falling-block game with piece rotation/movement, collision, completed-line detection, scoring, level selection, pause and game over in main.s. Classification: Original author’s revisit to Apple II assembly, recreating the block-stacking rules rather than disassembling another Tetris binary. It is independent of the catalogue’s Spectrum, NES and arcade transcodes. Source CPU: This is newly authored native game code rather than a recovered predecessor executable. No original-binary CPU is assigned from its target machine or the game that inspired it; source_platforms, source_cpu and source_language remain empty. Target CPU: README explicitly places the project in the author’s 6502-assembly work, and main.s is direct 6502 code using Apple monitor graphics/keyboard routines. No 65C02-only instruction requirement is established. Build: main.s uses ORG/EQU/DS/HEX-style native assembly. The file called makefile contains only main = "main.s", so it is not a demonstrated complete command-line build. A disk image is supplied but was not rebuilt or booted. Limitations: No compilation, launch, gameplay, hardware test or original-binary comparison was performed; every independent build flag remains null. Runtime profiles: README targets Apple IIe and documents loading the disk then BRUN TETRIS. Source uses low-resolution PLOT/HLINE/VLINE monitor routines and keyboard input. The README’s ambiguous disk-format wording is not upgraded to a verified DOS/ProDOS version; RAM minimum remains unknown. AI: No explicit development-AI disclosure was found in the inspected README, implementation, build and license sample or the available first-page commit messages (up to 20). Gameplay opponent AI, tool filenames and the age of the project are not development-AI evidence; usage stays unknown. Relationships: No same-code Tetris lineage found in the catalogue; shared rules/title are insufficient for deduplication. The complete repository has no LICENSE file and README provides no explicit reuse grant. Normalized root, title/alias and lineage were screened against the 1,798-project f003aa64 catalogue, source/decision files and expanded 2,198-root prior union; no same-code catalogue entry was found. events.title: fix(libretro): expose the Memory Track as SAVE_RAM on no-content boot (#810)
events.message:
fix(libretro): expose the Memory Track as SAVE_RAM on no-content boot (#810)

A no-content session never exposed SAVE_RAM (no_game_active), so Memory
Track writes made through a disc inserted via disk control were never
handed to the frontend. Two causes:

1. SAVE_RAM was gated on no_game_active, a #646-era rule ("no cartridge,
   no EEPROM"). #726 made no-content boot a CD session with the Memory
   Track plugged in from frame 0, so the gate is stale. It now follows
   jaguarMemTrackInserted. It is deliberately not keyed on a mounted
   disc: frontends size and load SAVE_RAM once after retro_load_game and
   libretro has no change notification, so exposing it first after an
   insert would write a file that is never read back.
2. The insert path never reinstalled the NVM BIOS module. The boot resets
   RAM, wiping the '_NVM' cookie; retro_load_game and retro_reset
   reinstall it, disk_set_eject_state did not. Found by the new test.

Tests: test_disk_control cases 6/7/8; test_boot_config's #646 size-0
assertion becomes the new contract. mtMem joins the test export lists.
No savestate change.

events.title: fix(ppc): fill polygons with the caller's pattern in FillPoly (#4187)
events.message:
fix(ppc): fill polygons with the caller's pattern in FillPoly (#4187)

FillPoly(poly, pat) draws the polygon's interior with the given pattern
in patCopy mode, ignoring the port's pen pattern, pen mode and
background pattern and leaving the pen where it was (Inside Macintosh
Volume I, p. I-192; Imaging With QuickDraw, p. 3-83); above 1 bit per
pixel, patCopy gives black pattern bits the foreground color and white
bits the background color (Imaging With QuickDraw, p. 4-32). The
PowerPC import shared PaintPoly's path and painted the interior solid
in the foreground color, ignoring the pattern. Read the 8-byte pattern
from the second argument, resolve the foreground and background pixels
once per call (honouring the port's explicit indices; a solid pattern
resolves only the foreground), and choose between them per pixel by the
pattern bit at the port-aligned position. The polygon scan is shared
with PaintPoly, whose output is unchanged.

events.message:
fix(ppc): keep async callbacks installed while they wait on 68K code (#4185)

A PowerPC callback that the runner enters asynchronously can call a 68K
routine through Mixed Mode, either with CallUniversalProc on a 68K
routine descriptor or through an import that starts a 68K operation.
These callbacks are the interrupt-level VBL tasks, DrawSprocket VBL
procs, Time Manager tasks, sound completions, sound doublebacks and File
Manager completions, plus Carbon event-loop timers, which run at task
level from the event loop. The import leaves an unstarted 68K frame and
halts the callback's slice, but every callback runner then reinstalled
the interrupted context unconditionally. The 68K frame starts later and
captures whatever registers are installed at that moment as its PowerPC
caller, so it captured the interrupted foreground's registers. When the
68K routine returned, the callback's continuation ran on the
foreground's stack and registers, returned through a stale LR to PC 0,
and the application halted. An application whose VBL task drives a 68K
music driver halts this way a few seconds after launch.

A callback that has not returned still owns the processor, so model
that: when a callback stops on a new, unstarted 68K call it submitted,
leave the callback installed and park the interrupted context, its
current resource file and the runner's post-return work on the loaded
application. The run loop recognises the callback's real return (a
halt at halt_pc with r1 equal to the callback's frame and the owning
task current), reinstalls the interrupted context and resource file,
and applies the deferred work (VBL retirement when vblCount stayed
zero, clearing the doubleback buffer's pending bit) once the process
records are back in place at the end of the slice. Callbacks that never
reach 68K code run exactly the old restore statements.

Masking follows the callback's level:
- A parked interrupt-level callback masks interrupt-level delivery
  until it returns: VBL and DrawSprocket VBL ticks do not count down,
  due Time Manager tasks stay due, and queued sound and file
  completions stay queued. Tick and subtick publication is unchanged.
- A parked event-loop timer leaves interrupts unmasked while its 68K
  call is pending, as for foreground code waiting on a 68K call. Once
  that call returns, its continuation holds the CPU, and interrupts wait
  until it returns, because one fired then would save the continuation
  as its interrupted context and could not park itself.
- Event-loop timers wait for any parked callback, so a timer is never
  re-entered, and only one callback is parked at a time.

The runner runs a parked callback's continuation before any other 68K
frame on its task. Readiness compares the task's top call ID with the
awaited call, so a callback that makes several sequential Mixed Mode
calls still runs each one.

A parked callback behaves like a handler that has not returned: its
continuation runs in the foreground's slices without the per-callback
cycle cap, and a fault after its 68K call halts the application rather
than abandoning the callback. If its 68K callee yields to another
thread, interrupt delivery stays masked until the owner resumes and
the callback returns.

Parking is limited to the case this change can resume correctly: the
current task has a native entry, owns the native CPU, has no 68K frame
(in flight, pending, or a 68K caller) when the callback starts, and no
other callback is parked. Other cases, including callbacks that
interrupt an in-flight 68K call and thread switchers, keep the previous
behaviour; a switcher that leaves a 68K call behind is reported under
SYSTEMLESS_PPC_THREAD_TRACE. Parks are counted on the loaded
application and traced under SYSTEMLESS_PPC_HLE_TRACE.

events.title: fix(ppc): auto-position dialogs against the live MBarHeight (#4184)
events.message:
fix(ppc): auto-position dialogs against the live MBarHeight (#4184)

PowerPC GetNewDialog, alert creation (the Alert family, StandardAlert,
CreateStandardAlert), and AutoPositionDialog hard-coded a 20-pixel menu
bar when evaluating System 7 auto-position codes, while the 68K Dialog
Manager (positioned_window_bounds) reads the MBarHeight low-memory
global. An application that hides its menu bar by zeroing MBarHeight, or
that uses a taller menu bar, therefore got its alert-positioned dialogs
at a different height on PowerPC than on 68K.

All three paths now read MBarHeight (0x0BAA) through one helper. Tests
cover GetNewDialog with an alertPositionMainScreen DLOG under a zeroed
MBarHeight and AutoPositionDialog under a 44-pixel MBarHeight; both
compare against the shared position evaluator fed the live height.

events.title: fix(ppc): call the application's ModalDialog filter proc (#4183)
events.message:
fix(ppc): call the application's ModalDialog filter proc (#4183)

PowerPC ModalDialog read its filterProc argument but never called it: it
popped the next event and ran only its own hit testing. A dialog whose
filter does the work, for example one that keeps a button inactive
(hilite 255) and hit-tests clicks on it in the filter, could never be
dismissed on PowerPC, while the 68K ModalDialog offers every event to
the filter first.

Each ModalDialog pass now offers its event, null events included, to a
native filter as filter(dialog, &event, &itemHit). A true result (the
low byte of r3) ends ModalDialog with the item the filter stored; false
continues with the event as the filter left it in the record. Null
events carry the current tick count, mouse location, and modifiers with
btnState.

The EventRecord lives in a 16-byte-aligned frame below the caller's
stack pointer (linkage area, parameter words, record), as it would in
ModalDialog's own frame, so an idle dialog that calls its filter on
every pass allocates nothing.

Alert, StopAlert/NoteAlert/CautionAlert, and StandardAlert run a
ModalDialog pass with ModalDialog's register arguments and restore the
caller's registers after it (#4134), which would discard filter
arguments staged during the pass. The pass therefore only prepares the
call; the filter's registers are staged after that restore, and the
pending-call state records the caller's stack pointer, link register,
TOC, and r3-r10. When the filter returns, the re-dispatched import restores
those before reading its own arguments, so an alert finds its alert ID,
filter, and output pointer again, and ModalDialog finds its own.

Tests cover a filter that declines a click (normal hit testing still
selects the button), one that claims a click on an inactive button,
null events on every idle pass, and filters on the resource Alert and
StandardAlert paths, including the caller's registers across idle
passes. The edit-text ModalDialog test now passes a NULL filter
explicitly instead of inheriting GetNewDialog's result in r3.

events.title: fix(tests): voicemodem pair test waits for its peer, not the wall clock (#796)
events.message:
fix(tests): voicemodem pair test waits for its peer, not the wall clock (#796)

voicemodem_pair_test flaked on a loaded runner: 'answer got F0DE, want
86D0' / 'dial: data byte 0 never arrived'. Nothing ordered the two
processes after the carrier query: the dialler finished its $8100 exchange
and sent its data packet while the answerer was still short of its own
$8100, so the dialler's first data byte (F0DE) landed in the answerer's
modem message queue ahead of the $86D0 reply it was waiting for.

- Explicit barriers (--sync DIR marker files, one dir per attempt from the
  driver): both sides pass the carrier query before either sends data, and
  both finish reading before either closes the socket. A peer that fails
  drops a .failed marker so the other side aborts instead of sitting out a
  timeout.
- The driver starts the dialler when the answerer announces 'listening',
  replacing the sleep 0.3.
- Every wait on the peer (rendezvous, message bytes, DTMF polls) is bounded
  in wall-clock time (30-60 s) instead of a ~1 s frame budget a starved peer
  blows through.
- The synthetic ROM path is per-process; parallel pairs shared one file and
  one rewrote it under another ('ROM is empty or unreadable').

Stress (12 parallel workers x 10 runs + 24 CPU burners, 120 pairs): 101/120
pass before (13x 'got F0DE, want 86D0', 3x 'want 8000', 16x 'data byte 0
never arrived'); 120/120 and 118/120 after (the 118 run predates the
per-process ROM fix and was one ROM collision plus one unexplained
connect stall).

events.title: fix(cd): serialize real-BIOS boot-stub flag and CD refill phase (v16)
events.message:
fix(cd): serialize real-BIOS boot-stub flag and CD refill phase (v16)

Run-ahead diverged mid-load on the real-BIOS CD path (Hover Strike,
warmup 400): video replay differed 44 frames after the rollback and the
state never reconverged.  Two statics sat outside the savestate blob:

- jagcd_bios.c cdBootStubInjected gates the 68K boot-stub injection at
  $050176.  A rollback to a pre-injection state kept the flag set by the
  replay that had already injected, so the replay never injected the
  stub and the game never started.
- cdrom.c fifoRefillAccum is the error-diffusion remainder that picks
  the next FIFO refill interval (2 or 3 ticks); stale, it shifted every
  later refill by one tick (fifoFillDelay 1 vs 2 in the state diff).
  cdPrevShouldIRQ, the CD IRQ edge detector, is saved with it.

Appended as two magic-tagged chunks ("CDB1", "CDX1") strictly after the
HLE chunk; STATE_SIZE unchanged.  This is the v3.7.1 savestate bump,
v15 -> v16: v15 and older states still load and leave the live values
alone (v3.7.0 behaviour; forcing "not injected" would re-arm the BIOS
hooks over a mid-game state's RAM).  Verified with a genuine v15 file
written by a v3.7.0 build.

Adds test_state_compat rows (v16 chunk restore, v15 load, damaged
accumulator), a ROM-gated real-BIOS Hover Strike run-ahead check next to
the HLE one, and VJ_RUNAHEAD_KEEP=1 to keep the three state files for
offline diffing.

project.status: Archived original Macintosh source release; legacy project/resources and rebuild unverified
project.notes: Identity: Preservation mirror of the original Macintosh Wolfenstein 3D First/Second Encounter source release, attributed in the preserved release note to Bill Heineman and Chris DeSalvo. The note dates the Macintosh commercial release to October 1994 and the source-release account to January 2000; the GitHub root itself is a later third-party archive. WolfMain.c implements the level/game loop, player/enemy/projectile movement and game progression. Classification: Historical original-source preservation with native Macintosh Toolbox support, C gameplay and separate 68k/PPC assembly renderers. The preserved note says this Mac version descends from the SNES adaptation and uses BSP rendering, so it is not collapsed into the tracker’s DOS-derived Wolf ports merely by title. No new decompilation is claimed. Source CPU: The release note explicitly distinguishes Macintosh 68000 and PowerPC editions. Wolf.68k contains D/A registers, MOVEM/MOVE/ADDX/DBF instructions, and Wolf.ppc contains PowerPC register, TOC and code-section conventions. These independently establish both source families; the SNES ancestry does not become a claimed source binary platform for this Mac archive. Target CPU: The archive retains distinct native 68k and PowerPC renderer paths and a CodeWarrior project. Both architectures describe preserved original outputs, not modern host targets or verified successful rebuilds. README’s historical runtime-generated-scaler description is not copied as current behavior: Wolf.68k explicitly records a revision to tight loops, and current SetupScalers68k.c builds a reciprocal table with a disabled older ScaleGlue call path. Build: The source-release note says the project was updated from CodeWarrior DR/4 to Pro 5. The tree contains Wolf3D.mcp, assembly/object artifacts and separate proprietary music libraries, but no complete game resource/asset pack or reproducible modern recipe. Source still uses resource IDs and GetResource/LoadAResource calls. Project-file strings name both MacOS 68K/PPC linkers and legacy libraries; they do not prove all dependencies are present. Limitations: No dependency installation, game compilation, tests, launch, gameplay, hardware check or binary comparison was performed. All build-verification flags remain null. README’s original author build claim is historical and does not verify this mirror. Runtime profiles: Mac.c’s 68k initialization explicitly rejects systems before 6.0.7, requires 32-bit Color QuickDraw, and selects an 8-bit monitor at least 512×384. Its 68000/68020/68030 cases display speed warnings rather than a reliable universal minimum-CPU rule. The PowerPC branch skips the OS gate with a 7.1 comment; no independently established PPC minimum or numeric RAM requirement is asserted. AI: The inspected README and complete available 1-commit message history contain no explicit development-AI disclosure or assistant co-author trailer. This does not establish non-use; age, coding style and filenames are not AI evidence. Relationships: One archived mirror of the original Mac source lineage, counted once. Existing records were compared without re-researching their roots: earok/AkikoWolf credits AWolf/PSP/id DOS source, agranlund/wolf derives from Wolf4SDL/id, and kweepa/wolf64 is a C64 assembly raycaster. In contrast, this preserved author note explicitly identifies a SNES-derived implementation rather than the PC version, with BSP visibility; RefBsp.c and separate Mac renderer paths corroborate material implementation differences, not merely a new target platform. No matching Blzut3/Heineman/Burger Mac source root appears in the complete prior-review union. No general root license is supplied; the release note expressly reserves Steve Hales/Jim Nitchals music-driver rights and requires separate permission for reuse. Public source availability is not treated as an unrestricted redistribution grant. project.status: Unfinished original game restoration; static review only
project.notes: Identity: The author identifies Sparks as the beginnings of a Macintosh game written around 2000 and this repository as an attempt to get its original classic Macintosh code running. The pinned tree contains the game loop, entity, player, star-field, renderer and resource source, rather than only an announcement. Classification: Original-source restoration of an unfinished game prototype. Main.cpp initializes the classic Toolbox and drives Game_RunFrame; this is neither a binary decompilation nor a modern independent remake. The README explicitly declines to characterize the historical work as a finished game. Source CPU: The preserved original Macintosh C++ tree has separate 68K object rules, CPlusOptions-68K with the near model, 68K runtime libraries and a Sparks.68k link target. Together with the author’s original-code statement, this directly establishes m68k source provenance rather than inferring it from the approximate date. Target CPU: The MPW makefile explicitly targets both Sparks.68k through ILink and Sparks.ppc through PPCLink. These are documented build targets; successful output was not established. Build: Inspected the MPW makefile, classic Toolbox bootstrap and complete tree inventory. The build requires the historical CPlus/PPCCPlus, ILink/PPCLink and Rez tools and classic Macintosh libraries; Resources.r and Resources.rsrc are present. No root license grant was found in the tree or README. The project remains explicitly unfinished. Limitations: No compilation, tests, execution, gameplay or binary comparison was performed. All build booleans remain null. Runtime profiles: Main.cpp tests Color QuickDraw availability and an 8-bit display mode, then allocates a GWorld backbuffer. These are implementation requirements, but the inspected material supplies no authoritative minimum CPU model or RAM for a usable game; no runnable hardware profile is asserted. AI: The inspected README and original-code/bootstrap material contain no explicit development-AI disclosure. This is a bounded negative search, not evidence of non-use; usage remains unknown. Relationships: The README mentions another copy in /game/space without identifying a repository. This record covers the author’s Sparks restoration root once; that undeclared copy is not promoted separately. The root was absent from the current catalogue and prior-review/source/decision root index. Limitations: The other copy’s provenance and current location remain unresolved.
