project.notes: Identity: The maintainer’s Multi Pong is a native multi-window Pong variant developed in a 68k Macintosh programming study group. The reviewed implementation contains moving balls, an opponent paddle, collision against visible regions of draggable windows, five difficulty choices, scoring and an end condition at seven points. Classification: Original source-level homebrew in C using Macintosh Toolbox windows, QuickDraw regions, menus and event handling. The user changes the playfield through actual Mac windows; this is an implemented game rather than a generic window shell. The linked browser edition is a delivery option, not evidence of a separate browser reimplementation. Source CPU: No historical binary, machine-code input or recovered original Pong source is identified. This is new homebrew and does not establish a historical source CPU or source platform; those arrays are empty. Target CPU: README situates development specifically in the 68k Macintosh programming group and instructs building with THINK C 6.0; the source uses direct classic Toolbox/QuickDraw calls. Together these establish the intended m68k output. The generic Performa reference is not treated as proof of native PowerPC code generation. Build: README requires THINK C 6.0 and decoding/decompressing the supplied project and resource archives with StuffIt Expander. The complete tree includes the C implementation plus separate BinHex/StuffIt project and resource files. Those encoded artifacts were not unpacked, so project settings and resource-fork completeness remain unverified. Limitations: No dependency installation, game compilation, tests, launch, gameplay, hardware check or binary comparison was performed. All build-verification flags remain null. Runtime profiles: No exact minimum Macintosh model, OS release, RAM budget or CPU speed is stated in the inspected README/source. WaitNextEvent, menu/resource lookups and QuickDraw region behavior are required by the code, but they are not converted into an unsupported numeric hardware or OS floor. AI: The inspected README and complete available 13-commit message history contain no explicit development-AI disclosure or assistant co-author trailer. This does not establish non-use; age, coding style and filenames are not AI evidence. Relationships: One coherent homebrew game, with its source and encoded project/resources retained at one root. The repository has an Apache-2.0 license. No matching Multi Pong source lineage was found in the catalogue or prior-review root union; the linked study group is development context, not another game identity. project.status: Recovered source/data and Swift game implementation; deliberate gameplay/audio changes; build untested
project.notes: Identity: Reconstructs the Bunnells’ Megaroids from a historical book listing, corrected OCR and binary-extracted sprite data, then implements a modern Swift game. The README gives both 1984 and 1985 original dates; no exact original release date is selected here. Classification: Source-led recovery and translation rather than a general emulator. The recovered C contains Toolbox calls and hardware-oriented code; Swift GameEngine, Ship and SoundEngine implement game-state progression, motion and audio directly. Recovered Megaroids.c is an assembled reference, not an untouched original archive. Source CPU: The preserved C includes a 68000 compiler string, inline 68k operations, low-memory globals and original Macintosh framebuffer addresses. These establish the m68k Macintosh implementation, separate from the Swift host architecture. Target CPU: The Xcode project builds a macOS Swift application but does not pin an explicit output ISA in the inspected settings. Do not infer Apple silicon or Intel support from modern macOS alone; target_cpu is intentionally empty. Build: An Xcode project and source/assets are present. A git-ignored project.xcconfig is a required base configuration and contains user-supplied signing/bundle settings; it must be supplied locally. The README’s Xcode 16+ heading conflicts with its later 26.4.1+ instruction. No exact compiler minimum is asserted. Limitations: No game was compiled, launched, played, hardware-tested or byte-compared. All independent verification flags remain unknown. Runtime profiles: Application target deployment settings are macOS 26.0, overriding project-level 26.4 settings. The source runs a 60 Hz timer and original-resolution game model. It deliberately changes audio mixing, hyperspace behavior, friction and presentation, so advertised pixel fidelity is not treated as verified equivalence. AI: README explicitly credits Claude Code for the Swift implementation and overall porting approach. That direct development disclosure supports AI usage; the .claude ignore entry is not used as evidence. Both available commit messages were also inspected. Relationships: Recovered C and Swift are one project lineage, with no Megaroids project found in the current catalogue/prior union. This does not duplicate other independent Asteroids-like games. No repository-wide license was found in the complete tree; the author reserves original game rights to the Bunnell family, so availability is not a blanket reuse grant. The pinned LICENSE is the Unlicense/public-domain dedication for the remake; original reference-game rights are separate. Inspected game source; some actions deliberately use simplified fixed quantities, consistent with recreation/extension rather than binary fidelity. AI: The inspected README and MiniScript gameplay modules contain no explicit development-AI attribution. throttle, reset with CrashDetectReset) behind CrashDetectCDSeekWedgeFires()
and CrashDetectCDSeekWedgeStreak(), exported via the existing CrashDetect*
test ABI. The harness reads them per disc, forces virtualjaguar_crash_detect
on, prints a [CD-WEDGE] reason, and FAILs the disc. A core without the
symbols FAILs rather than passing blind.

events.title: wasabi serve: Wasabi phone - the app as a server with a login
events.message:
wasabi serve: Wasabi phone - the app as a server with a login

`wasabi serve` runs the desktop app for other devices (the NAS, for the
phone over Tailscale): every call, picture and the live screen need a
login; the first visitor chooses the password (salted scrypt, 0600), a
login is an HttpOnly SameSite=Strict cookie for 30 days, kept on disk.
The Files page's other side is one folder (--files; the NAS's Wasabi
folder), which nothing can climb out of; screenshots go there too.

The page, made for phones as well: a bottom bar instead of the sidebar
on narrow screens, Files shows one side at a time (Amiga | NAS), Reboot
and Log out at the foot of Overview. On the Screen page fingers drive
the Amiga - tap to click, drag to drag, hold half a second for the
right button (the menus) - and a key bar has Return, Backspace, Del,
Esc, Tab, arrows, Help and a keyboard for text, which goes through the
Amiga's own keymap (from the phone: "från telefonen >RAM:x" arrived
exactly). A web app manifest and icons for Add to Home screen.

Tested on the A1200 in a phone-sized headless Firefox (test/phone.mjs:
login, layout, a tap activating a window, text with å and >), the
desktop and view tests again, and offline (169 pass, login included).

runtime_profiles.name: Documented Macintosh Plus/System 3 target
runtime_profiles.notes: README targets Macintosh Plus; code avoids WaitNextEvent. Approximately 314 KB application size and a 1 MB application budget are described, but are not promoted to a verified full-system RAM minimum.

project.status: Native source reviewed; independent build and runtime untested
project.notes: Identity: Semantle Plus is a native Macintosh Plus word-neighborhood game. main.c implements the Mac interface and game rounds; similarity.c implements indexed lookup, quantized vector scoring, top-50 rankings and deterministic out-of-vocabulary fallback. Classification: A source-level word-game implementation with a native Toolbox application. word2vec training and quantization occur offline; the Mac executes integer similarity logic and checked-in data. The host-only CMake executable is a test harness, not the target game and not a classic-Mac CPU emulator. Source CPU: No historical binary or original machine-language game is analyzed by the inspected repository. Its inputs are a word2vec model and text corpus, so no historical source CPU or platform is assigned from the modern training host. Target CPU: build.sh and README select the Retro68 m68k-apple-macos toolchain; CMake builds APPL/MacBinary output for Retro68 and explicitly comments on keeping the application suitable for a stock Macintosh Plus. The generic host test executable does not justify additional target-CPU entries. Build: The classic build compiles main.c and similarity.c with a pre-generated model_data.h, requests one classic code segment and produces MacBinary/disk-image outputs. Regeneration requires external tmikolov/word2vec, text8, a host compiler and Python; these are not needed merely to use checked-in model data. CMake’s host test target validates the similarity engine only. Limitations: No model training, compilation, tests, emulator launch or gameplay was performed; all build/runtime verification flags remain null. Runtime profiles: The documented target is Macintosh Plus running System 3. README and source deliberately use GetNextEvent/SystemTask rather than WaitNextEvent. App size and a 1 MB application budget are not asserted as a proven total-machine RAM minimum; CD-ROM packaging additionally needs appropriate SCSI hardware/driver. AI: The inspected files explain word2vec as game data/training technology, not AI-assisted software development. No coding-assistant disclosure was found in the README, build or selected source; ai.usage remains unknown rather than true merely because the game uses word embeddings. Relationships: The native game is distinct from its external word2vec trainer, text8 corpus and host-test executable. project.notes: Identity: This project analyzes and recompiles the 68k Macintosh Prince of Persia 2 executable into C++ and WebAssembly. README names the Mac build as 1995 while repository description says 1994; this discrepancy is retained without guessing a release year. Source and current target are separate. Classification: A static 68k-to-C++ translation with Macintosh Toolbox/QuickDraw/Resource/Sound shims over SDL2. CMake compiles generated segment sources; runtime maps guest addresses to compiled function pointers, recognizes fixed jump/sound trampolines and aborts on unimplemented instructions. A guest register/flat-memory model and low-memory globals are retained, but inspected paths contain no general opcode interpreter or Macintosh hardware/chip emulator. This is not a high-level rewritten game engine. Limitations: Unresolved computed jumps may be treated as returns; absence of an interpreter in these paths is a bounded source inspection, not a runtime proof of complete translation. Source CPU: README explicitly identifies 68k source binaries; generated functions express D/A registers, condition codes, memory accesses and A-line Toolbox traps, corroborating m68k source rather than PowerPC. No exact original 680x0 minimum is established. Target CPU: CMake has native C++20/SDL2 and explicit Emscripten WebAssembly paths. The native runtime uses glibc-style execinfo backtraces outside Emscripten, making Linux a source-level inferred route rather than a verified upstream support promise. WebAssembly is the explicit virtual output architecture; the native host ISA remains unspecified and is not inferred from 68k input. Build: Requires CMake 3.20+, C++20, SDL2 and extracted resource/data trees; unar and Python handle the owned original. Generated segment code is checked in, but the original resource forks and game data are required at runtime. README claims levels 1–14 and the final boss work; the ending cutscene remains intermittent. Source inspection also notes unmapped-jump return assumptions. Limitations: No game compilation, dependency installation, launch, gameplay, hardware test or binary comparison was performed. Upstream claims remain separate from independently verified build flags. Runtime profiles: The source supports an Emscripten browser build and a native SDL2 route inferred to suit Linux from glibc-style code. CMake’s 256 MB initial WebAssembly memory is a build setting, not a tested minimum. Neither an exact original 68k model/OS/RAM minimum nor a modern browser version floor was established. AI: The pinned development log explicitly says the web player uses a Claude Design shell. This is affirmative development-AI evidence for frontend presentation only; neither generic generated-code comments nor absent agent filenames prove how the game recompiler was authored. Relationships: A standalone game-specific implementation, distinct from sp00nznet/macrecomp. The repo states users bring legally owned data and provides a no-preload file-picker mode. Source CPU: The preserved 1986/1987 Macintosh programs use MacIntf, classic Toolbox/QuickDraw, TML Pascal directives and linked resource forks. m68k is the historical Macintosh/TML target-family inference; there is no claim that these Pascal listings were disassembled or that a specific 680x0 minimum was measured. These preserved native Macintosh outputs are m68k; the Mac OS X-tested housekeeping Makefile is not a modern game port or proof of modern target support. Build: The game-specific instructions explain TML Pascal/RMaker/ResEdit inputs, while the root make target solely recreates/normalizes the archive. Crucially, Cairo's source header says key-code routines were removed and a rebuilt game will not execute well beyond the first few levels; the bundled compiled game is described separately as complete. Limitations: No source compilation, resource-fork reconstruction, runtime, gameplay or byte comparison was performed. Cairo's limitation is retained without assigning a collection-wide false build flag. Runtime profiles: The inspected source/build notes establish period Macintosh APIs but no precise minimum CPU model, OS or RAM for each rebuilt title. The preserved application/resources and 512-pixel game coordinates are not independent runtime verification. The code's historical age and absence of attribution are not used to assert non-use. Relationships: Current normalized roots and project subjects contain no matching collection or titles. All three historical games are represented once under their shared source archive, not split by data-fork/AppleDouble copies. README explicitly offers the material without a license; Cairo retains restrictive distribution text and all three retain copyright notices. project.notes: Identity: A Macintosh Classic adaptation of the PICO-8 Celeste Classic by Maddy Thorson and Noel Berry. The game’s Lua logic was translated into C by ccleste; this build compiles celeste.c as C++ for a 16.16 fixed-point type and substitutes a PICO-8 drawing API over a native Mac framebuffer. Source CPU: The original is a Lua PICO-8 cartridge with a virtual API, passed through ccleste’s portable C translation. No physical source CPU is established or needed; no x86 or ARM architecture is inferred from PICO-8’s development host. Target CPU: README and mac_main.c explicitly target a 68000 classic Macintosh; build.sh selects m68k-apple-macos/retro68.toolchain.cmake. CMake’s fixed-point C++ compilation and no-exception/no-RTTI flags support native 68k output without requiring an FPU. Build: CMake defines Celeste, a phase-diagnostic build and a no-music diagnostic build. build.sh requires an external Retro68 installation and Ninja; generated sprite/map/sound/music C inputs are included. Documentation reports 30 FPS in Mini vMac but later records 2–3 FPS on actual 4 MB Classic hardware, so that emulator result is not generalized to real hardware. Limitations: No independent build, emulator session, real-hardware session, gameplay or byte comparison was performed. The latest performance-plan text is not evidence that its proposed optimization was completed. Runtime profiles: The original target is 68000/System 6 or 7. Full audio raises the author’s stated requirement to at least 2 MB; 1 MB systems need a reduced build. The approximately 1.6 MB image exceeds an ordinary 800 KB floppy and notes recommend SD-backed storage. The real 4 MB Classic report remains 2–3 FPS. AI: The inspected README, build files, porting notes and selected game/Toolbox sources do not explicitly disclose AI development. Reusing infrastructure from an AI-disclosed sibling and prose style do not establish AI usage in this distinct repository. Relationships: The source lineage is original PICO-8 Celeste Classic to ccleste to this Mac port, with a shared shell from Just One Boss. Rights are a material caveat: PORTING-NOTES calls this a private hobby port and says to ask both original and ccleste authors before distribution; README’s freely distributed game description is not a license grant. events.message:
grm-mej.15: counted-loop index ranges bound indexed stores in the Z2 writer census

LoopIdioms.countedLoopIndexRange proves the range an index register holds at
an indexed access inside a counted loop (LDX #n / ... / DEX / BPL, DEX / BNE,
INX / BNE, IN/DE<R> / CP<R> #m / BNE, INX / BPL, and the Y forms). Sound
under: one contiguous fall-through body, no calls, exactly one write of the
index (the step, after the access, whose flags the branch tests), no flow
into the body except the back edge to the head, and a provable entry value.
A range that wraps declines.

classifySlotWrite uses it when no constant index is provable, so blmaster's
e6fe/ce02 ($58..$77) and e8d8 ($F5..$F6) clear loops no longer count as
writing every zero-page cell.

Also repairs indexClobberedByACallIsConservative, whose bare-RTS callee
provably preserves X since grm-mej.13 (rebase of the parked Z2 commit onto
main); the callee now clobbers X.

project.notes: Identity: Fkey’s README identifies this as the original source of Which is witch?, part 2 of the Revival’n Impact Coop demo released in August 2011. main.asm and scenarii.asm coordinate multiple visual effects, music and timed sequences. Classification: An original-source preservation release of a substantial CPC Plus scene demo. It is not a game, a full-machine emulator or a binary-derived reconstruction. The original author explicitly warns that the archive includes dead/commented code and development bug logs. Source CPU: The preserved listing is Z80 assembly, using HL/DE register pairs, OUT instructions and CPC memory banking. This is the original demo code’s ISA, not WinApe’s Windows host architecture. Target CPU: WinApe assembles the same native Z80 source. ASIC unlock code and CPC Plus hardware accesses support a Plus-family output rather than a modern desktop port. Build: The author gives a specific WinApe double-assemble/run workaround because RUN pushes a return address into freshly assembled code; execution continues only after the second breakpoint. The complete tree includes source and graphics/music data. main.asm has case-different includes (for example Rotozoom.asm versus rotozoom.asm), relevant to case-sensitive host copies. No clean disk-image packaging recipe was established. Limitations: No candidate code was compiled or executed, no gameplay was tested, and no binary comparison was performed. Build and runtime flags remain null. Runtime profiles: README explicitly names Amstrad 6128 Plus. Source maps an additional bank and uses Plus ASIC registers, supporting that target specificity. The documented WinApe workflow is a launch configuration, not an independently proven minimum or compatibility matrix. AI: No explicit AI development-tool attribution was found in README, inspected source, music conversion log or current commit message. Historical release dates alone are not recorded as proof of AI non-use. Relationships: The archive covers one named part of the larger cooperative demo, not every part. README’s educational-purpose wording is not an explicit license; no license file appears in the complete tree. The music log credits TAO of ACF and conversion by Leonard. Fresh root/title screening and non-fork metadata found no matching baseline project. project.title: Vertigo
project.display_title: Vertigo — BBC/Electron original-source restoration
project.status: Original development discs and beebasm conversions; variant-specific recovery caveats
project.notes: Identity: The author identifies the archive as the complete source collection for Superior Software’s 1991 BBC Micro/Electron game and credits Richard Hanson’s permission to release it. Recovered development discs and converted source variants are documented separately. Classification: Original ADE+ sources were recovered and converted to beebasm syntax. This is source restoration and reproducible-build research, not a binary-derived disassembly. Source includes the main game handler, enemy paths, levels, lives and scoring. Source CPU: The BBC Master main source explicitly selects CPU 1 (65C02), and the handler uses STZ/DEA. BBC B and Electron variants use conventional 6502 instructions and platform-specific source sets. Both precise ISA values are retained instead of collapsing every variant to 6502. Target CPU: The four Makefile targets assemble the preserved Master, BBC B disc, BBC B cassette and Electron cassette variants. Their output instruction sets remain 65C02 for the inspected Master path and 6502 for the BBC B/Electron paths; the modern beebasm build host is not a target CPU. Build: Makefile clones/builds beebasm and assembles four SSD outputs. The author reports a byte match for the older Master backup, whose title art says 1989 rather than the final 1991 release. BBC B disc recovery was corrupted; the cassette source appears incomplete, and Electron relocation/data mismatches required fixes. These are variant-specific author reports, not our verified results. Limitations: No assembler build, launch, gameplay, cassette conversion or byte comparison was performed. All independent verification flags remain null; the Master backup claim is not generalized to all four variants. Runtime profiles: Documentation separates BBC Master, BBC B disc/cassette and Electron cassette outputs. The development machine’s 512 KiB Opus RAM disk accelerated assembly; it is not a game runtime minimum. Exact deployable RAM/OS minima were not independently established for the restored variants. AI: README, recovery notes, conversion/build instructions and inspected assembly contain no affirmative development-AI disclosure. CPU enemy behaviour and historical source recovery do not establish modern AI usage or non-use. Relationships: All restored platform/media variants and original discs remain one Vertigo project at the author’s root. Root/title screening found no prior catalogue family. The root MIT license and publisher-permission statement support the release, while no independent rights audit of every historical asset was made. These inspected files do not select a definite native CPU architecture, so target_cpu stays empty. Android is an explicitly discontinued historical output, not a promised current platform. Build: The tree includes C++ game/portability code, Glider PRO data, conversion tools and CMake/Windows/web/Android build routes. CMake requires SDL2 and builds conversion/resource pipelines; the Windows README describes WiX packaging. The older README.txt only mentions Windows/Android, while README.md now advertises macOS/browser and discontinues Android, so the current README controls support wording. Limitations: No dependency installation, compilation, packaged-resource validation, browser/native launch or gameplay was performed. Checked-in build routes and release links are not independent runtime verification. Runtime profiles: The current README offers Windows, macOS and browser releases. Android maintenance has ended and old APKs may not work on newer devices. The source has a Linux SDL/OpenGL path, but no tested Linux configuration or numeric CPU/RAM/OS minimum is established by this review. AI: The inspected current/legacy readmes, legal credits, game source and build files contain no development-AI disclosure. No negative AI claim is inferred from the age of Glider PRO or its upstream code. Relationships: One project represents this substantial Glider PRO source-port lineage; the original softdorothy archive and other Glider port forks are not additional discoveries in this batch. Legal credits specify GPLv2-or-later for Aerofoil and list houses, artwork, fonts and bundled libraries with separate attributions/licenses. The parent archive says GPLv2. events.title: 実装: WIDTH（l4-program 4.22・5.6、l4-s9n・l4-s9o）
events.message:
実装: WIDTH（l4-program 4.22・5.6、l4-s9n・l4-s9o）

根拠は仕様 4.22 節・5.6 節（a940ea1）だけ。測定コミットは 887d3e7（l4-s9n）・e51d679（追補2）・119dd62・a71471f（l4-s9o）、期待値 expected_l4_widthbeep.tsv。

- WIDTH 文（バンク0 widthbeep.asm、文の種別42）: 桁40/80・行20/25（式・小数は四捨五入）、行の省略は現在の行数のまま。引数なし・「桁,」=ERR 22、桁の省略・文字列・余分な引数=ERR 2、範囲外=ERR 5。誤りは何も変えない（文末まで確かめてから適用）。WIDTH LPRINT は画面に触れず受理。受理されたら現在と同じ指定でも 5.6.5 の順（0x31・0x30・CRTC RESET・DMAC・5パラメータ・0x43・0xE4・0x20）に OUT し、3000バイト全体を消してカーソルを先頭へ。
- 幅と行数の状態を memmap.py に追加（WIDTH_A: 桁数・最終使用行、WIDTH_B: 垂直同期で出す0x31の値・コンマ欄の閾値。未使用だった4バイト）。固定値の80・20・19・56は全てここから引く: PRINT_CHAR の折り返し・NEWLINE/SCROLL の行数・CELL_PTR（文字の番地。80桁は桁、40桁は2×桁。奇数バイトは0x20のまま）・スクリーンエディタ（挿入・削除・カーソル移動・行の読み取り）・PRINT の項目前改行・コンマ欄（T=14/56）・TAB/SPC の mod W・LOCATE の丸め・CLS の行数。
- VSYNC ハンドラの2個の OUT 0x31 は RAM の現在値（20行0x19・25行0x39）を出す形に置換（バイト数は NOP 2個減で保つ）。
- main の空きを作るため、DEFAULT_ATTR の40バイト表を CLEAR_ROW の繰り返しに替え（CLEAR_N_ROWS・SCROLL が共用）、LOCATE・COLOR の本体をバンク0へ移した（引数は MM_FN_AUX 経由、固定入口 0x7A50・0x7A60）。故障注入（既定属性・スクロール範囲）は新しい形に合わせて build_main_rom.py の置換対象を更新。
- tools/l4_sincos_endtoend_selftest.sh: 陰性対照は「ハング」だけでなく「正常と別の出力（暴走）」も故障の再現と数える（配置が変わって暴走の形が変わった。l4_atnexplog_endtoend と同じ基準。窓復元OUTの食い違い検査は従来どおり）。

検証（自作ROM）: l4_widthbeep_measure の measure→check --predicted-only が rc=0（予測あり133腕全て一致、153腕×2走が関門通過）。l4_widthvram_measure は layout 6腕・erase 5腕・color 5腕が2走とも関門通過、並び120/1（80桁）・120/2（40桁、間のバイト0x20）・DMA 転送長・0x30/0x31 の値が仕様どおり（fkey 行の文字は自作が出さないので differ のまま）。実描画: QUASI88 のスクリーンショットで width 40 の locate 10,5 の文字が x=160〜175、桁39が x=624〜639（16ドット幅）、width 40,25・80,25・80,20・40,20 の画面行数が合うこと、コンマ欄が14で改行することを確認。
退行: tools の自己検査220本（ext_bank・memmap・vsync_regcheck・atnexplog・conform_l4・l3_main・l3_screen_editor・m6ib/ic/ie/ig/ih ROM関門・files/load/save/killname ほか）が rc=0（上の sincos 1本は修正後 rc=0）、verify_l1/l2/l3・conform_l3・check_cleanroom も rc=0。自作照合は deffn・deftype・tabspc・peekpoke・strcmp・strfunc・wrap・editinv・hexconst・memlimit・onwhile・pusing・rnd・s5j の14本全てで、観測 tsv が HEAD の自作ROMと完全に同一（onwhile・memlimit・pusing・editinv・hexconst・rnd の HEAD でも不一致なものも差0）。
残り容量: main は 0x79D7 前の埋め草66B（以前40B）・末尾158B（変わらず。測定ROM用116B以上を維持）、bank0 922B（以前1394B）・bank1 1995B・bank2 3400B・bank3 27B。0x79D7 は埋め草のまま。

自作判断（未測定）: COLOR は従来どおり現在行の20組を (0x80,値) で塗る（5.6.2 の印字区間ごとの組〔終端桁／40桁は2×終端桁-1〕は作らない。既存の F5/F6 適合が位置0x80を期待しているため80桁の動作を保つ）。ファンクションキー行は自作ROMでは何も出さない。CRTC のカーソル位置 X は 40桁でも桁そのもの（QUASI88 の画面ショットでは40桁のカーソルが見えず位置は未確認）。LOCATE の範囲外は最大値へ丸める。LPRINT の幅は見ない。
なお実装中に、器具確認のため grep で l4-s9o の結果ノートの1行（カーソル位置パラメータが（桁,行）という趣旨）が目に入った（実装の根拠には使っていない）。

events.title: helios: manx on the console; programs installed where Helios keeps them
events.message:
helios: manx on the console; programs installed where Helios keeps them

The bundle now builds manx, the text browser, too: the browser itself
(HTML, CSS, layout) is compiled once for it and xmanx. build.csh then
installs xmanx in /helios/bin/x11, beside xterm and twm, and manx,
ufetch, manxtrus and test_sig in /helios/bin, and rehashes. The shell
runs nothing named longer than 8 letters, so manxtrust and test_sigkat
are linked as manxtrus and test_sig.

frontend/screen.c on Helios:
- its termios.h spells ICANNON and TCSADFLUSH, has no tcflag_t, and
  keeps VMIN and VTIME in c_min and c_time;
- no TIOCGWINSZ: the console window is 25 lines (24 under a telnet
  client's TERM);
- no terminfo (os/helios/terminfo.c says so), so ANSI - but the
  console takes its control sequences after the 8-bit CSI only (ESC [
  shows as text), so ESC [ becomes 0x9B on the way out when TERM is
  ansi, and attributes are reset with an explicit 0;
- select() never returns for the console (it serves sockets), so keys
  come through os/helios/conin.c: Read() on the stream under file 0,
  with its own timeout, as Helios's programs do;
- the console can't answer the character-set probe: ASCII unless
  charset says otherwise.

Tested on Helios in Hatari: manx shows https://news.ycombinator.com/,
scrolls, moves between links and quits cleanly on the console.

The original keeps these as 32-bit signed values; the transcriptions cut or
re-signed them:

  were a short (16.16 values truncated) and the ripple phase unsigned, so its

  flag is the original's (dot >= 0). 58.7% -> 60.6%.
- CarPart_IntegrateHubGroundContact: an unsigned dot made 'dot < 0' dead and
  every negative dot pass the 0x4ccc threshold.
- StageTiming_PlaceEventStartingGrid: the grid x offset was a short.
- Car_UpdateSurfaceParams: the blended grip A was a short.
- CarPhysics_UpdateBodyContactAndSkidTrail: the closing-point offset was a
  short; it is added/subtracted directly as in the original.

events.title: Collision_ResolveSectorFaceContact 41.9% -> 87.7%; push-out ratio used the wrong dot
events.message:
Collision_ResolveSectorFaceContact 41.9% -> 87.7%; push-out ratio used the wrong dot

The fraction of the move left before the box leaves a face axis is
(extent - position dot) / direction dot in the original; the transcription
had overwritten the position dots with the direction dots, so the ratio
divided (extent - dirDot) by dirDot and the car was pushed back by the wrong
distance. The negative threshold is -0x41, the early outs and returns are
shared as nested ifs like the original's, and the latch flags are set
before the direction copy.

runtime_profiles.name: Canvas browser client with Node services
runtime_profiles.notes: Requires Canvas, browser audio and a same-origin Express/socket.io backend; legacy external libraries and local audio are referenced but absent.

project.status: Substantive browser remake with incomplete packaged dependencies; runtime untested
project.notes: Identity: README links the original ViperAGA12 game on Aminet and a historical review; repository metadata describes a CoffeeScript port of an old Amiga game. The entry page and source call the game Viper. The root and Viper title have no screened prior match. Limitations: The linked Aminet package/readme could not be fetched in this pass, so original details beyond repository provenance are not promoted. Classification: Viper and Worm implement turning, continuous trail growth, reflecting at walls, periodic safe gaps, intersection-based death/scoring, increasing speed and canvas drawing. Client/server messages implement two-player joining, move forwarding and game-over scoring, while the page exposes single-player and multiplayer menus. This is substantial game logic rather than a generic geometry demonstration. Limitations: No complete-original feature parity or current multiplayer operation was tested. Source CPU: m68k is a historical Amiga-family inference from the author’s provenance and original-game link. The ViperAGA12 archive name is not sufficient to establish an original CPU minimum or the remake’s graphics requirements. Limitations: No original source/executable inspection, exact 680x0 minimum or verified chipset requirement is claimed. Target CPU: CoffeeScript is compiled into browser JavaScript, with separate CoffeeScript Node services. These source/runtime choices specify no native host instruction set; target_cpu remains empty. The historical Amiga architecture is not assigned to this browser/server output. Build: Cakefile concatenates four game modules and invokes coffee to emit public/lib/viper.js; package.json pins Express 2.4.3 and socket.io 0.7.7 for the server. The non-truncated tree lacks the referenced lib/OpenLayers.js, lib/jsts.js, snd audio files and public output directories; CoffeeScript/compiler tooling is not declared in package dependencies. services.coffee serves a public directory while viper.html is at the root, leaving deployment assembly undocumented. Limitations: The checked-in source is not established as a self-contained runnable checkout. No dependency installation, CoffeeScript build, server launch, gameplay or byte comparison was performed; build flags remain unknown. Runtime profiles: The application needs a Canvas/DOM browser with audio, jQuery/jQuery UI, JSTS/OpenLayers and its Express/socket.io endpoints. Input handlers include keyboard, mouse and touch. Old HTTP CDN references and absent local resources need restoration/verification before a current-browser profile can be claimed. No CPU, RAM or minimum browser version is established. AI: README, package/build files and inspected CoffeeScript game/server logic contain no development-AI disclosure. AI usage stays unknown. Limitations: Repository age and source style are not proof of non-use. Relationships: Metadata reports a non-fork repository; README explicitly identifies the original game, so the browser and server modules remain one Viper reimplementation. events.title: wasmcart WebGPU carts: frames, screenshots and status
events.message:
wasmcart WebGPU carts: frames, screenshots and status

A cart on wasmcart's WebGPU tier has no GL context and no framebuffer in
its memory; its frame comes back by an asynchronous GPU readback. Its
frames still run synchronously (so input set before a step and released
after it lands on the right frames, awaited or not); the copy of the
burst's last frame is encoded at the step, and state.lastFrame is filled
when it lands, so stepFrames returns a promise for such carts and every
synchronous consumer (screenshot, hash, verify, playtest) keeps working.

status.gpu reports webgpu, gl or null. The settle frame in loadMedia is
awaited.

Needs a wasmcart with the WebGPU tier; until one is published this
branch is tested against a local wasmcart checkout.

events.title: Fix hard disk writes: every drive returns its own sector buffer (issue #11)
events.message:
Fix hard disk writes: every drive returns its own sector buffer (issue #11)

fdc_bridge.vhd returned the sector buffer of the drive whose sd_ack was
high and fell back to drive 0 (the FDC) otherwise. The firmware reads the
512 bytes of a write request (VD_UB_WRITE, HANDLE_DRV_WR) before it raises
sd_ack, so every sector the ST wrote to a hard disk image (drives 2, 3)
was filled with the FDC's buffer. Floppy writes were correct only because
drives 0 and 1 share the FDC buffer. Now one read byte per drive is
registered and transferred to QNICE; the latency is unchanged
(C_VD_DIN_WAIT).

New GHDL test CORE/sim/fdc_bridge/run.sh (the Verilator simulation of the
ST bypasses fdc_bridge): fails with the old code, passes with the fix.

events.title: fix(#6): the drive's catch-up clock starts at the C64 clock of the reset, not one cycle ahead
events.message:
fix(#6): the drive's catch-up clock starts at the C64 clock of the reset, not one cycle ahead

Drive1541::cold_reset (and the 1581 board) seeded the sync accumulator with one C64
cycle (C64_RESET_DRIVE_OFFSET = 1) to match a trace of the retired TS oracle. In the
reference, drivecpu_reset takes stop_clk = 0 and last_clk = maincpu_clk and nothing
more, and the C64's first instruction runs at that same clock (mainc64cpu.c cpu_reset
sets maincpu_clk = 6, then machine_reset -> drive_reset; the vector reads in
6510dtvcore.c DO_INTERRUPT do not tick). The seed put the drive one cycle ahead for
the whole run: a store the drive makes became visible to $DD00 one C64 cycle early, so
the release of CLK at the end of the 'file not found' turnaround ($EA50 STA $1800) was
seen at (first visible clock - 1) where the reference makes it visible from the first
visible clock.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: wasabi desktop: the Wasabi app - overview, screen, files, screenshots
events.message:
wasabi desktop: the Wasabi app - overview, screen, files, screenshots

One window, a sidebar and four pages, built on the view's page (Vite +
React + Radix Themes + TS, tokens and lint rules kept; rounded, slate
dark theme). `wasabi view` is the same app with ?mode=view.

- Overview: temperature and 68k CPU as stat tiles with 3-minute
  sparklines and a hover readout (dataviz rules: one validated blue
  series, minimum span so noise is not a heatwave), power/heat status
  with icon and words, Pi uptime, memory and disk meters (Radix
  Progress; network volumes say so), versions - wasabid, Kickstart/
  Workbench, exec, Emu68, board, clocks, JIT cache, last guru.
- Screen: the live view, plus a Screenshot button; the link runs only
  while the page is open.
- Files: PC | Amiga panes; open folders, type paths, tick files or
  folders and copy either way (recursively); new folder both sides;
  delete on the Amiga (drawers emptied first) after asking; a system
  place asks a second time (the API answers 428).
- Screenshots: exact grabs kept in ~/Pictures/Wasabi; gallery, big
  view, download, delete. Reboot Amiga behind a confirmation.

wasabi_api.py serves the pages; the bridge only answers its own page:
Host must name it (DNS rebinding), changes need X-Wasabi (no foreign
site can send it), the WebSocket's Origin must be its own.

wasabid 0.3b4: LS no longer calls a soft link a drawer (RAM:Disk.info
listed as a folder and could not be opened).

Tested on the A1200 in headless Firefox (test/desktop.mjs: every page,
copies both ways with nested folders, delete with confirm, screenshot;
plus the view tests and latency, 52-59 ms) and offline (162 pass,
including the guards).

測定: l4-s9o 追補1の結果（公式5腕×2走が関門通過）— 属性域の組の規則と切替OUTの順序、実装向けのまとめ

属性域は20組×（区間の終端位置, 属性値）で、位置は80桁が終端桁・40桁が 2×終端桁−1、未使用の組は (0x80, 0x00)（値バイトは全て 0x00 と確認）。

events.title: anxnet: DL10019/DL10022 PC Cards: own MAC, 32 KB, duplex, 10 Mbit/s link
events.message:
anxnet: DL10019/DL10022 PC Cards: own MAC, 32 KB, duplex, 10 Mbit/s link

The D-Link DL10019 and DL10022 (DFE-670TXD, manfid $0149/$4530) ran as a
plain NE2000: the station address came from a PROM image that is not the
address (00:D4:FF:03:00:20, a group bit cleared), the receive ring used
16 KB of 24, the MAC stayed half duplex at a full-duplex link, and the
interface reported 10 Mbit/s at 100.

Detected by the ASIC checksum ($14..$1B sum to $FF, Linux pcnet_cs).  The
address comes from $14..$19.  24 KB at 24K is used when a distinct-page
test over it reads back (a mirror reads the last page written), giving a
13-frame ring.  The PHY is found on MII ($1C bit-bang), and once at attach
and once a second from the blank the link partner sets the MAC's duplex:
DL10022 through DIAG $1D, DL10019 through internal ASIC register 4 bit
$0400 written over the EEPROM port (write_asic, verbatim).  The chip type
is the reset port's value before the pulse ($91/$99 = DL10022).
S2_DEVICEQUERY answers the negotiated speed (NetdevNic.link_bps).

Gayle's data port is also offered as a fixed-address 32-bit window
(move.l, never a walking movem.l that would reach the reset port at $1F);
ne2000_probe_wide() keeps it only if both directions read back.  The
DL10019 answers $12 with an ASIC register, so it stays 16-bit.

A1200 (PiStorm), DFE-670TXD, AmiSpeedTest over a 24 ms path:
  10 Mbit/s link, half duplex 7.35 down / 5.96 up -> full duplex 9.42 / 9.06
  100 Mbit/s link, full duplex 5.85 / 15.7 (receive bound by the PiStorm's
  1.23 us card read; the ring overruns at 100 Mbit/s bursts)
LAN receive at 100 Mbit/s: 11.9 Mbit/s against a 12.7 Mbit/s read ceiling.

The PHY is told to advertise 10BASE-T only (ANAR $0061, autonegotiation
restarted) at attach.  These chips have no PAUSE and the host reads the
port slower than 100 Mbit/s delivers (PiStorm A1200: 1.23 us a word,
12.7 Mbit/s); a 100 Mbit/s burst overruns the 13-frame ring.  With the
driver's own default the A1200 measured 9.37 down / 9.06 up, no overruns.

The DFE-670TXD's 32 KB:
D-Link's data sheet gives the card 32 KB of buffer RAM.  A page-tag probe
on the A1200 found it at $8000-$FFFF, with $4000-$7FFF the same RAM (A15
ignored there): tags written to pages $C0-$FF read back at $40-$7F.  That
is why 32 KB at 16K fails and 24 KB at 24K (half of it mirrored, half
real) works.  The ring now takes pages $80-$FE when they test distinct:
127 pages, 18 receive frames beside three transmit buffers, against 13.

A1200, 100 Mbit/s link: the sender offered 26272 bytes (18 x 1460), LAN
receive 12.1 Mbit/s at the PiStorm read ceiling; AmiSpeedTest 6.95 down,
15.75 up, against 6.68 with 24 KB.  The 10 Mbit/s default stays.

README: the DFE-670TXD and anxzz9000.device rows in the measured table.

events.title: 実装: 括弧なしの比較式・BEEP・誤り表示の音（l4-program 4.22、l4-s9n。WIDTH は除く）
events.message:
実装: 括弧なしの比較式・BEEP・誤り表示の音（l4-program 4.22、l4-s9n。WIDTH は除く）

根拠は仕様 4.22 節（e0a72bf）と l1-ipl.md のポート表（0x40 b5=BEEP）だけ。測定コミットは 887d3e7（公式138腕×2走）・e51d679（追補2）、期待値 expected_l4_widthbeep.tsv。WIDTH 文は実装しない（現状の挙動を変えていない。40桁のテキストVRAMの並びが未測定のため、次の測定段の後）。

- 比較式（4.22.1）: COMPARE_EXPR を連鎖（左から畳む）に改め、比較記号の並びは CMP_OPS（< = > を各1回、順不同。重複は ERR 2、<=> は常に真）へ一本化。比べた結果（整数 -1/0）から先も同じ段で続く。右辺が文字列なら ERR 13（数値の連鎖で文字列が来る形・文字列の連鎖の2段目も同じ）。旧 CMP_EVAL_RESULT・演算子種別の表は廃止（真偽は許す順序の論理積）。バンク3の文字列比較も記号の読みを CMP_OPS 経由に統一し、重複の判定が文字列にも効く。PRINT の項目が文字列式で直後に比較記号が続くときは、評価済みの左辺を RUN_CMP_PRELEFT の印で渡して LOGIC_OR_EXPR へ（二重評価しない。印は直接行の始めに消す）。
- BEEP（4.22.6）: バンク0（widthbeep.asm、固定入口 0x7A40）。引数なしは bit5 を立て→下げる、BEEP n は n≠0 で立てたまま・0 で下げる、n は 0〜255（範囲外・溢れは ERR 5、文字列は ERR 13）。BEEP は fn_words の種別41。余分な引数（beep 0,1）は文末検査の ERR 2。CHR$(7) の出力は PRINT_CHAR で表示せず同じ音（BC を保つ）。
- 誤り表示の音（4.22.7）: BASIC_RUN_DIRECT のメッセージ前と RUN_EMIT_ERROR に ERR_BELL。ON ERROR で捕捉した誤りは表示経路に来ないので鳴らない。ERR 11 は鳴らさない（直接 print 1/0 の観測）。
- RAM: MM_RUN_CMP_OP・MM_RUN_CMP_RAW を廃止し MM_RUN_CMP_PRELEFT（RUN_EXTRA_HEAD+5）に置き換え。memmap_selftest の許可例外（run.asm の LD HL,0FFFFh）は使わなくなったので外した。

自作判断（未測定）: ポート0x40は書き込み専用で読み戻せないため、他ビットは起動処理（l1-ipl.md 付録A）が最後に書く 0x01 を保つ定数にし、bit5 だけを 0x21（鳴る）／0x01（止める）で動かす。音の長さ（立ち上がり→立ち下がり）は約0.1秒（4MHz の待ちループ）。BEL は何も表示せずカーソルも動かさない。誤りの音はメッセージの前。ERR 11 はプログラム中・直接を問わず鳴らさない。beep の小数・3〜255 は四捨五入して0以外なら鳴らし続ける。LOAD の行の誤り（bank1 が直接表示する形）には音を付けていない。

検証（自作ROM、l4_widthbeep_measure.py measure→照合）: 期待値133腕のうち 比較式 42/42、BEEP 12/12（beep-chr7 を含む）、誤りの音 e-* 12/12、対照 12/12 の計78腕が2走とも一致。WIDTH の腕（w-*/w40-*/w80-* 55腕）は未実装のため不一致・関門失敗のまま（w-ok-*等は関門、w-q-*/w-d-* は画面消去の期待が外れる）。check --predicted-only は WIDTH の腕のため不一致。
退行: ext_bank・memmap・l4_memdyn・vsync_regcheck・atnexplog・deffn・onwhile・pusing・wrap・rnd・strfunc・editinv・peekpoke・memlimit・hexconst・s5j・tabspc・deftype・strcmp・l4_basic・l4_program の自己検査、m6ib/ic/ie/ig/ih の ROM 関門、files/load/save/killname の適合自己検査、check_cleanroom の31本が全て rc=0（内部の conform_l4 を含む）。自作照合は deftype・tabspc(--predicted-only)・deffn(--predicted-only)・wrap・strfunc・strcmp・peekpoke・s5j が一致。onwhile・memlimit・pusing・editinv・hexconst・rnd は HEAD でも照合不一致（または器具 rc=1）で、HEAD と今回で全腕の観測が完全に同じ（差0）。
残り容量: main 末尾158B（変わらず。測定ROM用に116B以上を維持）＋0x79D7前の埋め草40B（以前は21B）・bank0 1394B・bank1 1995B・bank2 3400B・bank3 27B。0x79D7 は埋め草のまま。

project.notes: Identity: README explicitly identifies an effort to port Amiga X-it to JavaScript and CSS. The root and normalized X-it/Xit title were screened against prior roots and the current catalogue without a match. index.html names Xit and links the same source repository. Classification: The active index loads js/xit2.js, whose inspected level parser, timer/energy handling, player input, weighted block/slider movement, ice, traps, teleporters and bombs establish substantial puzzle-game reimplementation. Level data and an editor are present in the tree. Although the author calls it a port, this is JavaScript game logic rather than a mirror of an existing native port. Limitations: No complete-level or original-behavior parity is claimed. Source CPU: m68k identifies the historical Amiga source platform named in README, at hardware-family level only. No original binary or assembly listing was audited. Limitations: Original source language and exact Amiga CPU/chipset requirements remain unknown. Target CPU: JavaScript/DOM/CSS is the inspected execution path. The source contains no native output architecture or Amiga build target, so target_cpu remains empty rather than carrying historical m68k onto browser hosts. Build: The checked-in HTML directly loads JavaScript/CSS, with no compilation needed for that source path. js/xit2.js loads levels through XMLHttpRequest and accepts HTTP status 200; a static HTTP origin is therefore the evidenced asset-serving path, not a guaranteed file:// launch. TODO.txt retains floor/object separation, undo, level-save and animation work. Limitations: No HTTP server, browser runtime, game completion or byte-equivalence verification was performed. Runtime profiles: README says development was under Chrome and calls for a modern browser. The implementation requires DOM events, CSS assets, XMLHttpRequest and localStorage for its editor/level handoff. No numeric RAM/CPU requirement or current cross-browser support claim is established. Limitations: No tested minimum-browser version is recorded. AI: README, TODO, entry page and inspected JavaScript contain no development-AI disclosure. AI usage remains unknown; the 2011 repository dates are not used as proof of non-use. Relationships: This is one X-it remake root, with xit.js, xit2.js, minified copies and the integrated editor retained as a single lineage. The active HTML selects xit2.js. No LICENSE file was found in the complete non-truncated snapshot tree and the inspected entry/source files contain no reuse grant; source visibility and bundled sprites do not establish redistribution rights. Limitations: Original asset provenance and explicit project licensing need clarification; do not label this open source. runtime_profiles.name: Documented OCS/PAL A500 configuration
runtime_profiles.notes: README/source and runner specify 512 KiB Chip plus 512 KiB slow RAM, PAL and joystick port 2. This is the documented configuration, not independently measured minimum; slow RAM is not Fast RAM.

project.status: Source reviewed; independent build and runtime untested
project.notes: Identity: A distinct native A500 implementation of Space Invaders, with 55 aliens, destructible shields, UFO, waves, lives, power-ups and named high scores in main.asm. Classification: Newly authored native homebrew using familiar arcade rules and Amiga custom chips. No extraction or decompilation of original arcade code is established; source ISA/platform stays empty rather than inventing binary provenance. Source CPU: No separately analyzed legacy binary or predecessor source ISA is identified. This homebrew implementation’s 68000 architecture belongs to its output target. Target CPU: The build script explicitly selects vasm -m68000 and Amiga hunk output; source uses 68000 registers and OCS custom-chip access. No PPC/RTG target is implied. Build: Bash/PowerShell recipes assemble and link the single source with vasm/vlink. Toolchain binaries and the copyrighted Kickstart ROM are deliberately excluded. Emulation expects a separately obtained legal ROM; no original arcade data file is required by the reviewed recipe. Limitations: No compilation, execution, gameplay or byte comparison was performed; all independent build flags remain null. Runtime profiles: The documented OCS/PAL A500 configuration is 512 KiB Chip plus 512 KiB slow RAM and Kickstart 1.3+. The runner confirms those memory settings; the source’s vertical-blank wait at PAL line 303 does not justify NTSC compatibility. AI: The author-written introduction explicitly attributes the initial project to Claude Fable 5 and later guided fixes to Opus. Record Claude and affirmative AI use as author testimony; the remainder of the README is labelled LLM-generated, so its claims are checked against source/configuration. This is not an inference from CLAUDE.md. Relationships: A root GPLv3 license is present. events.title: wasabid 0.3b3: LIVE - the view sends only what changed, compactly
events.message:
wasabid 0.3b3: LIVE - the view sends only what changed, compactly

The view's speed was the Wi-Fi hop (~28 MB/s with spikes), not the
Amiga: every frame was a full 3.7 MB 24-bit grab. New LIVE (0x4E):
the daemon keeps, per connection, the last picture it sent and returns
only the changed rectangles - RGB565 for deep screens, pen numbers plus
palette for native ones - as self-describing messages the bridge
forwards to the page untouched. A still screen is 8 bytes a frame.

Reading the card: LockBitMapTags, each row copied out with
CopyMemQuick, compared a longword at a time against the card's own
pixels from last time, only the changed span converted. All measured on
the A1200, 1280x960 BGRA32, by an Emu68-counter timing message (flags
bit 1): ReadPixelArray 46 ms alone; byte-wise or interleaved card reads
200+ ms; per-pixel conversion of a copied row 62 ms; this ~20 ms. The
lock covers only the comparison - nothing is sent under it.

Key press to picture on the page, over Wi-Fi: 52 ms every time, was
90-245 ms (median 164). The bridge looks 20x/s while busy, 5x/s when
still (~5% of the Amiga's CPU idle), falls back to GRAB for an older
daemon (WASABI_VIEW_NOLIVE forces it, to compare). The page draws
RGB565 and pen8, and shows native screens row-doubled with the pointer
in that space. grab stays exact 24-bit.

Headless Firefox against the A1200: all pass, including the page's
picture against a real grab (every channel within 7). 152 mock tests.

events.message:
Printing: printer unit and density, TurboPrint

The print window offers the configured printer.device units (0-9,
ENV:Sys/Printer[N].prefs, named after their driver) and the density
1-7 with the resolution of each. The driver switches its resolution
with the density: it is queried with a classic PRD_DUMPRPORT and
SPECIAL_NOPRINT (XDotsInch/YDotsInch), set in io_Special and in
printer.device's copy of the settings (some drivers, AmiAirPrint, only
read that; restored afterwards). Tool types PRINT_UNIT and
PRINT_DENSITY replace PRINT_DPI.

TurboPrint (TPMATCHWORD) does not know PRD_DUMPRPORTTAGS: the page is
rendered as RGB24 and sent with PRD_TPEXTDUMPRPORT, at once if the
memory allows, else in bands with SPECIAL_NOFORMFEED (one job in
TurboSpool; tested in Amiberry without a real printer).

events.title: wasabi view: the Amiga's screen in a window, with its mouse and keyboard
events.message:
wasabi view: the Amiga's screen in a window, with its mouse and keyboard

Step 4 of ~/Projects/Ideas/wasabi-gui.md. `wasabi view` starts a bridge
(wasabi_view.py, stdlib only, WebSocket by hand) that serves a page
(view/: Vite + React + Radix Themes + TypeScript, tokens and lint rules
as in BBX's web part; dist/ committed so no Node is needed to run it).

- One Amiga connection per page; each cycle sends the page's input
  first (~3 ms a command), then grabs and sends only the rows that
  changed - 8-10 pictures a second on the A1200's 1280x960.
- Keys by position (KeyboardEvent.code -> raw key), so the Amiga's own
  keymap makes the characters. Settings choose which PC key plays Left/
  Right Amiga, Ctrl and the Alts (Ctrl, Alt, Super, Menu), saved in
  ~/.config/wasabi/view.json. Defaults: Right Ctrl = Right Amiga, Menu =
  Left Amiga.
- Two bugs found by testing on the A1200, both fixed: a separately sent
  key-up that waited behind a slow grab let input.device's repeat type
  "eeeeeee" (ordinary keys now go as whole presses, the PC's repeat
  repeats them); and waking from the frame wait re-queued the message
  behind newer ones, so Right Amiga+E could arrive as E-then-Amiga.
- Opens a Chromium-family --app window, else a new Firefox window
  (--kiosk for full screen); ends when the window closes (--stay).

Tested in a headless Firefox against the real A1200 (test/live.mjs:
picture, clicks, typing, Right Ctrl+E as Right Amiga+E with no stuck
keys, settings; test/settings.mjs: the dialog), right-button menus by
hand, and offline in `make test` (150 pass).

events.title: Share fonts, build rules and test harness in dev, shrink and speed up the libraries
events.message:
Share fonts, build rules and test harness in dev, shrink and speed up the libraries

One Beautiful Boot font: dev/lib/font/bbfont_glyphs.inc is the master,
bbfont.inc slices it for assembly (BBFONT_FIRST/LAST), bbfont_c.inc is the
generated C table and dev/tools/fonts.py serves the build tools; the three
divergent copies and the hand-kept MICRO-SOKOBAN subset are generated from it
(micro-sokoban/tools/hud_font.py). `fonts.py --check` runs in make test-assets.

dev/cc65/apple2.mk carries the tool variables, library paths, assembler
include path, the DOS 3.3 disk command and run/clean/distclean for every
program Makefile. dev/tools/a2test.py is the shared Python harness (ld65
labels, a2run/a2shot runs, dump decoding, test disks) and dos33.py now reads
images (catalog, read_file, replace_file); the MICRO-SOKOBAN, ARKABREAKOUT,
CHROMABREAK, Maze3D, dev/tests and dev/bench scripts use them.

Library size and speed, behaviour unchanged (a2run captures of every disk
and the full test suite): lib/apple2 and lib/hgr routines assemble only when
referenced (.ifref), a shared HGR_CLEAR_LOOP clears 8 KB in 51K cycles
instead of 90K, hgr_text8 computes its colour mask once per glyph and can
drop rev7_tab (HGR_TEXT8_HGR_ORDER); in hgrc the page flip is one asm EOR
loop (3.4K cycles instead of 16K), white 16x16 text goes through the colour
blitter, the 8x8 blitter works a row at a time (hgr_puts8 24K -> 9K cycles),
the C wrappers index hgr_col7/phase7/mask7 instead of dividing, the row
tables need no multiply, and hgr_mode_asm is split so DHGR programs do not
link the HGR init. Chess, LOGO, the demos and MICRO-SOKOBAN drop their private
copies of print_str_ax, clear_hgr and the scanline tables. Binaries shrink
by 42 to 459 bytes (ARKABREAKOUT 8129 -> 7670).

events.message:
TUNEFX: a richer title-tune player -- struck envelopes, the melody's vibrato, the chord arpeggiated, a noise bass at its true pitch

midi2snd.py --fx writes a stream of variable-length records (frames, a mask, a note for each
voice that changed, bit 7 where it is struck) with a header: tone 2's period for each note's
bass, the three envelopes (start, fall, rest), the vibrato and the arpeggio's rate.  menus.s,
under TUNEFX: the melody on tone 0 (envelope, vibrato after a delay), the chord's notes in
turn on tone 1, the bass as periodic noise clocked by tone 2 (silent) -- its own pitch, a
fifteenth of tone 2's, below the tones' 122 Hz floor; the bass and the chord ring on through
their rests; the chip given only what changed (MFX_A/PL/PH, low RAM with the rest of the
state).  A split (SPLIT, G3 by default) keeps an oom-pah's chord from being taken for its
bass.  Off by default: the plain stream is byte-identical and Commando's disc is too.
Measured in jsbeeb on both machines: a vsync's step about 680 cycles, 1,940 at most, and no
CRTC write of the menus' chain later than before.  GUIDE.md: the option.

events.title: Judge every garment vertex inside the body by the winding number
events.message:
Judge every garment vertex inside the body by the winding number

The penetration measurement only asked the winding number where the
nearest face's projection already exceeded the tolerance, so a vertex
inside the body with a small or negative projection (a crease, two body
parts crossing in a kneel) was never counted. fit.depths now decides
inside or outside for every vertex by the winding number and measures the
depth as the distance to the body's surface; the resolver pushes an inside
vertex towards its nearest surface point and searches its shortest way out
step by step.

A clip-filtered measurement now finds each pose's baked offsets by
(clip, frame, stride) instead of dropping them, the baked table is checked
against the current clips and body corners before measuring (failing loud
on a mismatch), and the resolved cache is rebuilt whenever the body,
clips, fitted garments or config it came from differ. The report's corners
run in parallel.

events.title: test(e2e): read the ROM signature from the ROM, not from whatever is mapped (#67)
events.message:
test(e2e): read the ROM signature from the ROM, not from whatever is mapped (#67)

beads-idt4. test_model_change_rebuild and test_profile_load_rebuilds_machine
fingerprint a model by 16 bytes at 0x02E0, read with a plain `mem read`. That
is the CPU view, and the firmware pages the lower ROM in and out constantly.
On a running machine the read got ROM ~93% of the time on a 6128 and ~50% on
a 6128+. Otherwise it got the zeros of the RAM underneath, or a byte-by-byte
mix while the Z80 ran. On a loaded CI Mac the reference machines read all
zeros: both failure shapes ("Initial ... != 6128 ref 0000..." and "Rebuilt
... != 6128+ ref 0000...") were the reference read, never the machine under
test. The bead's guess (config apply not awaited) was wrong.

A shared read_lower_rom_signature() pauses the machine, quiesces it with a
single step, then steps forward until the CPU view of the window differs from
its --view=ram read, so the bytes provably come from ROM. It doesn't depend
on the wall clock and leaves the machine running.

The context line's rom:LO flag is not used as proof. On a 6128+ it can lead
the memory device by one step right after the firmware's ROM-switch OUT at
&B9B2 (filed as beads-szc0).

profile, old-format rows) is repaired or reset on load.

SUCCESS, BRAVO and the other key screens wait for a quiet keyboard, so
a repeating or typed-ahead key no longer skips them, and IO ERR covers
the whole status field.

to a segment run from the level-pack buffer, which frees 290 bytes of
resident memory.

events.title: No anonymous labels: every ':' named, and the build rejects them (tools/noanon.py)
events.message:
No anonymous labels: every ':' named, and the build rejects them (tools/noanon.py)

An anonymous reference counts labels across the whole assembly unit -- macro expansions
and conditional arms included -- so a ':' added or removed anywhere retargets branches far
away, and a cold path escapes every test.  All ~150 converted: cheap labels in code; in
the macros cheap labels too (a .local name is a normal symbol and ends the caller's @
scope), a fixed name prefixed with the macro's where it expands once in a scope
(ringup, ringmod7, spnext, spcold, MIRDIRTY_BODY, recnext...), else passed in by the caller
(pagestep, runn, the loader's print); NIB_LOOPS's row join a normal label (ds_rowjoin: a
branch reaches it across ds_rowloop); the count-holding ':' lines that nothing referenced
removed.  tools/noanon.py runs first in build.sh.  Cleo's disc byte-identical, and every
build option that builds (ALLLEVELS, TIGHTBSS, B6PACK) byte-identical too; the options
that did not build before fail the same way.  Comments and DESIGN.md say the rule.

events.title: Resolve the garments out of the body frame by frame instead of by corrective shapes
events.message:
Resolve the garments out of the body frame by frame instead of by corrective shapes

The pose-driven corrective shapes (a linear blend of joint-angle shapes)
did not get every garment within tolerance: a hem pinched between thigh
and calf in a kneel needs an offset no blend of joint angles gives without
flaring the cloth in every other pose. scripts/villager/resolve.py now
resolves every pose the penetration report measures (each clip frame, a
gait's at each measured stride, on each body corner) on its own: pushed
out along the nearest surface's normal with the push spread over its mesh
ring, a vertex pushed back and forth or on a crease moved along its
shortest way out, and the result validated on the float32 offsets as the
game would draw them. The offsets are stored sparse per pose and corner in
the hung, baked frame; src/render/villagerGarmentBaked.ts evaluates them
like the pipeline (frame and stride interpolation, the corner blend of the
body morphs), checked against garment-baked-check.json.

The linear correction (correct.py, villagerGarmentDrivers.ts, its balance
values and check file) is removed. Penetration report: 32 of 32 garments
within the 0.003 tolerance in every frame (was 24 of 32). The table holds
5.69 M vertex offsets, about 43 MiB at 16-bit index and floats: not
shippable as is.

events.title: Konami's Synthesizer: la ROM original, no el volcado [a]
events.message:
Konami's Synthesizer: la ROM original, no el volcado [a]

El volcado [a] (sha1 73a40e7d) cambia 16 bytes en 0x4105-0x4114: donde
el original pone en la pagina 2 la RAM del ordenador con ENASLT (slot
guardado en 0xD854) y luego devuelve el cartucho (0xD855), [a] escribe
out (0xFE),3 / out (0xFE),1. Repuestos esos bytes, el sha1 es el del
GoodMSX original (2feff37d). El cartucho no lleva RAM: los samples van
en la RAM del ordenador, 0x8000-0xBFFF. Medido en openMSX (VG-8020):
durante SYN A8=0xF4 y lo escrito en 0x8000 se queda.

events.message:
finalfight: faster Lua harness (read_range dumps, cached memory methods), gated byte-identical

lib.lua M.ram/M.region use mem:read_range: equal to the per-word loop (work RAM 65,536 of 65,536 bytes, gfx RAM 196,608 of 196,608), about 100x faster per dump.
stagebot.lua and ffdrive.lua cache the memory methods, read fields only for in-use records, allocate no table per frame and hash the trace with the mask applied once:
34.6 s to 31.5 s over 20,000 frames of sb_s4 (1.10x; MAME is about 79% of a bot run's wall time).

Gates: sb_s4 frames 87,000 to 107,000 with the stage 2 to 5 options, work RAM, gfx RAM, bot.log and drive_trace.txt byte-identical to the unoptimised files, twice; default options
py/stage/run.sh boss and stage1 reproduce py/stage/README.md's hashes (sb_boss RAM a0cb6b52, sb_s1 RAM 6389dc8c, gfx 359a7c73) and are cmp-identical to the pre-change run.
README "Harness facts" records the measurements (read_range is the wrong tool for small per-frame scans; cached methods are 3.4x cheaper per call).

events.title: ttl_raster's comment: &FE21 is a 2 MHz access, so nothing realigns the loop
events.message:
ttl_raster's comment: &FE21 is a 2 MHz access, so nothing realigns the loop

The comment said every pass starts with a write to &FE21 "on the 1 MHz
bus", stalling the CPU to the same phase so the padded loop cannot
drift. The Video ULA (&FE20-&FE3F) is a 2 MHz access - jsbeeb's
is1MHzAccess, Master included (read 2026-10-06; beeb-port-kit's
hardware-facts already called the explanation unmeasured and probably
wrong). So a pass that takes a cycle extra - today the ttl_pal loads
cross a page for the later steps - carries into every later write on
the line, and what TTL_RASTER_PAD was tuned against is this layout:
moving ttl_pal or the loop moves the bars. Found by the BANK1 review's
skeptic (docs/dataflow-review-bank1.md, P1-P6).

Comment only: every disc file byte-identical to the build before it
but !BOOT, which carries the stamp.

events.title: runtime: backup RAM answers over 0x00180000-0x001FFFFF, as Mednafen
events.message:
runtime: backup RAM answers over 0x00180000-0x001FFFFF, as Mednafen

The Saturn's backup RAM repeats every 64 KiB up to 0x001FFFFF; the
runtime knew only the first 64 KiB and stopped on any other address. A
1996 -pic game loads its fighters' sprites by SCU DMA from a list and
reads one source past the list's end, at 0x001F0010: on the Saturn that
is backup RAM, and the 32 bytes land in a VDP1 command slot nothing
draws. Its first battle now opens.

An access there was fatal before, so no game that ran is changed: the
four others' runs byte-identical.

events.title: release: bundle the hatari-pist fork into the macOS app
events.message:
release: bundle the hatari-pist fork into the macOS app

The macOS archive shipped without an emulator because the fork links Homebrew's
SDL2 and libpng from /opt/homebrew, and rewiring those dylibs into the .app was
work nobody had done: Linux dodges it with the AppImage, Windows by staging the
MSYS2 DLLs beside the exe. The bundling step does the macOS version — copy the
transitive closure of non-system dylibs into Contents/Frameworks, rewrite every
load path to @rpath (the trick macdeployqt just played for Qt), add the rpaths,
then refuse the artifact if anything still points at the build host's prefix or
if the binary fails to load. The seal step now asserts the sealed app resolves
its own emulator and that it speaks HRDB and the media channel, so a bundle
that silently fell back to stock Hatari fails the release instead of shipping.

While here, fix the source offer the notices have been printing: the fork
component named tattlemuss/hatari at a hardcoded commit, but Linux and Windows
have shipped hatari-pist for weeks. The build-hatari action now reports the pin
it actually used and collect-notices consumes it — and fails rather than guess
when a fork binary arrives without one. `pist --diagnose` gains a `media:` line
so the sealed-app assertion, and any user, can see whether the discovered
emulator can drive the panel.

events.title: runtime: VDP1 takes the VBlank's end at the next HBlank, as Mednafen
events.message:
runtime: VDP1 takes the VBlank's end at the next HBlank, as Mednafen

Mednafen's VDP1 takes a change of the VBlank at the next HBlank
(SetHBVB), while the SCU raises VBlank-OUT at once, so a VBlank-OUT
handler that asks for a frame change (FBCR) right away gets it in the
same blanking. The runtime changed VDP1's frame at line 0, before the
interrupt was offered: such a handler always got its change a field
late, and a game that waits for the draw's end (EDSR) before it asks
changed frame every other field. The frame change, its erase and the
draw it starts now wait for a line entered by a later call than the one
that raised VBlank-OUT.

A 1996 -pic game's story scene changes frame every field, as in Beetle
(49.7 distinct pictures a second in its recording), in time with its
music; it had run at half speed. A 1995 FMV game's SEGA logo is shorter
(its opening starts 3.56 s after the logo appears, 3.15 s in Beetle,
6.4 s before), so its run reaches its title 290 VBlanks earlier.
Virtual Hydlide byte-identical; a two-disc SGL game and a 1997 SHC game
with overlays a frame apart in places (an object their title draws every
other field shows in the other field).

events.title: fix(ppc): report why a PowerPC context stopped (#4160)
events.message:
fix(ppc): report why a PowerPC context stopped (#4160)

When a PowerPC slice ends with the context stopped by a fault (an
unsupported import, an exception, an unimplemented instruction, a
memory fault, or a branch to address zero with a live link register),
the runner records the halt but prints nothing unless load tracing is
enabled, so the fault reads like a clean exit. Print one line naming
the unsupported import (looked up by symbol index) or the run result,
with pc, sp and lr. A plain return from the entry point, ExitToShell,
and stops inside 68K code reached through Mixed Mode stay silent; the
detailed load-trace dump is unchanged.

events.title: Add a profiler to the native app, and an example program to try it on
events.message:
Add a profiler to the native app, and an example program to try it on

The core keeps a call tree, a frame by frame timeline and the time spent at
every address (src/core/debug/profiler.hpp, owned by MachineDebug, fed by
both machines). Calls are followed through JSR, JSL, BRK, COP and every
interrupt taken, and popped by the stack pointer, so tricks with the stack
come out right. A IIgs is measured on its slow clock, fractions included.

Debug > Profiler shows it: a timeline of each frame split between the
costliest routines, routines, call tree, flame graph and hot lines, and the
selected routine's callers, callees and annotated code. Routines are named
by the debugger's symbols. examples/profiler-demo is a ca65 project whose
routines cost deliberately different amounts.

events.title: Landings: a return to an address no call returns to (a longjmp)
events.message:
Landings: a return to an address no call returns to (a longjmp)

A task system can leave a task at once: restore the scheduler's stack,
`mov.l #X,rn; lds rn,pr; rts`, and the scheduler goes on at X. A C++ call
cannot return elsewhere. Discovery now lists such X (Program.landings);
the recompiler makes them labels, wraps every call of the function that
holds one in a try that goes on at the landing an SH2Unwind names, and
writes them in the module's table (SH2Module.landings); the runtime,
when a return goes to a landing of an active module instead of its
call's address, throws SH2Unwind, which unwinds the frames between to
that function. A return anywhere else is fatal as before.

The four other games have no landings; their runs are byte-identical.

An older rip keeps the whole disc in one .bin, with track 2's pregap

The runtime's disc lays the sheet out as runs of sectors: each track of

events.title: runtime: the boot runs IP.BIN's initial program when a build has it
events.message:
runtime: the boot runs IP.BIN's initial program when a build has it

A game may put its crt0 in IP.BIN: the initial program after the area
block masks the interrupts, clears memory and jumps through a table at
the 1st read address, which is then not code; the game also calls back
into IP.BIN later. When a module covers IP.BIN (0x06002000), the boot
activates it beside the 1st read's and enters at the area block
(0x06002E00: each area's bra leads to the next, the last to the initial
program), as the BIOS does; if that returns, it goes on to the 1st read
address. Without such a module the boot is as before.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: discover: SHC's position-independent code
events.message:
discover: SHC's position-independent code

Code compiled with SHC's -pic calls through `mov.l #k,rn; bsrf rn`,
jumps far through `braf`, and takes addresses with
`mov.l #k,rn; mova T,r0; add r0,rn`. Discovery now resolves bsrf and
braf (outside switches) by constants, target = the jump + 4 + the
register, as the emitter already did; carries constants through
`add Rm,Rn`; and takes an address computed that way and never called
directly (a task's handler handed to the scheduler) as an entry when it
starts at a boundary (after a terminator, a tail braf or a literal pool,
reached or not) and descends into clean code that meets no known data.

On a -pic game: 944 unresolved sites of eight programs become 441, and
the run no longer stops on the task handlers. The four other games'
discovery is unchanged (the same vectors), their runs byte-identical.

events.title: fix(network): honour SO_RCVTIMEO/SO_SNDTIMEO in blocking bsdsocket calls (#2384)
events.message:
fix(network): honour SO_RCVTIMEO/SO_SNDTIMEO in blocking bsdsocket calls (#2384)

* fix(network): honour SO_RCVTIMEO/SO_SNDTIMEO in blocking bsdsocket calls

The POSIX bsdsocket emulation runs blocking recv/send on a non-blocking host socket and waited in select() without a timeout, so a guest that set SO_RCVTIMEO or SO_SNDTIMEO blocked forever when the peer stalled. recv now obeys SO_RCVTIMEO and send obeys SO_SNDTIMEO, returning EWOULDBLOCK when the timeout expires with nothing transferred, as Roadshow and BSD stacks do. connect and accept still wait without a limit.

* fix(network): cap the raw-socket recv override at the guest timeout

Raw sockets block in recv() with a forced 1 s SO_RCVTIMEO, so a guest timeout shorter than a second still waited the full second. Use the guest's value when it is shorter. The helper test now tolerates kernels that store socket timeouts in rounded-up scheduler ticks.

events.title: tools/dataflow: objects one array a field (layout='soa'), a game that builds its own records (game_bind), and type dispatch through jmp (ind) / jmp (abs,x)
events.message:
tools/dataflow: objects one array a field (layout='soa'), a game that builds its own records (game_bind), and type dispatch through jmp (ind) / jmp (abs,x)

Cleo's objects are OBJ_MAX records with one array a field (O_TYPE,y with Y = obj), built
by level_init, dispatched by process_object's jmp (jv) (Model B) / jmp (@tab,x)
(Master).  ranges.py now models that: a field access is the current record's when its
index register equals the current-record byte (kept across a call's projection); a jmp
through a per-type pointer or index splits the state by type as the rts dispatch did;
the game's own type store can bind the type.  With tools/dataflow_cleo.py, Cleo's
handlers are annotated per type (ty=bat ...) and process_object's jmp (jv) is resolved.
A run with no config is unchanged (Cleo's annotations without it identical).

events.title: wasabi: made for scripts - nothing hangs, wait, look, --json, a safety catch
events.message:
wasabi: made for scripts - nothing hangs, wait, look, --json, a safety catch

Step 2 of ~/Projects/Ideas/wasabi-gui.md, client only (daemon stays 0.3b1).

Nothing hangs: every reply has a --silence deadline (default 15 s); a
daemon that takes the connection and says nothing is exit 125 "the
Amiga stopped answering", never a hang. run used to wait forever: now
every 10 quiet seconds it pings the daemon on a side connection, so a
quiet command keeps going and a frozen machine is reported. run
--max-time S Ctrl-Cs a command that runs too long (exit 124) - proven
live on the A1200 with C:Wait 30.

wait window|task|file|change|still|up, with --gone, --contains and
--timeout (exit 124). debug/snoop --for S and --until TEXT end a stream
by themselves. reboot --yes --wait returns when the daemon is back.
All wait kinds proven live on the A1200.

look grabs the front screen or one window (--window TITLE) to a PNG
and prints only its path. windows now scales y/height by grab's row
doubling, so on a 640x256 screen its numbers match the picture.

--json on ls, ps, screen, windows, ping, run, wait, look. Exit codes:
0 ok, 1 failed, 2 unreachable/usage, 124 your limit ran out, 125 the
Amiga stopped answering.

Safety catch: put/deploy/del in SYS: C: L: LIBS: DEVS: S: FONTS:
LOCALE: ENVARC: or a config 'protect =' volume need --force; reboot
needs --yes.

136 mock tests pass, including a SIGSTOPped mock for both silence paths.

events.title: wasabid 0.3b1: keyboard, and every window as text
events.message:
wasabid 0.3b1: keyboard, and every window as text

wasabi key type TEXT [--enter] sends characters; the daemon maps each
with keymap.library's MapANSI() and the current default keymap, so the
PC needs no idea of the Amiga's layout - Swedish å/ä/ö/@/{[]} came out
byte for byte on the A1200. The whole text is mapped before the first
key goes out, so an untypeable character fails cleanly. Dead-key
sequences go out as one event with ie_Prev1/2Down filled, per the
autodoc.

wasabi key press NAME... sends key positions (raw codes) by name, with
modifiers: return, esc, f1, up, ramiga+e, ctrl+\. Proven live: Shell
history recall, ctrl+\ closing a Shell, ramiga+e opening Workbench's
Execute Command, its underlined shortcut cancelling it.

wasabi windows lists every screen and its windows - place, size,
borders, active/backdrop, the task reading it - walked under
LockIBase() into a buffer and sent after unlocking, so a slow network
never holds Intuition still. Positions are in grab/mouse pixel space.

events.title: ui: measure captured mouse deltas event-to-event, warp only at edges
events.message:
ui: measure captured mouse deltas event-to-event, warp only at edges

Re-centring the cursor on every captured move assumes the warp survives until
the next event. Under a guest driver that integrates the host pointer
absolutely — VirtualBox mouse integration, which is how a Windows VM is
normally driven — the next injected event overwrites the warp, so each delta
becomes the full offset from the panel centre instead of the hand's increment:
reported from Windows as a pointer that moves vertically at absurd sensitivity
and not at all horizontally, while Linux and bare-metal Windows are fine
because their relative mice honour the warp.

Event-to-event deltas are correct under both pointer models, and the host
cursor is blank while captured, so letting it roam costs nothing. The warp
stays only where it earns its keep: within 32px of a screen edge, where a
pinned cursor would stop delivering motion, re-based so the warp itself
contributes no delta.

events.title: Overscan: warm the whole bottom flick, for the Mega STE's cache
events.message:
Overscan: warm the whole bottom flick, for the Mega STE's cache

On a real Mega STE at 16MHz with the cache on, a frame that drew lost
the bottom border: a demo's overscan part lost it in 36% of frames.
The cache is 8192 one-word lines, direct-mapped, emptied whole by every
BLiTTER bus grant and replaced word by word by the CPU's own traffic,
and the ISR's warm-up - the tail of the flick with slot 15's entries -
left the poll's branch target, the nops slot 15 skips and both table
words of the slot actually caught to be fetched cold inside a window of
a few cycles.

The bottom ISR now reads all 32 table words in at its head on a cached
CPU (a calibrated dbra turn under 9 cycles), runs the whole path from
the poll's entry against a table of zeros, keeps its code, tables and
variables in one block of .text so none can share a line, and returns
from the flick through a4 so no stack write lands between the warm pass
and the 50Hz write. The timed instructions are unchanged, so every
measured constant still holds.

tests/hatari/ovcache.c, on the machine, one disturbance at a time in
one binary, 150 frames: a cache flush with no drawing at all opened the
border 0-30 times, one one-word blit 0-25, a 16-row fill 0-43; with the
whole path warm, 150 in every case (149 under a 24K CPU copy a frame),
and 150 everywhere with the cache off. The demo: 545 misses in 1525
frames before, 1 in 1524 after. Plain ST and STE in Hatari unchanged,
