project.notes: Tony Nicholson’s ZXCC maintains John Elliott’s ZXCC 0.5.7 lineage. It loads original CP/M .COM/.CPM programs at 0x100 and runs Ian Collier’s Z80 interpreter, while wrappers such as zxc, zxas, zxlink, zxlibr and zxobjtohex adapt host arguments for existing compiler tools. The original release and this maintained repository are one project family, not separate records. Canonical root was absent from the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and the prior deduplication index. Inspected default-branch head: c45e5065eca63dd045d60511a8b21ab7f567303a. Cross-development tooling executes original binaries with partial CP/M 2/3 API translation. The ED FE trap routes BDOS/BIOS calls to native C; CPMREDIR maps CP/M drives and FCB operations onto host files. Required bios.bin is the bundled tiny ZXCC-specific synthetic BIOS/BDOS shim, with Z80/bios.zsm source, not an original vendor ROM or full CP/M OS. Users separately supply HI-TECH or Digital Research compiler binaries, includes, libraries and overlays. The actual guest engine is Z80, confirmed by bin/z80.c, the shim and documentation. CP/M is the guest OS family, not a modern host target. The compatibility layer implements a restricted CP/M 3 subset useful for CP/M 2/3 toolchains; arbitrary BIOS/disk-layout programs are not established. Filename conversion enforces guest 8.3 expectations, user areas are unimplemented and unsupported BDOS calls terminate. README’s ZEXDOC success is a maintainer claim, not independent complete-ISA proof. README and Visual Studio instructions explicitly support Windows x86/x86-64; project configurations corroborate those outputs. README reports macOS Sonoma x86 and arm builds, and a recent commit specifically addresses Apple arm64 configure handling, supporting canonical ARM64 as well. Linux/Unix/macOS have documented Autotools routes, but no extra ISA is inferred from C portability. Current README explicitly drops MS-DOS/DR-DOS host support despite historical DOS references in older documentation. Autotools/configure/make builds C, CPMIO and CPMREDIR, with curses/ncurses and optional readline; --with-filetracker enables Unix-side open-file tracking. The Visual Studio solution supplies x86/x64 configurations and bundled PDCurses DLLs. README reports Debian Bookworm and macOS Sonoma builds, while recent commits describe Autotools compatibility repairs. Those claims were not independently reproduced. The complete tree contains no GitHub Actions workflow; no observed CI success is asserted. All four build flags remain null: compilation, execution, gameplay and byte-equivalence are independently unverified. Documentation establishes installation/search requirements for bios.bin, BINDIR80, LIBDIR80, INCDIR80 and required guest libraries/overlays; Windows builds also depend on the matching PDCurses DLL. These are software dependencies, not quantified hardware or minimum-OS requirements. types: experimental original-binary PowerPC user-mode emulator with imported API shims
project.status: Experimental; no license grant found; MacBinary saving and API coverage incomplete; independently untested
project.notes: Treeki/Ninji’s Rust runner loads original PowerPC PEF MPW executables and replaces imported Mac APIs with host callbacks through Unicorn. macOS is an implemented native-fork path, Windows is an incomplete MacBinary path, and Linux is a conditional user-reported path requiring a source workaround. src/main.rs reads the requested original tool through MacFile, parses its PEF data fork and resources, links it into emulated memory, forwards argv and returns the emulated exit status. README reports MWCPPC from CodeWarrior Pro 1 and DeRez results. These are upstream demonstrations, not independent compatibility tests; this record is the experimental runner rather than CodeWarrior/MPW itself. Root and record ID are absent from the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and the prior dedup index. Inspected main tip: a0d23d515987ae5b486da9430e0b78a02ac93b4f. Substantive emulator/development tooling: src/linker.rs builds transition-vector shims for imported symbols; src/emulator/mod.rs installs InterfaceLib/StdCLib and Toolbox/C-library callbacks and handles them through a PowerPC supervisor-call hook. Original PEF instructions run inside Unicorn without booting Classic Mac OS. Missing imports remain logged, the initialization vector is explicitly unimplemented, and the README lists missing PEF relocations and APIs. XCOFF support is not established. Unicorn is explicitly created with Arch::PPC and Mode::BIG_ENDIAN | Mode::PPC32. The original source platform is Classic Mac OS and source_cpu is PowerPC, specifically 32-bit big-endian PEF executables. This guest configuration says nothing about the native CPU used to run Rust/Unicorn. The inspected Cargo manifest, implementation and complete tree contain no explicit current native-output CPU matrix or host target triplet. The historical commit about Unicorn on M1 Macs is a dependency-workaround report, not a current minimum/support matrix, so target_cpu remains empty. Platform labels preserve implementation intent with important qualifications: native macOS xattrs, incomplete Windows MacBinary handling and Linux only after the manual xattr workaround described in merged PR #1. None is promoted to universal tested support. Cargo.toml selects Rust edition 2021, unicorn-engine dependency version range 2.0.1 and xattr 0.2.2 among the parser/runtime dependencies. No host build recipe matrix or CI exists in the complete tree. PR #1 reports Linux DeRez working only after manually commenting out the xattr::SUPPORTED_PLATFORM branch; that branch still exists at the reviewed tip and the same report reaches unimplemented fseek. Source availability and dependency declarations do not establish a clean build on all intended hosts. All four build flags remain null; no candidate compilation, guest execution, emulation, gameplay or byte comparison was performed. No explicit host OS version, CPU model or RAM minimum is documented, so runtime_profiles is empty. src/filesystem.rs uses com.apple.FinderInfo and com.apple.ResourceFork xattrs for the native path. Its MacBinary save branch calls unimplemented!(), after File::create has already opened/truncated the destination; Windows saving is therefore a material limitation, not just an absent test. Do not run against irreplaceable host files. Linux xattr modification and missing fseek remain conditional portability/API evidence, not a clean upstream runtime profile. runtime_profiles.name: Documented Linux terminal/headless host
runtime_profiles.notes: Original TOS executables run against the host terminal. TOSEMU_NO_WINDOW=1 suppresses windows; NO_WAYLAND=1 removes graphical build dependencies. No host CPU, RAM or OS-version minimum is documented, and no build/runtime was independently tested.

project.status: Substantive source reviewed; experimental compatibility; build and runtime independently untested
project.notes: TOSEMU is Johan Toverland Thelin’s hosted environment for original Atari TOS executables, not a decompilation of one guest application. The current PRG loader opens and maps the supplied file, checks magic 0x601A, constructs the guest environment and applies relocation entries. The tosemu executable runs a program directly; the separate tosaesd daemon supports shared GEM accessory sessions and is not a prerequisite for a single CLI invocation. README explicitly targets integration into Linux and excludes general games/demos. This repository is counted once; its hosted EmuTOS and Musashi components are dependencies, not additional runner discoveries. Canonical repository and lineage aliases were screened against the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and prior dedup index; no existing counted project matched. Source snapshot 443340b2dfcf9e691a080bc4e3722102bc9c2839, non-truncated tree with 274 entries. Tooling: original-binary CPU emulation plus TOS system-call reimplementation. src/musashi.c intercepts traps 1, 2, 13 and 14 for GEMDOS, GEM, BIOS and XBIOS, while src/gemdosfile.c maps guest file reads to host stdio and copies data into emulated memory. The guest instructions still execute in Musashi; native host API handling does not make the guest a source port or ahead-of-time translation. Hosted EmuTOS AES/VDI routines supply graphical APIs without booting an Atari ROM. Terminal usage, headless support and self-hosted retro development tests establish the requested runner category, without implying complete TOS or ST hardware compatibility. The guest ISA is Motorola 68000: tossystem.c selects M68K_CPU_TYPE_68000 and musashiconf.h disables later 68010/020/030/040 processors and the PMMU. Original .TTP/.TOS/.PRG guest binaries and TOS belong in source_platforms/source_cpu. The Musashi package’s broader M680x0 support is not TOSEMU support for those later guest CPUs. The FPU entry stubs abort and are not an emulated FPU. Neither the build’s __mcoldfire__ adaptation define nor EmuTOS source ancestry establishes a ColdFire host target. Linux is the explicit host target, but the inspected host Makefile and Ubuntu workflow do not establish a host ISA support matrix or minimum processor. target_cpu remains empty. GCC, C source, -no-pie, 32-bit GEM pointer fields and ubuntu-latest are not sufficient to label x86-64, ARM or another host architecture. The EmuTOS __mcoldfire__ define is a source-adaptation switch selecting portable C rather than a claim that the runnable host program targets ColdFire. README requires recursive Musashi and EmuTOS submodules and make; Makefile uses GCC, generates Musashi opcode tables and links hosted EmuTOS AES/VDI. NO_WAYLAND=1 removes the Wayland/xkbcommon headers, libraries and protocol-generation route; the Ubuntu workflow explicitly uses it for check and emuvdi-check. The GUI route needs Wayland tooling; optional detected integrations include D-Bus, libpng, FreeType/fontconfig and ALSA. The hosted EmuTOS build uses -fno-strict-aliasing and non-PIE flags because guest APIs contain 32-bit pointer fields. Devpac/Lattice tests are separate from building the host runner and require the original installations. project.notes: run68x is the maintained Human68k CUI emulator derived from run68. The README names rururutan/run68 and several run68mac forks as origins. The current C implementation has its own executable loader, 68000 interpreter, debugger and Human68k-compatible services. Modern tooling executes original Human68k .X and raw .R programs from argv, using host files and the existing terminal. load.c reads the HU header, performs relocation and initializes BSS; run68.c builds a PSP and enters the interpreter. DOS calls, IOCS and FE floating-point helpers are implemented in host C. The initialized HUMAN.SYS name represents a synthetic PSP, not a required OS image. The inspected direct-run path needs no original ROM or booted Human68k. The guest is the Motorola 68000 instruction set, explicitly retained even when the -himem option expands addressability. The interpreter dispatches instructions by their upper nibble. High memory is a non-hardware-compatible extension and does not imply a 68020/68060 guest. The X-file loader rejects bound executables; partial DOS/IOCS and graphics-related stubs do not establish arbitrary X68000 application or hardware compatibility. The host executable has explicit Windows x64 evidence in README and the win-x64 release workflow, so target_cpu is x86-64. Windows and Ubuntu under WSL are maintainer-confirmed build environments. project.notes: One riscose project family is tracked across its original SourceForge home, repo.or.cz lineage and the inspected hamishcoleman/riscose GitHub tree. The original site describes SWI-level execution of unmodified RISC OS applications without a RISC OS ROM. README demonstrates direct GNU grep invocation with host stdin and filenames. Current main.c and mem.c load an application image at guest address 0x8000 and execute it through arm_run_routine. Although README still says Absolute executables only, current code and man/riscose.1 also expose module and utility modes; this is evidence of implemented paths, not complete compatibility. The GitHub tip is 2023-10-25; a prior indexed repo.or.cz summary reported 2023-11-02, but its direct access was geographically blocked. That lineage is retained without pretending the GitHub tip is the newest commit anywhere in the family. Canonical repository and lineage aliases were screened against the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and prior dedup index; no existing counted project matched. Source snapshot ec85f120327ce37ecee8bbcb90f3111330bd5bae, non-truncated tree with 231 entries. Tooling: original ARM instruction execution combined with RISC OS SWI/SharedCLib reimplementation, focused on command-line software rather than a whole Archimedes machine. configure.ac selects ARMulator by default, sleeve as an alternate interpreter, or a separate native ARM backend. src/swi.c dispatches registered native handlers, and xosfile_load_stamped translates a RISC OS filename then uses host open/fstat/read. Guest instructions are interpreted for the default route; native SWI handling is not a translation of the guest binary. The optional same-ISA native backend remains a distinct execution design, not proof of general modern ARM compatibility. Runtime API coverage is partial, and unregistered SWIs return an error in the inspected tip. ARM is the explicit guest ISA in the man page, loader interface and ARMulator integration. The vendored armemu.c describes an ARM6 instruction emulator; historical native code uses 26-bit user-mode assumptions. These establish the old ARM/RISC OS execution model but not a complete per-CPU or per-RISC-OS-version guest support table. source_cpu therefore stays at the existing ARM family label rather than inventing a particular ARM2/ARM3/ARM6 minimum. RISC OS is the guest platform, not the operating system running the hosted command-line program. target_cpu includes ARM only for the explicitly selectable same-ISA native host backend: the man page says an ARM host can execute the instructions directly, configure.ac exposes native, and native-arm.c uses Linux ARM signal contexts and USR26_MODE. This is separate from ARM as the guest ISA. The default ARMulator/sleeve host CPU support matrix is not established and receives no invented x86-64 or other label. Recent history includes an i386 arithmetic-overflow fix, but a fix alone is not treated as an exhaustive supported-platform matrix or CPU minimum. No claim is made that the historical Linux native backend works on current ARM64 systems. The inspected route is Autotools plus C: a Git checkout needs maintainer tools, configure checks a C compiler, yacc, ranlib, awk and Perl, and src/Makefile.am links ncurses and readline. The checked-in Ubuntu workflow installs autoconf/libgdbm-dev, runs autoreconf -if, then configure and make; the workflow is a recipe, not a successful run verified here. ARMulator is the default backend, with sleeve/native selectable. The generated rom/romimage.o belongs to the compatibility runtime and is not evidence that an original RISC OS boot ROM is required. The original project explicitly says no RISC OS ROM is needed. Guest compiler tools are separate inputs, and the original test page explicitly withholds redistribution of Norcroft cc. No build, guest execution or binary-equivalence experiment was performed. All four build flags remain null; inspected recipes and upstream reports are not local test results. The original author documented Linux operation, including a historical Linux-on-ARM native route, while current Ubuntu CI supplies a Linux build recipe. An OS-only Linux CLI profile captures this without an OS-version, host-RAM or CPU minimum. riscose binary [args] passes command-line arguments; documented grep examples consume host stdin or filenames. The man page’s default 640 KiB wimpslot is a guest allocation, not host minimum RAM. The native backend depends on historical Linux/ARM signal and execution assumptions, so no modern ARM64 or specific-kernel runtime profile is asserted. README reports only partial grep behavior; historical SharedCLib/UnixLib filesystem gaps and the man page’s broad bug warning remain relevant limitations whose current extent needs testing. Windows and macOS are unverified. No explicit development-AI-use attribution was found in the selected documentation, substantive source/build/license material, or the latest 30 default-branch commit messages inspected at ec85f120327ce37ecee8bbcb90f3111330bd5bae. ai.usage remains null and ai.tools empty; absence of attribution is not proof of non-use. No inference is drawn from project age, author/provider addresses, configuration filenames or ARM emulation behavior. SourceForge/repo.or.cz history is not included in this bounded GitHub-history check. The SourceForge site, repo.or.cz location and hamishcoleman GitHub copy are recorded as a single riscose lineage, not three discoveries. The current tree incorporates ARMulator, sleeve, OSLib-derived SWI definitions and native compatibility handlers; none is independently promoted in this fragment. The original author states a GNU GPL distribution license, ARMulator armemu.c specifically carries GPLv2-or-later, and mod/LICENSE contains Apache-2.0 text for that directory’s separate material. The tree has no repository-root license file in the inspected listing, so dependency/module licensing must not be flattened into a claim that every bundled file has identical terms. The author’s 2001 diary reports Norcroft cc plus Acorn’s linker building and running Hello World, which is historical upstream evidence only. The separate test-input listing includes grep, unzip and zipinfo, explicitly excludes distribution of Norcroft cc, and does not establish complete correctness. project.status: Substantive source reviewed; experimental compatibility; build and runtime independently untested
project.notes: ParaTos is an experimental direct runner for original Atari TOS/MiNT command-line applications. README identifies Linux and explains the system-call translation approach. gemdos/loader.c reads and endian-converts the PRG header, builds the basepage/environment, copies text/data, applies relocation fixups and appends ARGV data. paratos.c loads the named executable and enters the CPU engine directly, without an ST machine boot. A 2023 upstream commit explicitly added OSX support, and current Apple-specific executable-path and byte-order code remains present; this refines the earlier discovery’s Linux-only evidence without asserting that a modern macOS build was tested. Canonical repository and lineage aliases were screened against the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and prior dedup index; no existing counted project matched. Source snapshot 9d43e70bce3ed4f82ee43e35375994332fc2ac4b, non-truncated tree with 106 entries. Tooling with CPU-emulator and GEMDOS/API-reimplementation capabilities. ParaTos invokes Musashi to execute original 68k instructions and dispatches guest trap calls to native host implementations; gemdos/path.c converts TOS/MiNT filenames to POSIX paths, with case-insensitive and 8.3-name lookup. It accepts U: and rejects other drive-letter mappings in this snapshot. This is not a compiler translating the guest to host source and not an ST hardware emulator. README restricts the intended programs to clean command-line tools avoiding direct hardware and OS trap-vector patching. The implementation is incomplete, and minimal BIOS/AES/VDI paths do not establish a desktop compatibility environment. The historical binaries are 68k TOS/MiNT programs. README calls the bundled engine m68000, while current paratos.c explicitly chooses M68K_CPU_TYPE_68020 for execution and disassembly. source_cpu records the documented 68000 family entry point and the concrete 68020 guest engine rather than silently retaining the discovery’s m68000-only description. paratos.c states that the FPU is not emulated. The test cross-toolchain prefix m68k-atari-mintelf- produces guest .tos binaries; it is not evidence for the CPU of the Linux/macOS host. memory.c contains an explicit __x86_64__ host branch that reserves the 68020’s four-gigabyte address space; this supports recording x86-64 as an implemented host target, not a tested runtime minimum. The alternative branch reserves 512 MiB and is not an identified support matrix for every 32-bit or ARM host; no additional CPU is inferred from that fallback, C11, Clang or macOS. memory.i explicitly assumes host unaligned loads/stores. Source-level Apple portability exists, but Apple Silicon support is not verified and is not implied by target_platforms including macOS. CMakeLists.txt declares CMake 3.10, C11, bundled mushashi and gemdos subdirectories and a paratos executable. Clang warning adjustments and the later explicit opcode-table definitions document maintenance of that route; they do not prove current build success. The original OSX-support commit adds Apple byte order and executable-path logic, with guarded host API differences, retained at the inspected tip. The guest test directory requires make plus a m68k-atari-mintelf- cross-toolchain and produces hello.tos, echo_args.tos, exit_code.tos and syscall proxies. Those generated guest outputs are ignored build artifacts, not prebuilt executables present in the tree. No boot-ROM dependency appears in the direct loader/build recipe. The host virtual-memory and unaligned-access assumptions require validation on any selected platform. All four build flags remain null; inspected recipes and upstream reports are not local test results. README documents direct Linux CLI execution as ./paratos hello.tos, so an OS-only Linux host profile is retained without numerical CPU/RAM/OS-version minima. macOS is a source-supported porting target evidenced by the explicit OSX commit and surviving __APPLE__ paths, but no macOS runtime profile or independently tested compatibility claim is added. Windows is unverified. Current memory.c reserves guest virtual address space and commits an initial region; these are implementation details, not host hardware requirements. The syscall-proxy suite shows intended testing scope, not successful commercial compiler execution. Trap #1 coverage remains incomplete, FPU operations are unsupported, and direct hardware/trap-vector dependencies remain outside the stated intended scope. The latest 30 default-branch commit messages include three explicit named Copilot co-author trailers, on 96db56afe7190d8c314a0265f23a9f7c202439f3, 8006a12cd116c395d71f9023bcde75895f4e68a7 and 612d761cc2df93fcd927dadef7f640f20a114565. ai.usage is true and the canonical tool label is GitHub Copilot. The full named trailer is preserved in evidence; this conclusion does not rely on a bot email, a branch name, AGENTS.md or the _codeql_detected_source_root filename. Other contributors or commits are not assumed AI-assisted, and this is not an exhaustive history review. README explicitly credits Vincent Riviere’s 68kemu as inspiration; that relation is not a same-project alias or proof of shared source. The bundled mushashi directory supplies Musashi CPU code under its MIT-like grant. ParaTos COPYING contains GPLv3; README also identifies GPL-licensed TOS syscall documentation taken from the Atari Compendium/TOSHYP site. Original guest programs retain their own licenses; the runner’s license does not authorize redistribution of commercial tools. The repository provides source for small cross-compiled syscall tests, but no primary source checked here establishes that an original commercial compiler runs. The OSX-support and macOS alignment commits show deliberate host-port work, while current usability and broader binary compatibility remain untested. project.display_title: ntvdm — 8086 DOS command-line executable runner
project.status: Substantive source reviewed; independent build, runtime and equivalence untested
project.notes: David Lee’s NT Virtual DOS Machine is an independent portable 8086/text-mode DOS runner, distinct from Microsoft’s system NTVDM component. ntvdm.cxx loads .COM and MZ/ZM .EXE files, applies relocations and runs i8086.cxx. README documents direct console/script use of MASM, Link, Microsoft C, Turbo Pascal/C, QuickBasic and other legacy tools. Original test software is included but does not become reconstructed source or separate runner records. Canonical root was absent from the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and the prior deduplication index. Inspected default-branch head: 0649657d912f23e60b32971d1c45653d48b440e3. Tooling combines an 8086 interpreter with partial DOS 3.00-style APIs, BIOS/text-console and selected interrupt behavior. The loader creates PSP/environment and synthetic interrupt stubs; DOS file calls use native host fopen/fread/fwrite and -r maps a host directory to C:. Original executables run without a booted DOS OS or vendor ROM in the normal path. Optional boot-sector loading does not establish a complete PC hardware emulator. The guest CPU is explicitly Intel 8086 and source_platforms=DOS; a compiler producing other target code does not change the executed guest ISA. README excludes graphics, sound and mouse and cautions that CPU/cycle fidelity is incomplete. It documents application-specific limitations such as QuickC incremental linker access to missing memory control blocks and a COBOL linker requiring 286. The 8086 capability must not be expanded to general 286/protected-mode compatibility. README explicitly lists Windows x64/ARM64, Linux x64/x32/ARM32/ARM64/RISC-V, and macOS ARM64 M1/M3. It also reports big-endian builds for 68000 via m68 and SPARC v8 via sparcos, which are emulated-runtime outputs rather than independent tests on physical legacy machines. Canonical x86, x86-64, ARM, ARM64, RISC-V and m68000 labels are retained. The pinned m68/ntvdm/mntvdm.sh recipe explicitly selects 68000 and builds ntvdm.elf using the newlib/BSP route; it assumes guest source files have been made available locally, and was not run. The SPARC-v8/Linux route through sparcos remains an explicit maintainer runtime claim in notes: no concrete ntvdm SPARC build/output recipe was identified, so SPARC is omitted from target_cpu. No cross-product guarantee across all hosts and CPUs is claimed. MSVC/g++ scripts build the C++ interpreter/runtime; Linux release links statically with OpenMP and macOS uses pthread/signed-char settings. mr.sh deliberately uses -O2 and documents a maintainer-observed g++11.4 -O3/-Ofast code-generation problem. The pinned-head Windows-2022 MSVC CI run succeeded and archived ntvdm.exe, but its workflow runs no guest regression suite. README and commit test reports remain upstream claims; no compiler, test harness or DOS guest was executed here. All four build flags remain null: compilation, execution, gameplay and byte-equivalence are independently unverified. README’s Windows11, Debian10/12, openSUSE15.4, Ubuntu20.04 and MacBook models are maintainer test configurations, not declared minimum requirements. Linux console use assumes VT-100 behavior, CR/LF inputs and suitable filename/Alt-key handling; these are operational caveats rather than numeric hardware floors. runtime_profiles remains empty. Guest segment memory and simulated 8086 clock rates are not promoted to minimum host RAM or clock requirements. project.title: ntvcm — CP/M 8080/Z80 command-line runner
project.display_title: ntvcm — CP/M 8080/Z80 command-line runner
project.status: Substantive source reviewed; independent build, runtime and equivalence untested
project.notes: NT Virtual CP/M Machine is a standalone C++ command-line runner for CP/M .COM tools. ntvcm.cxx loads a selected host file at guest 0x100, creates CP/M entry hooks and enters x80.cxx. README documents asm/load, Turbo Pascal, Aztec C, WordStar and many other tools; they are compatibility examples, not separately reconstructed projects. The current head has removed the former GDB/MI debugger-host mode, so it is not advertised as a current capability. Canonical root was absent from the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and the prior deduplication index. Inspected default-branch head: be598f65c1b649f5250dcd6d8fef266b1b86413e. An emulator with native CP/M BDOS/file and console translation, an 8080/Z80 trace disassembler and optional per-PC CSV profiling. It executes original instructions and synthesizes BDOS/BIOS hooks rather than booting a CP/M disk or requiring an original ROM. Host fopen/fread/fwrite implement FCB file operations. Original guest tools must be supplied with their own overlays/data; this record is the runner, not a full disk/hardware emulator or compiler reconstruction. x80.cxx and README explicitly implement Z80 with optional -8 8080 mode, making both guest source ISAs. CP/M 2.2 is the main guest API, supplemented by selected CP/M 3 and nonstandard services. README excludes BIOS disk-layout access, undocumented 8080 instructions and precise cycle accuracy. Recent commits distinguish optional Z80 R/MEMPTR accuracy and unattached I/O gaps; upstream validation reports do not establish universal instruction/hardware compatibility. msvcenv.bat explicitly selects Windows x86, x64 and ARM64 native toolchains. README documents a RISC-V Linux output runnable under RVOS and a real-mode DOS Watcom output; mwatcom.bat uses -0 with the DOS target, grounding 8086. Canonical target labels refer to these host executables, while source 8080/Z80 remains separate. RVOS’s AMD64/ARM32/etc host list does not automatically prove native ntvcm ports on every such system. Linux/macOS recipes do not establish an exhaustive ISA matrix. Native MSVC/g++ recipes and the Watcom real-mode DOS route are present. Unix release scripts default to RSS disabled; enabling RSS introduces cpp-httplib/OpenSSL dependencies, and README reports unresolved macOS RSS-enabled builds. Windows mr.bat enables RSS. A pinned-head Windows-2022 MSVC CI run succeeded and archived ntvcm.exe; the workflow contains no guest-test step. These observed upstream build results remain separate from maintainer CPU-test claims and this unrun review. All four build flags remain null: compilation, execution, gameplay and byte-equivalence are independently unverified. The real-mode DOS output and explicit host toolchain choices are preserved in target fields, but no numeric RAM or supported minimum DOS/Windows/macOS/Linux version is established. Guest 64 KiB layout, 80x24 console mode and emulated MHz are not host memory/CPU minima. runtime_profiles stays empty. CR/LF inputs, uppercase/lowercase handling, terminal escape conversion and optional RSS dependencies materially affect actual workflows and need chosen-host testing. types: original DOS binary emulator with host DOS and BIOS API translation
project.status: Substantive source reviewed; build and runtime independently untested
project.notes: Takeda Toshiya’s MS-DOS Player family, represented by cracyc’s maintained vt branch, runs original DOS command-line utilities directly against Windows files and console services. The official site and maintained fork are one counted project family. readme.txt explicitly targets 16-bit DOS command-line utilities and demonstrates msdos lcc sample.c followed by msdos sample.exe. msdos.cpp identifies Takeda as author, loads MZ/ZM EXEs with relocation and otherwise uses the COM entry at 0x100. The selected maintained source root is cracyc/msdos-player, default branch vt. Its README credits imported fixes from the cracyc fork; the official Takeda distribution is lineage/context, not a second project. Root and record ID are absent from the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and the prior dedup index. Inspected vt tip: b3ebaa8452be478afec604361db32e9451eb43e2. Emulator/development tooling with CPU execution plus DOS/BIOS service translation. The INT 21h dispatch sends 3Dh/3Fh/40h/4Bh to host-backed open/read/write/execute handling. The direct console workflow does not boot a DOS disk image, but this is not a CPU-only layer: text-mode hardware scaffolding, memory services and optional driver/VDD support exist. README excludes Win16, graphics/sound hardware and gaming as the project’s goal; protected-mode capabilities vary by CPU build. Original COM/MZ DOS binaries are x86 guests. README lists separate 8086, 80286, 80386, 80486, Pentium4, NEC V30 and IA32 emulation variants, including protected-mode capabilities and an optional V30 8080 mode. Canonical source_cpu=x86 describes the principal DOS guest ISA without mistaking the emulated model labels for host CPU requirements or claiming full PC compatibility. README explicitly distinguishes _x86 binaries for 32/64-bit Windows and _x64 binaries for 64-bit Windows; msdos.vcxproj independently contains Win32 and x64 output configurations. These support host target_cpu x86 and x86-64. The i86/i286/i386 suffixes and HAS_I286 macro select the emulated guest core, not the native output ISA. No native Linux or macOS support is established by these Windows/MinGW recipes. Source includes Visual C++ projects and build batch routes, plus MinGW Makefile.mingw. Current CI is configured on windows-latest for i86, V30, i286, i386 and i486 variants; it is configuration evidence rather than an observed successful run. The older simple Makefile selects an i586-mingw32msvc cross compiler and Windows libraries, so it does not establish a native Unix build. README’s packaged-binary count says 12 but lists 14 variants; record variant names rather than repeating that count. All four build flags remain null; no candidate compilation, guest execution, emulation, gameplay or byte comparison was performed. Two host-output profiles retain explicit _x86 versus _x64 Windows requirements from the README. No Windows version or numerical host RAM minimum is established from the reviewed pinned material. The emulated 1/16/32 MB memory configuration is guest memory, not host RAM. Direct commands use host paths; original COMMAND.COM is needed for batch execution. VDD support is limited to selected 32-bit process builds with companion ntvdm.exe and is not available in x64 process builds. project.display_title: m68 — CP/M-68K and 68000 executable runner
project.status: Substantive source reviewed; independent build, runtime and equivalence untested
project.notes: m68 directly loads 68000 CP/M-68K .68K, Linux-style ELF and Motorola hex programs. The repository contains a substantial custom C++ 68000 interpreter, executable loaders and host OS-service implementations. README and cpm/m.sh show original Digital Research compiler/assembler/linker stages being invoked through m68; MT Pascal, CB68 BASIC, DDT, SVS tools and Forth examples are documented uses of this one runner. Canonical root was absent from the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and the prior deduplication index. Inspected default-branch head: 45b0c7378c7adc4433141d33cf5dd119b9cca612. A tooling emulator and partial OS-API reimplementation, not recovered source for the guest compilers. load_cpm68k reads the 0x601a executable header, creates a basepage and relocates text/data/BSS; trap 2 implements BDOS and trap 3 BIOS, with host fopen/fread-backed files. Trap 0 handles supported Linux-style services and trap 15 Fondse-style calls. The direct-run path constructs runtime state without booting CP/M or loading a ROM. 68000 is explicit in README, m68000.cxx and the loaders. CP/M-68K is retained under canonical CP/M; Linux here means the supported m68k ELF/syscall convention, not every Linux executable. README requires its newlib startup/BSP stubs for sample applications, and source explicitly limits BDOS to calls used by tested compiler families. Addresses are not constrained to physical 68000 24-bit behavior. Nested 6502/Z80/x86 interpreters running as guests do not expand m68 itself into those guest ISAs. README explicitly reports host tests on AMD64 Windows/Ubuntu, ARM64 Raspberry Pi OS/Ubuntu/macOS, ARM32 Raspberry Pi 4 and RISC-V64 Debian. Canonical target labels preserve x86-64, ARM64, ARM and RISC-V. c_tests/mm68.sh also targets -mcpu=68000 with m68k-elf-gcc to run m68 recursively in an existing m68 instance; target_cpu=m68000 refers to that distinct emulated-runtime output, not an asserted physical CP/M host port or arbitrary Linux/m68k compatibility. MSVC and g++ release scripts compile the emulator; the Linux recipe links statically and the macOS recipe sets signed-char behavior. The nested 68000 build uses m68k-elf-gcc, explicit 68000 options and newlib BSP support. Guest cross-compiler construction is separate: README reports GCC 8.2 build difficulties on macOS/Pi 5 and a GCC13 guest-test issue. These are maintainer claims, not independent failures here. No .github/workflows entry exists in the complete tree; no CI result is asserted. All four build flags remain null: compilation, execution, gameplay and byte-equivalence are independently unverified. The documented host test matrix and build toolchains do not specify a minimum supported CPU generation, RAM or OS version for a runnable m68 output. The default 40 MiB heap/mmap spaces and command-line size options describe guest address-space allocation, not minimum host RAM. The special Forth83 0x500 load address is a guest compatibility caveat. runtime_profiles remains empty rather than generalizing test machines or nested emulation into hardware minima. The selected primary documentation, implementation/build/licence sources and latest 30 default-branch commit metadata contain no explicit affirmative development-AI attribution. ai.usage remains null with no tool names; absence is not proof of non-use. This is a bounded latest-30 review, not full-history proof. Agent/config filenames, provider/bot email domains, implementation language, project age and gameplay AI are not authorship evidence. Root LICENSE dedicates the emulator work under CC0-1.0. Checked-in Digital Research, Manx/Aztec, SVS, Forth and other legacy tools/support files retain their own rights; CC0 does not relicense third-party binaries or libraries. The README explicitly says the DOS-hosted Aztec C68K distribution requires a DOS emulator such as davidly/ntvdm: that compiler is not itself a native m68 guest. ntvcm/ntvdm nested builds and RVOS/ARMOS are related independent runners, not aliases of m68. Wider author, dependency and fork-graph coverage remains partial. events.title: Use the two-half touch joystick in every layout; drop the two-finger turn
events.message:
Use the two-half touch joystick in every layout; drop the two-finger turn

Portrait touch fell through to the mouse gestures (tap to walk,
double-tap to leap, self-tap for the menu) because side touch was only
switched on by the fullscreen and landscape classes.  That was
accretion, not design: portrait was not a target when the joystick
went in.  Touch now always uses side touch; the mouse keeps its
gestures.  A tap on the status panel no longer opens the menu on
touch in portrait, matching landscape: the two-finger hold does.

Two fingers tapped together now trigger, like any other tap, instead
of turning the figure around.  Saul: "unnecessary and provisional
anyway".

What's left to teach a touch player is three things: hold or swipe to
move, tap a second finger to jump, hold two fingers for the menu.

Tests: the portrait browser check now walks with a held half and opens
the inventory with a two-finger hold (after the opening fall and
knockdown in B8, since airborne touches steer at once).  The browser
tests that drove the pointer gestures by touch now drive them by
mouse; the touch EAT block and the touch tap on the menu button are
gone, as touch can no longer reach those paths.

The spec, README and port Status describe one touch scheme.  The
spec's lone-tap row now says the game ignores the trigger with the
stick centred.

events.title: Click the power button on press, not release
events.message:
Click the power button on press, not release

The power button toggled on click, which waits for the mouse or finger
to come up, so the click sound trailed the press.  It now toggles on
pointerdown.  Keyboard and programmatic clicks (detail 0) still toggle
through onclick.  A pointer's own click only re-unlocks audio, since a
touch pointerdown is not a user activation and the context may only
start then.  mousedown's default is prevented so the button does not
take focus back from the screen.

The click files lose their 5 ms of leading silence as well.

project.notes: Scala/JVM graphical editor and serializer for real AmigaOS keymap Hunk files. README describes learning Amiga keymap layout/OS concepts to create a Colemak keymap; the resulting resource is copied to DEVS:keymaps. events.title: fix(cd): serialize the HLE CD streaming state (#803)
events.message:
fix(cd): serialize the HLE CD streaming state (#803)

* fix(cd): serialize the HLE CD streaming state (#787)

The HLE BIOS streams CD_read data into RAM at drive rate from statics in
jagcd_hle.c (hleStream, the CD_read/CD_poll bookkeeping, the #766 align
phase) that were never in the state blob. Measured with
test_runahead_determinism: Hover Strike (HLE) failed all four checks at
warmup 200/400/700/1000; Myst (HLE) failed while its reads were in
flight (200/400) and passed after. Cart (yarc) and Hover Strike with the
real BIOS at 1000 pass, so the leak was the HLE path.

Append an HLE chunk strictly last, behind a magic word ("HLE1"),
extending v15 in place (v15 is still develop-only). Field by field, never
the raw struct (padding, sizeof(bool)). hle_active is boot-strategy
configuration and is not saved. A damaged bufOff/written drops the
transfer rather than reading past the sector buffer.

Backward compatibility, measured by saving at frame 400 (mid-stream) and
loading into this build:
- v14 states from v3.6.1 load and run byte-identically (per-frame hash
  CSV) to v3.6.1 loading its own state, for Hover Strike and Myst.
- v15 states written by develop before this change (zero-filled tail)
  load with the in-flight transfer dropped, as before.
- New states resume the transfer (Hover Strike: 200 distinct frames
  after load vs a frozen black screen without the chunk).
A pre-#787 state saved mid-read still cannot resume that read on any
build -- that data was never saved.

After: all eight runs above pass all four checks. make test gains a
ROM-gated Hover Strike HLE run-ahead check at warmup 400 (passes here,
exits 1 on the pre-#787 build).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cd): validate a restored HLE stream; synthetic mid-stream round trip

Review on #803:
- Copilot: a damaged or crafted state could set dest near $FFFFFFFF,
  wrapping HLEStreamFinish's dest+total bound check into an out-of-bounds
  write, or point the GPU data base where CD_poll's +0/+8 reads land
  outside RAM. Load now requires dest/total/reqTotal/written and the
  CD_poll range to fit main RAM, and both data bases to be 0, main RAM or
  GPU local RAM; otherwise it drops the transfer and those pointers.
- Copilot: CI has no private discs, so nothing exercised an active
  stream through save/load. test_cd_synth_read gains
  inflight_stream_survives_savestate_round_trip on its synthetic disc:
  save mid-stream, finish, restore, and the same transfer must be in
  flight and complete byte-exact. Red with the chunk load disabled.
- Kimi: check room for the ~2.4 KB chunk before writing it, not after;
  JaguarCDHLEStateSize() is pinned to what Save writes by the same test.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

The grip slid between the carry's and the dig's by dig / (dig + carry), while
the bones layer the dig over the carry: at a full dig with the carry still
fading the arm was already in the dig pose but the shaft kept sliding through
the fist, pulling the other hand off its grip. The carry's share now counts
only what the dig leaves of it (and only as far as the clips own the arm). A
Vitest case checks the dig grip exactly while the carry still fades.

events.title: Ease each arm's clip ownership so a hand taken or given back blends
events.message:
Ease each arm's clip ownership so a hand taken or given back blends

When the code took the right arm (a gesture, a contact, a steadying hand) the
gait swing and the shovel carry dropped off it in one frame, snapping the arm
from the clip pose to the code pose (about 3 rad on a carrying walker). Each
arm now has a clip weight eased toward its free state over the transition
time, and the gait and carry layers blend by it. A Vitest case hands the
right arm (and briefly the left) to the code mid-walk and back.

events.title: Fade a lifted foot's hold correction over the gait cycle instead of dropping it
events.message:
Fade a lifted foot's hold correction over the gait cycle instead of dropping it

The held contacts' mean miss divided its own fading weight back out, so a lone
contact restored the full correction until it crossed the touch height, and
the foot jumped the whole miss after a turn or shove. The mean is now held
only as firmly as the firmest contact, and once no contact holds firm the
correction eases toward what is left over plantFadeCycle (calibratable, 0.15
of the cycle) of the phase walked, since the contacts lift within a frame or
two. A Vitest case shoves a walker sideways and bounds every later per-frame
foot step across the release.

events.title: Folders of the first Finders; startup application in any HFS folder
events.message:
Folders of the first Finders; startup application in any HFS folder

MFS: the Finders of 1984 (1.0, 1.1g) record a folder in 58 bytes plus four
per item, with its name only as the resource's name. Such folders were not
shown - the files of Apple's MDS 1.0 disks all appeared at the top level.
They are read now, files can be added to them, and their records are left
as the Finder wrote them. Tried on a Macintosh 128K with System 1.1: it
shows a file added to such a folder, and a folder made by mkdir.

HFS: startup takes a path and records the application's folder in the
volume header (drFndrInfo, second long). Without it System 3.2 and System
6.0.8 do not find an application at the top level and start the Finder;
with it they open the application from the top level, from a folder and
from the System Folder (Mac Plus, eight disks made by the tool). A plain
name is looked for at the top level, then in the System Folder, as before.
info and startup say where the application is opened from.

events.title: 実装: TAB(・SPC(・POS・XOR・EQV・IMP・CSNG（l4-program 4.20、l4-s9l）
events.message:
実装: TAB(・SPC(・POS・XOR・EQV・IMP・CSNG（l4-program 4.20、l4-s9l）

根拠は仕様 4.20 節（63fcd50）だけ。測定コミットは 44d055a（公式101腕×2走、期待値 expected_l4_tabspc.tsv）。
- 本体はバンク0（tabspc.asm、deffn.asm の後ろへ連結）。mainに足したのは入口の中継だけ。
- XOR・EQV・IMP: 両辺を16ビット整数へ丸め（範囲外ERR 6）、優先順位は OR>XOR>EQV>IMP。mainのLOGIC_OR_EXPRはOR段（LOGIC_OR_LEVEL）の後で次が英字のときだけバンクへ入る。
- TAB(・SPC(: PRINTの項目（FN_IS_STRINGの入口経由）。TABは n mod 80 の桁へ、同じ桁なら何もせず前なら改行してから。負は桁0・32768はERR 6・SPCは n mod 80 個・区切り無しで終わる文は改行しない。式の中の TAB(・SPC( はERR 2。
- POS（桁・0始まり）・CSNG（倍精度は既存のMBF_DTOS）・CSRLIN（行・0始まり。4.20に記述は無いが測定器具が行の増分の観測に使うため実装）。
- 数値比較（4.20.3: csng(1/3#)>1/3# は真）: どちらかが倍精度なら倍精度で比較（以前は単精度へ丸めてから比較）。整数どうしはバンク内で完結。
- listnum.asm: 数字の後の「 E」を指数と見るのは ELSE の EL を除いていたので、EQV の EQ も除く（5 eqv 3 が LIST で 5!QV 3 に化けていた）。
自作判断（未測定）: POSの引数は評価するだけ、HEX$(TAB( のように直前が '(' のときはPRINTの項目として扱わない。
自作ROMで l4-s9l の101腕×2走が関門通過、tabspc の check --predicted-only は照合一致（予測あり96腕＝食い違い20腕は公式の観測、予測なし5腕も観測と一致）。
退行: 自己検査39本が全て rc=0（ext_bank・memmap・l4_memdyn・vsync_regcheck・atnexplog・deffn・onwhile・pusing・wrap・rnd・strfunc ほか、m6ib/ic/ie/ig/ih のROM関門を含む）。自作照合は deffn・wrap が照合一致、onwhile は期待値の全84腕×2走が一致。
残り容量 main 116B・bank0 2119B・bank1 1995B・bank2 3400B・bank3 27B。

events.message:
Pose the glTF villager from its clips on the hung skeleton, with the planted foot held

A pure module carries a clip pose onto the skeleton the settlement figure
binds (each limb's hang taken out, the hips scaled onto the drawn body),
advances the walk/sprint cycle by the ground walked, warps the stride to the
blended cycle by leg IK and holds every sole contact where it touched down,
giving way by a slip rather than a jump. The sprint threshold moves to where
the walk's stride saturates.

events.title: Cut the first load from 2 MB to 0.56 MB and flatten its request chain
events.message:
Cut the first load from 2 MB to 0.56 MB and flatten its request chain

Measured on an emulated Pixel 7 at slow 4G (150 ms, 1.6 Mbps, 4x CPU)
over HTTP/2 + brotli: the title frame drops from 6.2 s to 2.9 s cold and
from 1.75 s to 0.91 s on a repeat visit.

- Desk tray images are 2x webp thumbnails (tools/thumbs.py, make thumbs)
  instead of the full scans: about 95 kB instead of 990 kB.
- The open box image is lazy, and a book fetches pages only while on
  screen; neighbouring spreads preload once the reader hovers, focuses,
  or turns.  The box still shows during loading, so its cover loads then.
- Dev notes are a separate dev-notes.html fetched on first open; the game
  pages shrink from 192 kB to 22 kB.
- Game pages carry modulepreload hints for main.js's whole import graph
  and fetch preloads for every data, charset and sprite file, and
  charsets/sprites no longer wait for rooms.json.
- _headers caches images, fonts and sounds for a day with a 30-day
  stale-while-revalidate; HTML, JS and data still revalidate because
  their names are not fingerprinted.  netlify dev overrides
  Cache-Control locally, so this only shows on a deploy.

The book browser test now opens the box before turning it, since a
hidden book no longer loads pages.

events.title: Stop the status panel flashing on touch; keep its taps off the menu button
events.message:
Stop the status panel flashing on touch; keep its taps off the menu button

Saul wants to play one-handed with two fingers on the status panel, and
the panel blinked on every touch.  The panel is covered by the
transparent #command-menu button, and Chrome flashes its default tap
highlight (18% black) over a tapped button.  #play now sets a
transparent tap highlight.

Touches on the panel already reached the side controls.  The button's
click skipped side-touch taps only when the click carried pointerType,
which Safari's does not, so there a panel tap could also open the menu.
The click now falls back to the pointerType of the press on the button;
keyboard activation (detail 0) still opens the menu.  Whether Saul's
phone hit this is unknown.

The landscape browser test now walks, leaps and opens and closes the
menu with two fingers on the panel alone.

events.title: helios: xmanx on the ATW800/2's T425, under Helios X (HTTP only)
events.message:
helios: xmanx on the ATW800/2's T425, under Helios X (HTTP only)

xmanx now builds with Helios 1.31's C compiler and runs on the
transputer itself. tools/helios/bundle.sh lays the sources out in 8.3
names with a build.csh to source on Helios; the link takes libx11.a
first, then the X shared library's stub (-lX), as Helios's own X
clients do.

There is no TLS in this build: Helios C has no 64-bit integers, which
BearSSL needs, so os/helios/tls.h and tls_none.c stand in for tls/ and
https fails with a message. os/helios also has poll() over select()
and the clock.

Shared code, all still C89: no trailing comma in enum display, no
second declaration of a struct already defined, char * casts where
Helios's socket calls want them, no initialised auto array. Under
MANX_HELIOS: snprintf declared (os/sysv4's), the data directory is
~/manx (GEMDOS has no names starting '.'), temporary files replace the
extension rather than add one (8.3 would make "a.html.tmp" "a.htm"
itself), and a file is removed before another is renamed over it
(GEMDOS won't replace one).

Tested in Hatari with the T425 emulated: fetches over slirp, follows
links, revalidates its cache, Helvetica and CSS colours (once the X
font lists are fixed).

events.title: Rebuild landscape touch as a two-half joystick and trigger
events.message:
Rebuild landscape touch as a two-half joystick and trigger

Saul asked for a simpler model: the screen splits into left and right
halves, a hold or swipe on either is the joystick at that moment, a
tap is the trigger, and a hold plus a tap leaps.  The touch layer now
ignores game state except for a lone tap in the air, menus, and a tap
while pointing down; the C64 code already decides what a held
direction means (centring stops a walk and leaves a glide alone).

Gestures, as written into docs/spec/input.md:
- One finger held without a swipe points the stick at its half after
  120 ms, at once in the air.
- A swipe points it the swipe's way on either half; the vertical part
  outranks the sideways one, and back near the start centres it.
- A lone quick tap triggers on the ground and nudges in the air (Saul:
  every fall, not only the glide).
- A second-finger tap triggers on lift, and does nothing while the
  stick points down (the C64 maps fire+down to the menu).
- Two fingers held 200 ms without swiping open the command menu, or
  close it; this replaces the both-sides chord.
- Two quick taps landing together turn the figure around.  Saul wants
  to see whether he notices this one at all.  In menus they confirm.

Dropped: the top up zones, the dead middle and the picture-middle tap
rule, the glide's newest-finger steering, the airborne button role,
the two-holds brake from 02b48ed, and 46060f8's climb-on from a plain
hold mid-ladder (Saul chose to try the C64 rule; swipe to climb).

The second-finger leap now starts at its lift, about 100 ms later than
at its landing, because a held second finger means the menu.

events.title: ACKPACE: an opt-in acknowledgment pacer for a card without flow control
events.message:
ACKPACE: an opt-in acknowledgment pacer for a card without flow control

A sender whose window is the limit sends what each acknowledgment opens,
back to back.  On an A3000 (68060/50, X-Surf 100, no 802.3x) the ACKs left
evenly, 543 us apart with GROFRAMES=2, but each opened two segments: a
sender clocked at ~43 Mbit/s against the ~22 the machine sustains, so the
eight-frame ring overran on a long path.

ACKPACE=<kbit/s> holds a pure IPv4 acknowledgment (no data; SYN, FIN, RST
never) in a 16-slot queue until the bytes the previous one opened -- its
move of the sender's right edge, ack + window scaled by the shift our own
SYN/SYN-ACK offered -- have had their time at the rate.  The SANA-II
reader releases them at the top of each pass and from a timer.device
MICROHZ request when nothing else would wake it.  Only an acknowledgment
advertising more window than the card holds (hw_rx_bytes) is paced, so it
is inert under PAUSE and for a LAN connection at its ring fit; while it
paces, GROFRAMES cuts only the paced connection's runs.  Full queue or no
reader: the acknowledgment goes at once (ShowNetStatus counts both).

Measured on that A3000 only, one build, TCPWANWINDOW=46720 GROFRAMES=4
TCPACKMAX=5840 ACKPACE=24000, Mbit/s:

                       no flow control      flow control
                       before   ACKPACE     before   ACKPACE
  iperf LAN            18.9     18.2        22.6     21.6-22.1
  iperf 25 ms path      3.3     11.1-11.6   10.5     10.5
  HTTP 100 MB           6.0     10.7        14.9     14.0-14.2
  FITZ read 8 MB       14.2     13.6        16.4     16.2

Experimental and per interface: the rate, GRO size and window come from
one 060/50 and are not a default anywhere.  Host: test_sana2_ackpace (61
checks against an owned E-clock), the GRO paced-connection test in
test_sana2_rx, config parse tests; 555 host tests.  own-tools.tsv
regenerated: the reader's timer request.

events.title: test: gate key injection on the program-entry stop, not a media frame
events.message:
test: gate key injection on the program-entry stop, not a media frame

The readiness signal was the guest's blue start frame, but the media
stream is change-gated and drops a frame that cannot go out whole, so
that one early change can be missed and the gate times out even though
the program ran — it failed on macOS, and flakily on Linux. Use the
session's own signal instead, exactly as debuggerStopsAtProgramEntry and
mediaDisplayFeedsThePanel do: arm the program-entry breakpoint, wait for
that stop, resume, then inject. An entry stop cannot be missed, and
injecting only after it keeps the early presses that make EmuTOS abandon
the autostart (PLAN.md §9) from happening at all.

events.title: Five options for Commando's footprint, all off by default (Cleo's disc byte-identical):
events.message:
Five options for Commando's footprint, all off by default (Cleo's disc byte-identical):
- GAMESPRLIST: the game writes the sprite list itself (no add_sprite);
- MASTERONLY: bank 7's placement pads zeroed (the unpinned Master's image ends at the kernel, so
  the pinned values place nothing: 166 bytes);
- TIGHTBSS: the dirty lists interleave the buffers, and REC_H holds the column's high bits low;
- RINGARITH (Model B): a row's ring slot from the window's (wrow + row - wcy, one fold: every
  caller's row is in the window) and the slot's address by arithmetic ($80 x (5r+1) from the base
  page), not ringmod_tab and the three slot tables (bank 6), and ring_addr7 in constant time;
- B6PACK: scroll_validate placed before draw_rect (engine/scrollv.s), in the room draw_rect's
  placement pad held; the pad is the old one less its length, mod 256, so draw_rect lies as before
  (bank 6: -186 bytes on the Master, -185 on the Model B).

Checked: Cleo built with all off: byte-identical; with RINGARITH and B6PACK on: Model B windows
identical to off on eight levels (three of them 600 frames of random keys), the Master's on three,
both machines' menus identical; Commando's twelve levels, sound and menus identical.

events.title: release: don't tilde-expand the pre-release separator
events.message:
release: don't tilde-expand the pre-release separator

`PV="${V/-/~}"` expanded the literal "~" in the replacement to $HOME,
so the v0.9.0-alpha tag produced "0.9.0/home/runneralpha": the deb/rpm
version, and the check against it, would have been garbage. Only the
tag-triggered Release runs this, so a green CI run cannot catch it.

Take the tilde from a variable instead: "0.9.0-alpha" -> "0.9.0~alpha",
numeric tags unchanged.

events.title: test: make the media readiness gate and panel compare race-proof
events.message:
test: make the media readiness gate and panel compare race-proof

Follow-ups from the fork's frame path: a frame that cannot go out whole is
dropped ("never queue two"), so comparing the panel to the newest
received frame races a repaint and cannot converge while the guest's
screen keeps changing. Compare only after the stream is quiet — no new
frame for 400 ms — so the panel has caught up.

The key-injection readiness gate now accepts any blue frame, not only the
newest: the guest paints it once and then blocks in Cconin, so a later
non-blue frame must not hide that it was up.

events.title: fix(loader): count LEA abs.L into any An when inferring a raw binary's load address (#739)
events.message:
fix(loader): count LEA abs.L into any An when inferring a raw binary's load address (#739)

InferRawBinaryLoadAddress only counted LEA abs.L,A0 ($41F9) as an absolute
reference.  PlaySFX V1.0 is a headerless BJL image linked at $4000 whose
startup uses LEA abs.L into A1-A7 (library base in A6), so it scored 2 for
$4000 against the minimum of 8 and fell through to the sub-1 MiB headerless
cart fallback.  HLE then took cart+$404 ($00004436, mid-instruction-stream)
as the entry point and the 68K slid through zeroed RAM until its PC left RAM
(pc_escape, final_pc=$200002) by frame 19.  Matching (op & 0xF1FF) == 0x41F9
scores it 14 for $4000 and 0 for the other bases; it now loads at $4000 and
plays its sounds on keypad input.  Across the 155-ROM private corpus this is
the only file whose inferred load address changes.

release: order the pre-release package version before the final

Passing the tag version to CPack fixed the deb metadata, but
"0.9.0-alpha" is not a pre-release to Debian or RPM: both read the
hyphen as a package revision, so the alpha would sort *after* a later
"0.9.0" and hide the final release from upgraders. Encode it as
"0.9.0~alpha", which both order first; asset names keep the readable
form. Mark a hyphenated tag a GitHub pre-release too — the release
action does not infer it, so otherwise the alpha becomes "Latest".

events.title: test: wait for the running guest before injecting keys
events.message:
test: wait for the running guest before injecting keys

keyInjectionReachesTheGuest injected scancodes from t=0, while the guest
was still booting. TOS flushes those presses, so the guest reached the
program's Cconin and the test passed; EmuTOS instead abandons the
autostart when a key arrives during boot, so the program never ran and
the test failed on every EmuTOS run — CI's ROM — while passing on real
TOS. It was the only tst_emulatorhost failure in CI.

The program now paints blue before its Cconin, and the test waits for
that frame before injecting: proof the guest is actually running, with
no input during boot to cancel the launch.

events.title: Leap once per side-touch button press; both sides held stand still
events.message:
Leap once per side-touch button press; both sides held stand still

Saul: holding one side and then holding the other leapt over and over.
He wants a press on the other side to leap once, further taps to leap
again, and two holds to stop all movement.

- A button finger now taps fire once when it lands (or when the chord
  window resolves) instead of holding fire until it lifts.  In the air
  the tap waits for the landing read as before.
- Once that tap has been read, the held side stops supplying its
  direction while the button finger stays down; lifting either finger
  walks the side still held.
- Behind the figure, the button tap waits until the turn has been read,
  so the turn and the leap stay separate reads.
- A held button no longer holds fire in the air.  The glide still opens
  from the steering side alone, as fireFree tries it with any sideways.

The off-picture Pointer sidebar keeps its held trigger.

events.title: New option "Keyboard as printed" (issue #6); docs for 0.4.8
events.message:
New option "Keyboard as printed" (issue #6); docs for 0.4.8

Controllers & ports -> "Keyboard as printed": digits and symbols give the
character printed on the MEGA65 key (US ST layout) instead of the ST key
at the same position. keyboard.vhd presses or hides the ST's Shift key
as needed; the symbol key follows 20 ms after a change of the Shift
state, so the IKBD never sees it with the wrong Shift. Extra characters:
Shift+: ; @ * = [ ] { }, Pound = \ |, Shift+- = _, Arrow left = ` ~.

The menu has one more line (OPTM_SIZE 95): C_MENU_* from 57 on shift by
one, /atarist/stcfg must be the new 95 byte file. GHDL keyboard test
checks the mapping and that no symbol key is ever seen with the wrong
Shift state.

events.title: Cold boot after changing the machine type or memory size (issue #7)
events.message:
Cold boot after changing the machine type or memory size (issue #7)

TOS keeps memvalid/memctrl/phystop in RAM and trusts them at the next
reset, so after a change of the machine type or the memory size in the
menu the ST crashed until a TOS was loaded again. tos_loader now watches
these menu bits: on a change it keeps the core in reset, clears the
system variables (like a TOS load from the menu) and lets the ST make a
cold boot. GHDL test: tb_tos_loader -gMEMCHG=true.

events.title: release: stamp the tag version into the deb and rpm
events.message:
release: stamp the tag version into the deb and rpm

CPACK_PACKAGE_VERSION came from PROJECT_VERSION, which CMake requires to
be numeric, so the v0.9.0-alpha tag built a deb reporting '0.9.0' while
the workflow's own metadata check — and the asset name — say
'0.9.0-alpha'. The release run failed on the mismatch after the tag was
pushed.

Pass the tag-derived version through to CPack. Debian accepts the
pre-release suffix verbatim; CPackRPM rewrites the '-' to '_', the only
form RPM's Version field allows.

events.title: MFS folders of later Finders, and DiskCopy 4.2 images
events.message:
MFS folders of later Finders, and DiskCopy 4.2 images

Later Finders record an MFS folder with 98 bytes in front of its name, the
Finder 5.3 with 94; both kinds can stand in one DeskTop file. The name was
read at 94 only: such folders came out without a name or with a garbled
one and could not be addressed. It is now the Pascal string that ends the
record, or else the resource's name.

DiskCopy 4.2 images are read and written: the sectors behind the 84-byte
header, both checksums set after a change, the tags of the changed sectors
cleared. info names the format, and a header whose checksums are wrong.

Tests: a folder record rewritten the later way; DiskCopy images with and
without tag data and with a wrong checksum. The checker verifies the
checksums and no longer objects to a folder window in a list view; the run
over foreign images leaves a full disk unchanged.

events.title: A landing stops on the platform; a hen draws at its own x
events.message:
A landing stops on the platform; a hen draws at its own x

Two alignment fixes carried over from the working repo.

A landing: AirPhysics replays PHYSICS_STEPS Spectrum main-loop iterations for
one GB frame, and on the iteration he lands CheckBelow clears PlayerInAir --
the Z80 takes the ground path from the next iteration on. Replaying the fall
regardless carried him up to 3 px into the platform he had already landed on
and left PlayerInAir clear at a y that is not y+1 % 8 == 0, a state nothing
recovers from except a jump: on screen, Harry sunk into the platform he had
just dropped onto, and a jump shook him out. The replay now re-reads
PlayerInAir (and PlayerDead) after every step and stops when he lands. Sink by
frame phase was +3 +1 0 +3 +2 +1 0 +2 on two platforms; it is 0 in all eight
phases now. tools/verify_player.py section 11b drives the drop from all eight
phases of the falling counter, which is what makes the sink deterministic --
section 7 lands him on the floor, where an overshoot has almost nothing to sink
into and the frame usually ends first, so it passed throughout.

A hen: climbing hens drew 4 px right of their ladder. The Z80's hen art is
shifted 4 px inside its cell and the game compensates in the draw; the port was
applying the shift to the wrong frames, so frames 2/3 and 4/5 are now
de-shifted at extraction, with a generator refusal and a sprite-sheet check to
keep it that way.

Upstream reports fourth place in CPCRetroDev 2015 and credits Bruno Kukulcan, Tom & Jerry/GPA, CED and testers. Original competition game with a Back to the Future theme. README requires manual WinAPE assembly and BASIC autotype, plus separate image conversion, compression and DSK preparation tools. An automated complete reconstruction of the distributable was not established; no build/run/play/byte-exact result is asserted. Reviewed on 2026-10-05; no independent build or execution was performed. events.title: Fit the dress round the glTF body's measured trunk sections, and let each dress station cover the girth up to its neighbours
events.message:
Fit the dress round the glTF body's measured trunk sections, and let each dress station cover the girth up to its neighbours

Skin showed through the glTF women's bodice (worst on the heavy Hausa
build) for two reasons. The dress envelope was the code-built profile with
the trunk's widest and deepest extents plugged into an ellipse — but a bust
or a belly off the front line, or a square flank, lies outside the ellipse
through those two extents. And a wrap's stations sit ~0.055 of stature
apart, the cloth running between their girths, so it cut the chord through
the bust and the belly between them.

The glTF body now measures its trunk every 0.01 of stature from crotch to
neck as ellipses that enclose every point of each cross-section, and the
dress follows those sections; the code-built body keeps its profile. Each
wrap station takes the largest girth as far as its neighbours, so the
cloth falls straight from the bust. A new test casts rays from the trunk
axis through every trunk vertex of every sex, age and build and asserts
each people's dress layer lies beyond the skin.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: hardware: Leave Gary timeout mode unchanged during SCSI probes
events.message:
hardware: Leave Gary timeout mode unchanged during SCSI probes

Fat Gary's timeout register reads status rather than the programmed
mode, so saving and restoring it can leave short DSACK timeouts active
for unrelated hardware accesses.

Use guarded reads for NCR and SDMAC detection and configuration. Keep
controller writes conditional on accessible, idle hardware and restore
the saved transfer count before handling a failed readback. Check WD
register access before entering the timed diagnostic section.

Update identify to use guarded NCR detection and remove the unused
Gary timeout definitions.

events.title: grm-mej.13: registers a callee provably preserves keep their value across the call
events.message:
grm-mej.13: registers a callee provably preserves keep their value across the call

StoredValueScanner.resolveStoredValue and constantValue no longer treat every
call as clobbering the register being resolved: a plain JSR to one resolved,
disassembled, non-banked target whose CalleeRegisterSummary preserves the
register is stepped over (CalleeRegisterSummary.summarizeCallSite; per-program
memo invalidated on modification number).

The register surviving does not mean the BANK survived -- the callee may switch
it. So resolveStoredValue resumes with hooks.stateAt(call) after the crossing,
exactly as a call-crossing PHA/PLA pairing does (resumeStateAfterPairing); with
no state there the walk goes blind: it may still finish on a state-free
definition (immediate, transfer, immediate AND/ORA) but stops at any read that
would consult the in-state WITHOUT asking the hook (the ironsword rule).
constantValue was already safe: it resolves loads under BankState.unknown().

banktest2 C5 (LDA #$35 / JSR sub / STA $01, sub = bare RTS) now resolves to
bank 5; criterion C5 updated (it asserted the old clobber warning) and the
generator comment with it; golden re-blessed. No real-ROM row moved (check nes:
wizwarr held + shenlong/dragonpower symbol flaps only).

CalleePreservedRegisterScanProgramTest: 13 tests, incl. the bank-state hazard
(mutation-checked: both fail without the at-call resume / blind guard).
Unplumbed, future: HelperArgumentRecovery prologueOutcome, reload walk,
inboundArgumentCell.

events.title: Steer touch glides with the newest finger and treat a leap as airborne
events.message:
Steer touch glides with the newest finger and treat a leap as airborne

Three side-touch fixes for leaping and gliding on the sky platforms.

- Gliding: the newest side finger steers, so a press on the other
  side turns at once with the first thumb still down, and lifting it
  turns back.  The fall rule from deb5eb5 (a second side is the
  button) now applies only before the glide opens; in the glide the
  button does nothing until landing, and holding back the turn until
  the first thumb lifted was the long press it took to change course.
- A leap now counts as airborne.  A finger landing mid-leap took the
  ground route: a lone press waited 120 ms to tell a tap from a hold,
  and a two-thumb press waited up to 250 ms to rule out the menu
  chord.  Either could miss the single landing read, so a re-leap
  worked only sometimes.  In the air every press is live at once.
- Lifting the steering finger hands the steer to a remaining button
  finger on the ground too, not only in the air, so the figure walks
  whichever side is still held instead of holding fire alone.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Drop taps made during a knock-down when the figure gets up
events.message:
Drop taps made during a knock-down when the figure gets up

The player step reads no input for the 2.75 s knock-down, so presses
made meanwhile queued for the first read after it.  A button tap made
during the fall's last row or while lying down then joined a held side
in that read and leaped, where the player expected a walk.

The step that ends the knock-down now flushes queued presses through a
new `flush` on the input.  Held keys and fingers stay held, so the
figure gets up doing what is held at that moment.  Playback reads its
recording and ignores the flush.
